- **My connections joins the redesign under the rail chrome.** The page trades the gradient page-shell hero for the flat account-page anatomy `/me/profile` and `/me/activity` already wear (head band + surface cards + shared controls); every behavior contract — OAuth Connect/Reconnect/Disconnect, token save/test/remove, the revoked-access and no-tools-yet card states — is unchanged, and the card guards now run against both templates. Default (topnav) instances keep the pre-redesign page byte-for-byte (frozen `me_connections_legacy.html`, same pattern as the other redesigned pages).

- **Under the rail chrome, the Library is now the one browse surface for memory domains and hosted data apps.** The Memory band carries the item/required counts the standalone cards had and hides empty optional domains; the Files band is renamed **Artefacts** and holds the caller's sub-kinds in stable blocks — folders, loose files, then their visible data apps (rows keep the "Data app" type for the Type facet; gated on `data_apps.enabled`) — fulfilling the old "Data apps coming soon" badge literally. `/corporate-memory` and `/apps` now 302 to their Library sections under rail — the interim rail nav rows for both are gone again, and a memory-domain detail's back link points straight at the band. Default (topnav) instances render exactly what they rendered before; detail pages (`/memory/d/…`, `/apps/detail/…`) stay live in both chromes.

- **Web chat streams markdown progressively.** Tokens used to append as plain text, so the reader watched raw `**bold**`, `|table|` pipes and fence markers until turn end flipped the whole bubble at once. The accumulated text now re-renders through the same sanitized markdown pipeline as the final answer, throttled to one paint per 150 ms; a trailing wire-format trailer (```sources / ```next_actions) is hidden while it streams in — by fence parity, so the trailer's own closing fence is never mistaken for a fresh opener and its body can no longer flash raw at the instant of close — and the heavy passes (syntax highlighting, mermaid, table sort, copy buttons) still run once at turn end.

- **Web chat tool blocks are headlined by a human label** — "Querying data", "Reading a file", "Running a command" — derived from the tool name and, for shell calls, the command line itself, instead of a raw tool id. Unknown tools get a humanized name (`mcp__` prefix off, underscores to spaces), the raw id stays in the tooltip and the args panel, persisted history uses the same labels, and the copied-transcript export writes `tool: <label> (<raw id>)` so a transcript pasted into a bug report keeps the real id.

### Fixed

- **A table named for a SQL keyword poisoned ordinary queries — `ORDER BY` on an internal table was rejected as a join with it.** Both `/api/query` name guards decided "does this SQL reference table N?" by scanning the SQL text for N as a word, so a registry row called `order` matched the `ORDER BY` of any query: the internal mixed-plane guard 400'd every sorted query against `agnes_sessions`/`agnes_telemetry`/`agnes_audit` ("can't be joined with registered table 'order'"), and the non-admin master-view denylist 403'd with a not-in-stack error whenever such a view was outside the caller's stack. The collision was never limited to `order` — a view named `limit`, `filter`, `date` or `list` broke `LIMIT 5`, `count(*) FILTER (…)`, `CAST(x AS date)` and `list(x)` the same way, since the scan cannot tell a table reference from a keyword, a type, a function, a column or an alias.

  Both guards now ask **DuckDB itself** which tables a statement references, via `json_serialize_sql` — the engine's own parser, which parses without binding or executing (an unknown table serializes fine, a non-SELECT is refused outright, and serializing an `INSERT` inserts nothing). The SQL is passed as a bound parameter and parsed on a dedicated in-memory connection with nothing attached, so parsing touches no data, no catalog and no locks. Using the engine that will run the query is the point of the design, not an implementation detail: a third-party SQL parser can disagree with DuckDB about what a construct means, and for a deny check every such disagreement is a bypass. sqlglot, the obvious alternative, reads DuckDB's `(TABLE v)` shorthand as a *column* named `table` and lexes `values` as a keyword, so `SELECT * FROM (TABLE values) t` reads a view while appearing to reference nothing — those constructs are now regression tests. DuckDB cannot disagree with itself, and an engine upgrade moves the guard with it.

  The word-boundary scan survives only as the fallback for SQL DuckDB will not serialize (a `PIVOT` subquery, a backtick-quoted BigQuery path, anything malformed), where it stays deliberately over-matching because nothing is known about the statement's structure; it also skips the `BY` of a two-word clause, so the reported symptom does not come back on that path. Known and unchanged: a table macro hides its body from the parser, but equally from a text scan — neither can see a name the SQL does not contain — and SQL smuggled through a string-taking table function or `EXECUTE` never reaches these guards, being blocked by `_assert_select_only` first.

- **A Library row for a stack membership you created yourself now offers Remove, matching /catalog.** Adding a granted data package or memory domain from the Library (classic membership mode) used to flip the row to a locked pill claiming "only an admin can remove it" — false for a self-subscription, and read in testing as an admin mandate — while /catalog offered a working Remove for the very same membership. The lock now follows droppability: required-tier and auto-membership rows keep it (there really is nothing the caller can drop), classic self-subscriptions render the same Remove control both views agree on, live through any number of add/remove cycles without a reload.

- **Postgres-backed instances now count required memory items — the Library's "· N required" suffix was hardcoded to zero there.** Two reads in the PG memory-domains repository (`count_items_by_domain`'s `0 AS required`, `list_items_of_domain`'s `FALSE AS is_required`) still claimed `knowledge_items.is_required` "does not exist in the PG schema" — stale since `0012_duckdb_v59_parity` added the column, which the PG writers have been persisting all along. So on a Postgres backend the Library rendered "3 items" where DuckDB rendered "3 items · 1 required", a governance mandate invisible by backend choice (Devin review on PR #1278). Both reads now use the real column (`NULL` counts as not-required, matching DuckDB's `DEFAULT FALSE`), and the cross-engine contract test seeds a required item so the two backends must agree on `(3, 1)` — the old all-FALSE fixtures let the hardcoded zero pass by coincidence. No schema change: both ladders already carried the column.

- **Web chat no longer fronts raw JSON at the reader.** Non-tabular tool results used to render as a pretty-printed JSON `<pre>`; they now collapse behind a one-line "Structured result — show raw JSON" summary. "Show all rows" on a tabular result expanded to a JSON dump contradicting the mini-table right above it; it now expands to the same sortable table, capped at 500 rows — with a lazily-built "Raw JSON (all N rows)" route past the cap, so the cap bounds the DOM without losing data.

- **A turn that stops early now says so in the transcript.** The per-turn tool-budget frame (`confirmation_required`) was silently dropped — no assistant message follows it, so the turn just froze with no explanation. It now renders a visible note ("Stopped early… send a message to continue"), and errors and cancellations land in the transcript too instead of only flashing through the status bar. Each stop frame also flushes the streamed bubble's withheld tail (the progressive painter holds back a trailing half-fence, which only a further repaint would have shown) without dropping the stream pointers — a trailing partial-answer `assistant_message` is common after a stop and must finalize into the same bubble, not a duplicate — while `done`, a conversation switch and the next submit close out a bubble that never finalized — giving the orphan the same finishing tail a normal answer gets (highlighting, sortable tables, the copy/actions row; sources chips excepted, since no server verdict exists) — so a pending repaint can never land in a detached node and the next turn can never append into a stale bubble.

- **The magic-link "check your email" page claimed the link expires in 15 minutes; the token actually lives 1 hour.** The expiry sentence is now rendered from the real TTL constant (`MAGIC_LINK_EXPIRY`) instead of a hand-copied number, so the copy can no longer drift from the behavior.

- **`GET /login/email` now renders the magic-link form instead of the password form.** The route was always meant to be the email-only sign-in door, but it rendered `login_email.html` (whose forms post to `/auth/password/*`) by mistake. That was harmless while every provider's routes were always mounted, but the new `auth.providers` allowlist puts `Depends(require_provider("password"))` on the whole `/auth/password` router — so an instance configured with `auth.providers: [email]` 404'd on every form submit from its only login page, locking the instance out of the web UI entirely. `/login/email` now renders the previously-orphaned `login_magic_link.html`, and its form posts to a new `POST /auth/email/send-link/web` (the HTML-form sibling of the existing JSON `/auth/email/send-link`, mirroring the password provider's `/login` + `/login/web` pair).

### Removed

- Dead `auth.disabled_providers` example config (never consumed) — superseded by `auth.providers`.

### Internal

- Semantic-layer groundwork: `src/semantic_validation.py` — pure validator core over semantic-model documents (used-object detection, constraint evaluation with static/post-execution split, dialect checks incl. `locally_executable`). No user-visible surface yet; REST/CLI/MCP wiring and the UI land with the storage slice per `docs/superpowers/specs/2026-08-14-semantic-layer-ui-and-agent-parity-design.md`.

## [0.83.18] - 2026-08-14

### Internal
- New `tag-release.yml` workflow (`workflow_dispatch`): creates the semver tag + GitHub Release for a release-cut already merged to main, entirely server-side (`gh release create` makes the tag ref — no git tag push). Validates before acting: tag shape, target reachable from main, `pyproject.toml` version at the target matches, `## [X.Y.Z]` CHANGELOG section exists (it becomes the Release body); an already-tagged-and-released version is a no-op, a tag missing its Release gets the Release created (repairing a half-finished run), and a mismatched tag refuses. An over-limit CHANGELOG section (several historical ones exceed the Release-body API cap) is truncated at a line boundary with a pointer to `CHANGELOG.md` instead of refusing to tag. Exists because remote/CI-managed operator environments commonly allow branch pushes but refuse tag pushes, leaving `docs/RELEASING.md`'s post-merge step undoable from there.

### Changed

- **A stdio MCP server is kept warm between calls instead of started for each one.** Measured on a live instance against a connected Keboola project: **~6 s per tool call**, of which the `uv` launcher accounts for 0.13 s. The rest is the upstream's own import tree — `import fastmcp` alone is 2.4 s, its server module 5.6 s — so nothing about *how* we launch it can move that number, and an agent reaching for five tools in one answer was spending half a minute inside process startup. Sessions are now pooled per launch spec. Three properties make reuse safe, and each is pinned by a test. **The pool key is the whole launch spec, resolved secret included** (hashed, so the bookkeeping never holds a credential in the clear): a rotated token, an edited `env` or a bumped runner version each produce a different key, so the next call builds a fresh process and the stale one ages out — there is no invalidation hook to forget. The same property is what stops a `scope='per_user'` source from handing one analyst's warm process to another, since their resolved credentials differ. **Calls on one session are serialized**, because the streams underneath are not documented as safe for concurrent writers and nothing was concurrent before — every caller was paying a full spawn. **A failed call evicts the session and never retries**: retrying is the caller's decision, since a retry of a mutating tool can run it twice; the pool only guarantees the next caller does not inherit a broken process. Idle sessions close after `AGNES_MCP_SESSION_IDLE_S` (default 180 s) and at most `AGNES_MCP_SESSION_POOL_MAX` (default 8) are held, since each is a Python process with the upstream's imports resident. The reuse itself is a registered switch — `mcp_session_pool` (`mcp.session_pool` / `AGNES_MCP_SESSION_POOL`, on by default), editable from `/admin/server-config` — so an instance can go back to a process per call without a redeploy. HTTP and SSE sources are untouched — they have no spawn to amortize.

- Six hardenings of that pool, from Devin Review on this PR. **A warm session is only reused on the event loop that made it**: the session, its keeper task and the futures it parks on all belong to that loop, and the sync call paths (`list_tools`, `call_tool`, `_materialize_one_tool`) run one `asyncio.run` each — so the entry cached by the previous call named a session whose loop was closed and whose subprocess had already been torn down with it. Bookkeeping is now per running loop, and a closed loop's is dropped rather than served (the shape `_get_oauth_refresh_lock` already uses in the same connector). **A session is reserved before it is handed out**: the idle sweep and the size cap ran while the caller was still on its way to the lock, so a just-started process looked idle — with every other session busy it was the only eviction candidate, and the caller that had asked for it got a dead one. A claim is now registered under the same guard the sweeps run under. **Starting a process no longer holds a pool-wide lock**: one source's ~6 s startup queued every other source's tool calls behind it (and teardown could add 10 s), which is slower than the per-call spawn this change exists to remove; spawns are now single-flighted per launch spec and teardown runs after the guard is released. **A cancelled call evicts too**: `CancelledError` is not an `Exception`, so a caller whose `asyncio.wait_for` fired unwound past the eviction branch and left a session with a request still in flight upstream for the next caller to inherit. **Pooled sessions are closed on graceful shutdown**, wired into the FastAPI lifespan teardown, instead of being left to process death. And the on/off toggle is a registry switch rather than a hand-rolled `os.environ.get` — which also means `off` now turns it off (the inline parser accepted only `0`/`false`/`no`, so `off` read as ON). The two numeric knobs stay env-only and say why in `docs/feature-flags.md`: they gate nothing, and they are read once at import, so a live-editable field would show a value the running process is not using.

- Five more hardenings of that pool, from Devin Review's second round. **Idle sessions now age out on a timer**: the idle timeout was enforced only when the next tool call happened to arrive, so a quiet instance held its warm subprocesses — up to the pool cap, each with the upstream's import tree resident — until process exit, the opposite of what the switch text and the operator docs promise; a per-loop sweeper task (alive only while the pool is non-empty) now runs the same guarded sweep on a schedule. **A call abandoned during startup takes the starting process down with it**: the wait for the spawn was guarded by `except Exception`, and a cancellation — a caller's `asyncio.wait_for` firing, an HTTP client disconnecting — is a `BaseException`, so the keeper task stayed parked forever with a live subprocess that no sweep and no `close_all` could ever reach, since the entry was never registered; the same window existed between the spawn returning and the entry landing in the pool, and both now shut the orphan down. **A call abandoned during checkout gives its claims back**: the reservation taken under the guard — and the per-key spawn marker — leaked on a cancellation delivered inside the teardown wait that follows, pinning the entry as in-use forever (unsweepable, and once enough piled up the cap stopped bounding the pool) and wedging every later caller for that spec on a spawn nobody was doing; every await between claim and return now undoes the claim before re-raising. **A session whose upstream died on its own is detached, not handed out**: the keeper's exit resolved its future but left the entry registered, so the next caller ran on a dead transport and failed before a fresh process was spawned; an exited keeper now counts as stale everywhere the pool selects a session. **`aclose()` waits out in-flight spawns**: it snapshotted registered entries only, so a spawn racing shutdown re-inserted its entry after the sweep and the subprocess outlived the "graceful" stop — the spawn marker is now released only once the entry is registered, which is what makes waiting on markers sufficient. The default-on posture exception for the `mcp_session_pool` switch is now documented in `docs/feature-flags.md`.

- Four more hardenings of that pool, from Devin Review's third round. **A `scope='per_user'` source now isolates users by construction, not by the accident of differing tokens**: the pool key was the launch spec alone, and the claim that two analysts can never share a warm process rested on their resolved credentials differing — with no stored secret, or an identical shared value, both users built the same spec, hashed to the same key, and shared one upstream process that can retain per-session state; the caller's user id now salts the key for per-user sources (the caller-less scheduled materialize path stays unsalted — it is a single identity). **A server that starts but never answers `initialize` no longer wedges every caller of its spec**: the spawner's wait for session readiness was unbounded, and concurrent same-spec callers park on the shared single-flight marker behind it, so one hung startup was a permanent per-spec outage; the wait is now bounded (`AGNES_MCP_SESSION_SPAWN_TIMEOUT_S`, default 60 s, `0` disables) — on expiry the half-started process is cancelled, the marker is released, the spawning caller gets a typed error naming the knob, and the next caller spawns fresh. **A tool call that never returns no longer freezes its source**: calls on a warm session are serialized, and both the call and the wait for the serialization lock were unbounded — one wedged upstream call queued every later caller of that source forever, for every user; a pooled `call_tool` now carries a default ceiling (`AGNES_MCP_SESSION_CALL_TIMEOUT_S`, default 300 s, `0` disables; a caller-supplied `read_timeout_seconds` still wins), on expiry the call errors and the existing eviction path closes the process, and a caller waiting for the lock gives up with a clear busy error once the call ahead of it must itself have timed out. **A non-finite tuning value no longer takes the connector down at import**: `_env_number` guarded only `ValueError`, but `nan`/`inf` parse as floats — `int(float("nan"))` then raised at import (killing the whole MCP connector, the exact outcome the fallback exists to avoid), and a `nan` idle timeout made every expiry comparison false so sessions never aged out; non-finite values now fall back to the default with a warning, like any other unparseable input.

## [0.83.17] - 2026-08-14

### Fixed
- **Hosted apps now appear in the Library.** When this work started, a `rail` instance had no way to click to a data app at all: `data-ui-layout` picks one of two hand-written navs, and the "Apps" entry shipped in `_app_header.html` (topnav) only — reported by a user looking for an app they had just watched get built. The nav half of that has since shipped separately (the rail regained its own gated "Apps" entry alongside four other missing destinations — see the five-pages bullet above), so the claim that the Library row is the rail's *only* route is stale (Devin Review on this PR); what this adds is the listing itself: hosted apps in the **Library**, next to data packages and memory domains, which is the route those kinds already take — "everything you have", and an app you built from chat is as much yours as a collection you uploaded. Rows carry the app's state (running / sleeping / error) as their meta line, link to `/apps/detail/<slug>`, and are hidden entirely when the feature is off — a row leading to an empty-state page is worse than no row. Draft exclusion reuses `list(include_drafts=False)`, matching what `/apps` already does; a draft is an iteration branch of an app, not an app.

- **Credentialed CORS is no longer opened app-wide to every data-app subdomain.** The subdomain readiness-poll fix above first rode in as an `allow_origin_regex` over `*.{subdomain_base}` on the app-wide `CORSMiddleware`, paired with `allow_credentials=True`. Those subdomains serve user-authored app code, and the session cookie already travels from them to the main host (`Domain=.<parent>`, and subdomains are same-site, so `SameSite` never blocks the send) — CORS readability was the one barrier left, and the regex removed it: any hosted app's JS could `fetch` any authenticated Agnes endpoint as its viewer and read the answer (Devin Review on this PR). The poll needs exactly one readable cross-origin response, so that is what it gets now: the readiness handler itself answers with `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` for the app's OWN `<slug>.<base>` origin only — route-scoped, per-app (a sibling app's origin gets nothing), no preflight needed since the poll is a simple GET. The middleware regex is gone; `CORS_ORIGINS` semantics are untouched.

- **Two more preview/readiness hardenings from the same review.** (1) A preview mint whose slug failed the cookie-name safety check refused *after* creating the JWT and persisting the `access_tokens` row — so the refusal left a live, orphaned 30-minute credential behind and surfaced as a 500. The check now runs before any side effect, and `POST /{slug}/preview-grant` maps the refusal to a clean 400 `slug_not_cookie_safe`. (2) Moving readiness auth out of the `Depends` chain had put the registry read first, so an anonymous probe got 404 for a made-up slug and 401 for a real one — free enumeration of which hosted apps exist. The caller is resolved first again: anonymous is a uniform 401 either way, exactly what the old `Depends(get_current_user)` signature enforced. (Devin Review on this PR.)

- **Library app rows share like every other owner-held kind, and linked rows show the admin's wording.** Data apps are a real grantable resource type (`resource_grants` on the app's slug is what `_can_view` honours), yet the new Library row rendered share-less — for the one kind a user builds from chat, `/admin/access` was the only sharing surface, while collections, files and agents all carry an owner Share control. The row now wears the same control, wired through the owner-sharing service (`data_app` joins `_OWNER_RESOLVERS`, slug-keyed so the grants it writes are the grants the proxy reads), and its Sharing badge reflects the grants that actually exist instead of hardcoding "Private". Separately, the row read the raw `description` column, which for linked apps the MCP lister rewrites on every sync — an admin's `description_override` was shown on the app's own detail page and dropped here; the row now reads `effective_description`, same as every other surface. (Devin Review on this PR.)

- **`agnes status` reported `Parquets: 0` for a workspace holding hundreds of parquet files — a wrong zero in the one command an analyst runs to ask "is my data here?".** Measured on a real workspace: 6 tables present as 331 part files, reported as 0. The count globbed `server/parquet/*.parquet` **non-recursively**, but a partitioned table is a *directory* of parts (`<tid>/month=…/data.parquet`), so a workspace of partitioned tables counted zero however many parts were on disk. It also ignored `.claude/data/_shared/` entirely, the store the per-type stack sync writes.

  The line now counts **tables, not files**, and reports the two trees **separately** rather than summing them: `Tables    : 6 queryable, 37 downloaded (no local view)`. Summing was the first attempt and was wrong in a way worth recording — the DuckDB view rebuild only walks `server/parquet/`, so nothing registers views over `.claude/data/_shared/`, and a single `43` would have promised local data that `agnes query --local` cannot resolve (confirmed against a live workspace: 37 parquets in `_shared`, zero matching views, `--local` failing with a catalog error while the default server-side scope answers fine). One number could only ever hide real bytes on disk or overstate what is reachable. The second clause is omitted when everything is queryable. The "never initialized here" explanation is chosen on whether ANY tables were found rather than on the queryable count alone — a workspace whose data all sits in the stack-sync store has zero queryable tables and was otherwise told to "bootstrap" one line after being told it holds dozens of tables. `--json` keeps `parquet_tables` as the queryable count and adds `tables_downloaded_no_local_view`.

  Cross-tree matching reads the recorded id↔name relation from `<workspace>/.claude/sync_state.json`, because the trees are keyed differently — the legacy stem is the flat manifest key (`sync_state.table_id`, which is `table_registry.name` by convention) while `_shared/` uses `table_registry.id`. Slugifying the name is only the fallback for workspaces whose state predates this, and it is not sufficient on its own: Keboola auto-discovery derives the id from the fully-qualified source id (bucket included), so `id != slug(name)` there and one table would be reported as both queryable and missing. Empty and `.staging-<tid>` directories left by an interrupted partitioned sync hold nothing queryable and are skipped, matching the view rebuild. The rule for "what is a local table?" now lives in `cli/lib/local_tables.py`, shared with `agnes diagnose`, which already had an identical private copy that this would otherwise have drifted from.
- **`agnes status` no longer answers `Initialized: no` beside a populated table count without explaining it.** The two lines answer different questions and can legitimately disagree: `agnes pull` writes into any directory that is workspace-*shaped* (`is_workspace_shaped` accepts a bare `server/parquet/`), whereas "initialized" means `agnes init` ran *there* and installed the Claude Code hooks and workspace template. A directory receiving pulls but never initialized therefore reported `no` and was advised to "bootstrap", which reads as though the data were absent. That case now names the half that is actually missing — the hooks and template, not the data — and asks for `agnes init` to finish setting it up.

- **`customer-instance`: the state-applier's uid is now pinned everywhere it is created, not just in the startup-script's primary block.** `/data/state/instance.yaml` is written `0600` (#1214), which makes its owner load-bearing — the app container can read its own config only while `agnes-applier` resolves to the same uid as the app (999). #1214 pinned that in the startup-script's main `useradd`, but left two other call sites allocating an uid by chance: a belt-and-braces `useradd` further down the same script (before the `.env` chown) and, more significantly, `scripts/ops/agnes-state-applier-bootstrap.service` — the systemd unit that is the *only* user-creation path on any infra that doesn't run the OSS module's own startup-script. All three now pin the same uid (a single `AGNES_APPLIER_UID` variable in the template, referenced by both `useradd` attempts and the readback check, so they can't drift apart again), with the same fallback and posture as before: if the uid is already taken by a different account, provisioning falls back to an allocated one and logs a loud, non-fatal warning with remediation steps rather than bricking the boot — a 0600 file the app cannot read is no worse than the pre-#1214 world, and a hard failure over a file mode is a worse trade than a warning. `docs/postgres-cutover-runbook.md`'s manual migration command is updated to match. (#1217)

  **That fallback was not survivable, which made the warning a lie.** Provisioning gates its `chmod 600` on the readback, and both the runbook and the bootstrap unit told operators the overlay simply keeps its looser mode and everything keeps working — but the applier's own `write_instance_yaml` chmodded the temp `0600` unconditionally on both its writer paths and renamed it over the file, which re-owns it to whoever wrote it. So on any host where `agnes-applier` did not land on the app container's uid, the first rewrite left `/data/state/instance.yaml` owner-only under a uid the app is not, and the app's fail-closed strict boot read refused to start the instance. Every backend flip, cancel and stuck-job recovery rewrites that file, so ordinary admin activity took the instance offline — hours or weeks after the operator was told the state was fine, with nothing connecting the two. The mode is now computed once, from the uid the file will come to *rest* on (the writing process, or `agnes-applier` when running as root, since the chown after the rename can still move it there), and handed to both writers: `0600` where the app container will own the result; anywhere else, never an owner-only mode — `0640` with the app's gid (999) as the group wherever the applier can actually grant it (probed on a scratch file before each rewrite, because the post-rename group re-assert is best-effort and a `0640` whose grant never landed is the same lockout), falling back to the documented `0644` degradation otherwise, with a warning at every rewrite naming the uid it found and the mode it chose. Preserve-don't-tighten was this fix's first shape and had two holes of its own: the app-side writers (`write_backend_state`, the admin config editors) run as uid 999 *inside the container* — where owner-only is exactly right — and chmod `0600` unconditionally, so preserving carried that `0600` across the applier's re-owning rename and stranded the overlay unreadable one rewrite later anyway; and on a fresh overlay "preserve" bottomed out in a stat-fallback that *created* the file world-readable, database url and password inline. Warn-only stays the posture for a pre-existing mis-numbered account (`usermod -u` on a live system account orphans the files it already owns, which is a worse surprise than a warning), but it is now a warning about a hardening that did not apply rather than about a pending outage. Found by Devin Review on this PR (two rounds).

## [0.83.16] - 2026-08-14
### Added

- **A whole MCP source can be granted to a group in one action** — only its **enabled** tools, and it says how many it skipped. — `POST /api/admin/mcp-sources/{id}/grants` (`agnes admin mcp source grant <src> --group <id>`, plus a group picker on the Chat tools row of `/admin/data-sources`), with `DELETE …/grants/{group_id}` to take it back. The per-tool grant is the right granularity for an upstream curated a few tools at a time; it is the wrong one for a source that arrives with its whole toolset at once. A connected Keboola project registers around forty tools, so granting them one page at a time reintroduced by hand exactly the friction the chat-tools switch removes — registration was automated and the admin was left forty clicks later. The revoke half matters more than the convenience: an admin who granted a whole project in one action must be able to withdraw it in one, rather than clicking through forty tools while access stays live. Idempotent per tool. It refuses (409 `no_tools_registered`) rather than reporting success over a source with no registered tools, and returns `granted` / `already_granted` / `total` separately, because "granted 0 of 37" and "granted 37 of 37" are different news and look identical otherwise. Deliberately **not** MCP-exposed: a tool an agent can call that widens which tools a group may call is a privilege-escalation seam, and this one widens by a whole source at a time.
- **A connection can carry `config.workspace_schema`**, passed to its derived chat-tools source as `KBC_WORKSPACE_SCHEMA`. This is what makes a **non-master, read-only** token usable: only a master token gets a workspace created for it behind the scenes, so an admin who narrowed the token to read-only — the obvious thing to do when lending a project to an agent — got a source where every tool worked except `query_data`, the one they most wanted. Absent unless the connection sets it, because with a master token inventing one would be wrong.

- **A data package has a page: `/admin/data-packages/<id>`.** The package is the unit an analyst actually receives, and it was the one object in the Data section with no home — its composition was edited inside the package-grouped layout on `/admin/tables`, its sharing on `/admin/data-packages`, and the card's own drilldown left the admin area entirely for the analyst-facing `/catalog/p/<slug>`. Three surfaces, none of them about the package. The new page states its whole life in reading order: **Tables** (add/remove members), **Sharing** (one row per group with the Optional/Automatic tier, the same `/api/admin/grants` rows a group's Access tab writes), and **At a glance** (source, freshness, reach). It adds no endpoint and no repository method — composition rides the existing `/api/admin/data-packages/{id}/tables` junction. Package cards on the Packages lens now drill here.
- **The delivery read-out — shared is not delivered.** A grant is a *permission*; the data lands only when `agnes pull` runs, and nothing in the product could state the difference. The Sharing panel now reads it off `users.last_pull_at`: how many people get the package automatically, how many actually have it on their machine (pulled within 7 days), and how many are shared-but-not-yet-delivered. Only **Automatic** grants count toward reach — an optional grant merely makes the package offerable, and counting it would overstate delivery.

### Changed

- **A group's Rename and Delete live on the group, not on the pane.** The Access workspace put a `⋯` in the header of the right-hand card, which meant it could only ever act on the SELECTED group — renaming `finance` while looking at `sales` required selecting `finance` first, a navigation performed to reach an edit that has nothing to do with what the pane is showing. It also competed with the group's name for the same corner. The menu is now on the row in the group list, so it acts on whatever you are pointing at, and it appears only there: `opacity` rather than `display` so the row does not reflow under the cursor, `pointer-events: none` while transparent (an invisible control that still takes clicks is a trap, and this one opens Delete), `@media (hover: hover)` so touch input keeps it permanently visible, and `:focus-within` / `:focus-visible` for the keyboard path. Only editable rows carry one — `Admin` and `Everyone` are renamed and deleted where they are owned. Using the menu no longer changes the selection, and deleting a group from its own row leaves a different open group open rather than navigating the pane as a side effect.

- **The data package page states each standing fact once.** `/admin/data-packages/{id}` opened on a strip carrying the table count, the sources, the category, the status, the newest sync and a "View as analyst" link — and every one of those was already on the same screen. The table count, the sources and the newest sync were three rows of **At a glance**; the link is the button on **Appears as**, beside the sentence about how analysts see the package. A banner that repeats the column next to it is not a summary, it is a second copy free to fall out of step with the first. The strip is gone and the two facts it alone carried — **Category** and **Status** — have joined At a glance, so the page now opens on the work. The two warning bands above the columns stay: those are conditions to meet before acting, not facts to read.

- **Removing a table or a group from a data package asks first, and the ✕ appears on the row you are pointing at.** `/admin/data-packages/{id}` drew a remove button on every table row and every sharing row at rest — a column of destructive controls, inches from the Optional/Automatic buttons beside them — and the per-row ✕ deleted immediately while the *bulk* remove was the one path that confirmed. Both single-row removals now open the app's shared confirm, and each dialog names the consequence rather than asking "are you sure": removing a table says analysts stop receiving it on their next sync and that the table stays registered so it can be added back; un-sharing says everyone in that group loses the package and every table in it unless another of their groups also carries it. The bulk dialog picks up the same anatomy, so the three confirmations on the page no longer explain themselves three different ways, and each confirm button says what it does ("Remove table", "Stop sharing") instead of "Confirm". The control itself is revealed by row hover, via `opacity` rather than `display` so no row twitches sideways as the pointer crosses it — with `pointer-events: none` while transparent (an invisible button that still takes clicks is a trap, and this one deletes something), scoped to `@media (hover: hover)` so it stays permanently visible on touch input, and revealed by `:focus-within` / `:focus-visible` so the keyboard path is unaffected.

- **The Tables lens runs the product's own toolbar, not a private copy of one.** `/admin/tables` wore `.fbar`'s chrome over its own engine — a page-local facet matcher, comparator and badge bookkeeping — so the one lens with the most rows in it filtered by rules nothing else in Agnes used. It is `filter_toolbar.js` now, the engine the Library, /chats and the Add-tables drawer share, and it brings the two things the private copy could not do. The **Filter menu has two levels**: it lists the families (Source · Project · Mode · Data package), each opening its values beside it, with a search field inside any family past ten options — the flat popover it replaces ran to one option per Keboola bucket in a single scroll. And the applied filters are **removable chips on a row under the bar**, one per family reading `Source: bigquery, jira`, each its own edit affordance with a trailing **Clear all**; a filtered list used to be legible only as a number on the Filter button, which said how narrowed the list was but never by what. Each family row also carries its own count, so the menu says which one is doing the narrowing before it is opened. Sorting, the count, the no-results state and the `?unpackaged=1` / `?package=` deep links all ride the shared engine; the mount is torn down and rebuilt when the registry is re-fetched, so nothing stacks.
- **Bulk actions on Tables float at the foot of the viewport, the way /chats does it.** Ticking a row used to **swap the toolbar out in place** for a tinted bulk strip — so selecting one table took search, Filter and Sort off the page, exactly when an operator is most likely to want to widen or re-narrow the set they are building. The toolbar now stays put and a floating bar appears instead, carrying the verbs for a set. Selected rows are tinted, since with the verbs pinned to the bottom of the screen "which rows did I pick" has to be answerable without scrolling back to the checkbox column. `Unregister` is **disabled with the reason in its title** while any selected table is still in a package, rather than failing in a dialog after the click. The list reserves the bar's clearance unconditionally, so its arrival never moves the row under the pointer that ticked it. The bar itself is promoted into the shared component as `.fbar-bulk` (`filter_toolbar.css`), and `FilterToolbar.init()` now returns a `destroy()` for pages whose rows and menu are both rendered by a fetch.
- **The Tables list, re-hierarchised.** **Mode** was a coloured pill per row — green, blue, purple — beside its plain-language label, a stripe of four hues down a list whose subject is the table name two columns to its left; it takes the Source column's own two-line anatomy instead (`Saved query` over a quiet mono `materialized`), so the two cells on a row that still carry colour are the two that carry a state worth acting on. An **unpackaged row now says "Nobody" quietly**: the Package cell beside it already carries that alarm in the colour of the thing that can be fixed, and most rows on a fresh instance are unpackaged, so the pair made the list read as entirely on fire. Packaged-but-reaching-nobody keeps the warning, because nothing else on the row says it. The instance-level connector warning moved **above** the toolbar, next to the note it belongs with, instead of sitting between the controls and the rows they act on; the no-results panel gained a **Clear filters** button and now hides the empty table header above it. The row checkboxes ride the row's own ink at rest rather than the brand accent, and the Filter menu's footer is the shared component's again (the page had been restyling it).
- **The rest of the Data section speaks the same vocabulary.** `/admin/data-packages` drew the unpackaged pile as a private dashed amber tray with a wall of up to 24 mono table names in it, saying the same *kind* of thing the Tables lens says in one shared `.apg-strip--warn` line, in a second object three times the height, on the adjacent tab; it is that strip now, and the names went with it — 24 of 450 is a sample, not a list, and the strip's link lands on all of them in the surface that filters and acts on them. Its two package verbs move from a bare button row under the tab strip into the section head's own action slot, where Sources puts `+ Add source`. `/admin/semantic-layer`'s "Also connected, but not syncing" list becomes the shared strip with its fix pinned to the end. `/admin/sync` — a Data lens that renders the Data tab strip — drops the gradient hero and `DATA PIPELINE` eyebrow the Tables lens had already retired for the same reason, adopts `.fbar` (its search box's magnifier was a data-URI SVG with a grey baked into it, so it stayed light-grey on the dark theme), and has its stat cards, row cells and toasts retokenized off `--ds-*` — they were legacy names with raw-hex fallbacks, which is a card that resolves to white-with-near-black-text whatever the theme decides. Its two tinted counts now tint **only when non-zero**: `0` errors was being reported in alarm red.
- **A data package looks the same to the admin who publishes it and the analyst who receives it.** The Packages lens drew each package as a 120px coloured banner with two-letter initials over it, a `NEW` badge, an `In stack` pill and an `Owned by` line — an admin-only card carrying an analyst's vocabulary, four of which filled a screen while the facts an admin scans for (what is in it, who gets it) sat below the fold. Both grids on `/admin/data-packages` now render the Library's own card: `.fbar-card` from `filter_toolbar.css`, through a new `macros/_fbar_card.html` that emits the same DOM the Library's grid builds in JS — so the component has one definition and two hosts instead of two lookalikes. Admin facts ride the pattern's own slots rather than justifying a second card: the table count, category and owner on the one-line meta, source types as tags, and the footer's two — who can use it on the left (a named group, or a count, or **Not shared** in warning ink), and the one thing worth acting on on the right (**No tables**, linking to the assign flow, which outranks the tier because an empty package delivers nothing however it is shared). Memory Domains get the same card and the same read-out, from their own grants.
- **Sharing is stated on the package card, not edited there.** The card's `Share…` button and its group-tier modal are gone. A grant is consequential — *Automatic* puts a package into every member's workspace on their next pull — and an index card shows none of its consequences; the package's own page sets it right beside the delivery read-out ("14 people get this, 11 have pulled it") that answers for it, and a group's Access workspace remains the other end. Both still write the same `/api/admin/grants` rows, so the two surfaces cannot disagree.
- **The package page is a detail page, and both its flows are drawers.** `/admin/data-packages/<id>` now wears the anatomy `/admin/users/<id>` already had. The way back is the page's **first line, above the heading** — it rendered inside the page body, which sits below the hero, so the link out of the page appeared under the title it is meant to precede (`{% block page_prehead %}` in `base_page.html` is the slot, available to every page on that base). The two states that strand analysts — no tables, shared with nobody — are **bands above the columns**, each carrying the control that fixes it, instead of being legible only by counting rows in a panel further down; the unshared band clears itself the moment a grant is written. **Add tables** and **Share with a group** moved off page-local centred modals onto the shared right-side drawer (`css/drawer.css`) — the same chrome the Add-data wizard, the group editor and the invite flow ride.
- **Creating a data package is one shared drawer, opened on the lens you are standing on.** Three faults, one cause — the create form was page furniture on `/admin/tables` rather than a component. It was the tallest form in the admin surface (name, slug, description, lifecycle, category, icon, colour, cover image and a group-access matrix) inside a 520px centred card, so on a laptop its footer sat on top of its own last field; the `<select>`, the colour input and the file input inside it were undressed browser chrome beside fields that were not; and because the Tables lens owned the only copy, **`+ New package` on the Packages lens was a link to `/admin/tables?new_package=1`** — asking for a new package on the Data packages tab switched you to the Tables tab to fill the form in. It is `js/components/package_drawer.js` now, on the shared right-side drawer (`css/drawer.css`) that the Add-data wizard, the group editor, the invite flow and the package page's own two flows already ride, and both lenses open it in place over the grid or list it adds to. The controls that a browser draws in its own house style are dressed in the shared sheet — the status select borrows `.fbar-select` (the product's own select chrome), the access tier borrows `.fbar-seg` (its segmented control, now reading **Optional / Automatic** per group rather than a raw `available|required` dropdown), and `.ds-drawer__color` / `.ds-drawer__file` / `.ds-drawer__disclose` / `.ds-drawer__row` join the drawer's own field vocabulary for the colour swatch, the file button, an optional folded-away section and a two-up field row. Two bugs went with the move: the slug now follows the name **as you type** (it was derived only when the form opened, so typing a name into an already-open form left the slug empty and the create bounced on a required field), and the created package's name reaches the caller — `POST /api/admin/data-packages` answers with `{id}` alone, so the chip added back to a table's edit form was showing the raw `pkg_…` id and the toast read *Data Package "undefined" created*. Every existing entry point is unchanged: the chip-input's "+ Create new" tail row still hands the drawer its host and gets the new package back as a chip, and `?new_package=1` still opens it on `/admin/tables` for the legacy catalog CTA.
- **The Add-tables drawer carries the product's own toolbar.** A substring filter is not a way to work three hundred registered tables, and that is all the modal had. The picker is now `.fbar` + `filter_toolbar.js` — the same engine the Library and My Stack run on — with search over name/bucket/source, a Filter menu of **Source · Query mode · Bucket** (each vocabulary built from the candidates themselves, so a filter can never offer a value that matches nothing), an **In no package** toggle carrying its own count, and sorting by name, source, bucket, freshness or row count. Each candidate row states its source, bucket, mode, size and sync age. Selection survives filtering, so narrowing to Keboola, ticking four, then narrowing to BigQuery and ticking two adds six — the footer keeps a running count and the button reads `Add 6`. The package's own table list gains the matching end: per-row checkboxes with a select-all, and one **Remove from package** for everything ticked.
- **The Add-data wizard: buckets collapse, a bucket picks itself, and the step strip is the way back.** Step 2 rendered every bucket open and every table under it — 164 buckets and 576 tables on a real Keboola project, one flat wall with no way to pick a whole bucket and no running answer to "what have I selected". A bucket is now a single line that is **closed by default** (a one-bucket project opens, since there is nothing to choose between), carrying its own **tri-state checkbox** — checked, unchecked, or the indeterminate dash for a partial pick — that selects or clears the bucket in one gesture without touching rows that are already registered. Per-table checkboxes are untouched for the granular case, and each bucket line reports `N selected · M tables` so a closed bucket still answers what is in it. Above the list: a **filter** over bucket and table names that springs matching buckets open (and restores the reader's own open/closed layout when cleared, not the filter's), **Select all / Clear** scoped to what the filter is actually showing, **Expand all**, and a running `N of M selected` that counts the whole picker — with an explicit *"(k hidden by the filter)"* rather than letting a filtered view imply that a selection went away. Registering re-opens the buckets it writes to, so the per-row `registering… / ✓ registered / ✗ failed` report is on screen while it is written. The same picker renders in a source card's inline **Browse tables** panel, which gets all of it too.
- **"Already connected" is an offer, not a grey strip above the real form.** On an instance that is already running, adding tables to a project Agnes *has* is the more common of the two things the Connect step does — and it was drawn as chrome: one line of small secondary text, a bare `<select>` and a ghost button, on the dim surface this page uses for things that are switched off. Admins read past it and filled in the URL-and-token form underneath for a project they had already connected. It is the shared connect-banner shape now — the same `.cbn--bar` the Library and the chat landing use, and the same tokens: the Agnes soft surface, the connector's mark in a lifted tile, a headline that states the connector-level fact (*"Keboola is already connected."*), a sentence that names what you are spared and carries the count when there is more than one project to choose between, and one filled pill for the action at the CTA weight the analyst surfaces use. The picker carries what each project actually holds (`Keboola AI · 3 tables`), read off the same per-connection count the source card behind the drawer is showing, so choosing between five projects is not a guess at names. Below it, *"or connect a new project below"* — a muted sentence **inside** the box, which is the one place it could not do its job — becomes a real labelled divider between the two paths, because the thing this step has to make obvious is that there are two. The tile takes the connector's own `-soft`/ink token PAIR rather than the lifted white of the shared component: `--ds-kind-data` is a light-only ink and measured 2.16:1 on the dark theme's surface, where the mark simply vanished.
- **The wizard's step strip is a control, not a picture.** `Connect → Choose tables → Bundle → Share` was four `<span>`s behind `aria-hidden` — an admin who mistyped a package name or missed a table had to cancel and start the whole flow again. Each step is now a **button**: one you have already been through is enabled and takes you back to it, one you have not earned is `disabled` (dimmed, cursor-blocked), so "not yet" is carried by the control's own state rather than by a click that silently does nothing. Nothing is re-fetched or re-rendered on the way back, so **everything survives** — the connect form's fields, the picker's checkboxes and open buckets, the board's trays and their names, the share grid's ticks and tiers. Returning to Choose tables and adding more merges the new tables into the board that was already arranged instead of re-seeding it. Three states are distinguishable without relying on colour: a completed step swaps its numeral for a ✓, the current step's numeral takes a halo, a future step's is an empty outline. Because creating packages is a real side effect, a tray that has become a package is **frozen** on re-entry — read-only name, its rows unselectable, a `✓ created` chip, the seed chips disabled and the CTA reading *Back to sharing* — so stepping back can never mint a duplicate; renames, merges and splits belong to `/admin/data-packages` from that point, which the step now says. The last screen is a receipt for work that has landed, so from there the strip stops offering a way back. The shared drawer (`css/drawer.css`) carries the done/current/disabled step states, so the invite-person drawer picks them up too.
- **Inviting a person is a drawer, and the groups they belong to are part of it.** `+ Invite person` opened a centred card that asked for an email and then told the reader to go and do the half of the job that matters somewhere else: *"New users start with no group memberships — assign them on the user detail page after creating."* Nothing is granted to an account directly, so that card's product was a person who reaches nothing plus a chore to remember — and the People table it left you on says exactly that back to you in the **No data access** cell. The flow now rides the shared right-side drawer (`css/drawer.css`, the one the Add-data wizard and the group drawer already use) with two steps: **Person** (email, optional name, the invitation link) and **Groups** — a pick-list of the groups this person joins, each row carrying its member count and how many resources it actually carries, with the Admin row saying in its own colour that it hands over the whole instance. Two kinds of group are absent rather than disabled, for the same reason the person's own page omits them: `Everyone` (every account is in it at creation) and Google-synced groups (membership belongs to `admin.google.com`). **The group can also be made from inside the invite** — the one that ought to exist usually turns out to be missing while you are looking at the list it is missing from, and the alternative was abandoning the invite, going to Access and starting again. `+ New group` writes the same one-field `POST /api/admin/groups` the group drawer does (naming a group is all that drawer does now), and the new row arrives ticked with a line saying it carries nothing yet — a person in an empty group still reaches nothing. It commits immediately while the memberships wait for the end: a group is an object other people will use, and cancelling an invite is no reason to delete it. Both empty states point at that button instead of sending the reader away mid-flow, and Escape backs out of the name field before it backs out of the invite. The account and its memberships are written together at the END of the flow, so cancelling on the group step leaves nothing behind; a membership that fails after the account exists is reported by name rather than dropped silently. No new endpoint and no second writer: `POST /api/users` then `POST /api/admin/users/{id}/memberships`, the same call the detail page's add-to-group row makes.

- **Instance secrets: the "Google Workspace" card says which Google Workspace it is.** The name covers three unrelated roles in this product and the card is only one of them — the **analyst-side** Drive/Gmail/Calendar connector, whose credentials `agnes init` writes into the analyst's workspace so each analyst signs in to their own account from Claude Code. It is not the identity provider (sign-in and group sync read `auth.google_client_id` from `instance.yaml` and use a separate web-application OAuth client), and it is not a server data source (the connector is a laptop-side skill; it produces no `extract.duckdb` and therefore no tables). An admin who filled it in expecting Workspace login got no login and no error. The card is now titled **Google Drive, Gmail & Calendar** with a note naming where the credentials take effect and where sign-in is configured instead; its save/clear toasts follow the title. The **Sources footnote** carried the same conflation from the other end — "the identity provider, not a data source … instance-level credentials live in Instance secrets", which reads as the *identity provider's* credentials being in that card — and now answers the question a reader of that list is actually asking (why is Workspace not here?) once per role: the identity provider produces people, the connector extracts nothing onto the server. Its groups link follows them to `/admin/access`, where a group has been edited since they left People. The stored key names (`AGNES_GWS_CLIENT_ID` / `AGNES_GWS_CLIENT_SECRET`) are unchanged — they are the wire contract with `/api/connectors/params` and the analyst's `.claude/agnes/.env`, and a label is not a reason to rotate a secret every deployed instance already holds.
- **Tables reads as a lens of Data, not a page of its own.** It rendered a gradient hero card titled *Tables* under a *DATA* eyebrow, while Sources, Data packages and Semantic layer all render the plain **Data** head — so moving between lenses changed the heading, its size and its treatment. It now shares the section head; the tab strip names the lens.
- **Registering a table opens in the shared right-side drawer.** Both register surfaces (BigQuery, Keboola) moved off the centred `.modal-overlay` onto `.ds-drawer` — the chrome Connect-source, the Add-data wizard and the group editor already use. Setup flows in this product come from the right. Every field id is unchanged.
- **Bulk selection on the Tables list.** Assigning twelve tables to a package meant twelve trips through the row menu. Rows now carry checkboxes, and ticking any of them swaps the toolbar for a contextual bar — *N selected · Add to a data package · Sync now · Unregister · Clear* — that appears only while a selection exists. Select-all covers the **filtered** set, not the hidden remainder, and filtering out a row deselects it, so a bulk action can never take something the operator was not looking at. Unregister enforces the per-row rule for the set: a table still in a package must be detached first.
- **`/admin/tables` is denser.** The standalone count row (~40px for three words, separating the controls from the rows they act on) folds into the toolbar, and the per-row *"Keboola not connected"* warning — an instance-level fact repeated once per Keboola row, costing each a third line — is stated once above the list, with the link that fixes it.
- **The Tables lens is rebuilt in the shared table + toolbar vocabulary.** It rendered its own `.registry-table` — a second table in a product that had agreed on one — with its controls scattered across a card of buttons above the list, a search box inside the list panel, a checkbox beside it and cache freshness floating at the card's right edge. It is now the `.data-table` People, Groups and the Library render, under ONE `.fbar` toolbar: search, a grouped-checkbox **Filter** popover (source · Keboola project · mode · data package · in-no-package, each option counted and built from the rows so an empty facet never appears), a **Sort** control (name, source, package, reach, last synced), then the page's own actions — cache freshness and *+ Register new table*. Row actions collapse from five icon buttons into one `⋯` menu (a fixed-position portal, since the table clips its own overflow). The name cell takes the bucket as a second line, freeing the width five columns had been splitting. Nothing was removed: Edit, Sync now, Add to a data package, Sync history and Unregister are all in the menu, and Unregister stays gated on the table being in no package.
- **Data tab names carry their own meaning; the stage captions are gone.** Each lens briefly shipped a caption under its name ("where data comes in", "who receives it"), which doubled the strip's height to gloss four words — the tell that a label was doing too little. **Semantic** (an adjective with no noun) is now **Semantic layer**, and **Packages** — the word whose meaning nobody could state, which started this reshape — is **Data packages**, the term the API, the CLI and the analyst's Library already use. The pipeline arrows stay.
- **The Tables lens stops sorting freshness by nothing.** `/api/admin/registry` joins `sync_state` on the table's NAME while the orchestrator and every other consumer key it by ID, so its `last_sync` is null on instances where those differ. Freshness now comes from the same server-side map as reach, keyed by ID.
- **The Data lenses stop overlapping: `/admin/tables` is a flat cross-source lookup.** It rendered one collapsible `<details>` per *package* with its member tables inside, plus an Unpackaged bucket — which made it a second list of packages beside `/admin/data-packages`, with a package's composition on one lens and its sharing on the other. Composition moved to the package's own page; what is left here is the question only a flat list answers: **where is this table, and does it reach anyone?** Columns run to the end of the chain — Table · Source · Mode · **Package** · **Reaches** — so "a table reaches nobody until it is in a package" is visible per row instead of being a rule in the page subtitle. New **In no package** filter (deep-linkable as `?unpackaged=1`, which the Packages tray now points at). `query_mode` is worded in plain language while keeping the system word (**Synced copy** `local`, **Live query** `remote`, **Saved query** `materialized`) so CLI and API vocabulary stays learnable; one mapping (`_mode_words()` in `app/web/router.py`) feeds both Data surfaces. Row actions keep the full edit surface; *Remove from package* moved to the package page, where you can see what else you are emptying.
- **The three package verbs moved off the Tables toolbar.** *+ New Data Package*, *Group tables by bucket* (now **Suggest packages by bucket**) and *Bulk assign tables* sat above a list of tables — the same category slip as the package-grouped layout under them. They live on the Packages lens now and carry the caller in with the flow named in the query (`?new_package=1`, `?group_by_bucket=1`); the flows themselves are unchanged.
- **The Data strip reads as a pipeline.** `Sources → Tables → Packages` are not three categories you choose between but one flow seen from three places, so the strip now draws arrows between them and gives each its stage in a line — *where data comes in* / *what there is* / *who receives it*. Semantic keeps its tab and sits past a divider with **no arrow into it**: `metric_definitions` is one instance-wide registry several Keboola projects write into, so it lies across the pipeline rather than after Packages in it. Every tab is still a real URL; every other admin section keeps the unchanged `ds.tabs` strip (the flow variant fires only where the inventory declares a `purpose`).

- **Every source lives in the Sources list, and a source card ranks its own contents.** `/admin/data-sources` said *Keboola projects*, its primary button said *+ Add Keboola project*, and its list asked the API for `?source_type=keboola` — while the drawer behind that button offered Keboola, BigQuery, CSV and Jira. A BigQuery table registered through that very drawer then appeared nowhere on the page that had just registered it. The section is now **Connected sources** with one **+ Add source** button that opens the connector picker, and the list is every connector on the instance: `_source_inventory()` (app/web/router.py) synthesizes a card for the connectors that keep no `source_connections` row — BigQuery (credentialed once in Instance secrets), Jira (webhooks), uploaded files — from the tables they actually registered, and BigQuery earns a card from a configured service account alone so there is somewhere to press *Add tables*. Each card's pipeline strip is per-connector: BigQuery trades the permanently-"never synced" Sync cell for **Cost guard** (the live `bq_max_scan_bytes` / `max_bytes_per_materialize` caps), Jira reads **Webhook**, files read **Freshness**. A card's own contents are now ranked rather than flat: the head carries the connector mark, one identity line, **one status word** folded from the strip (`Healthy` / `No tables yet` / `Reaches nobody` / `N failing syncs` — a missing semantic-layer token stays a cell-level warning, since an opt-in feature being off is not a broken source), an **Actions** menu and a disclosure caret; the five-button action strip, the chat-tools row, the master-token row and the two hidden input rows collapse into a settings body that is closed by default. Nothing was removed — Test, Add tables, Rotate storage token, Semantic-layer token, Chat tools, Make default project, Unbind and Delete are all still there, in a menu whose dividers rank them and whose Delete sits alone at the bottom. Derived cards get the verbs that are real for them plus a line naming where their credentials actually live, instead of controls that would do nothing. New shared component: `.apg-menu` in `admin_page.css` (fixed-position portal, broad dismissal — the cards clip their own overflow). Terminology: *Master token (semantic layer)* → **Semantic-layer token**, with the Keboola noun kept in the hint. Two page-wide restatements are gone above the list: the **semantic-layer status strip** (a full-width "Never synced yet." band, when Semantic is its own tab in the same tab row and every card already carries its semantic cell) and the paragraph under **Connected sources** explaining what a source is and where the Actions menu lives — the cards now say both.

- **A group is edited in one place.** Groups and "who can use what" were two tabs of the Access section that were both, in substance, a list of groups — and behind them sat two more editors over the same rows: `/admin/groups/{id}` (Members and Access as tabs) and the create drawer's steps 2 and 3 (its own member picker, its own grant matrix). Four surfaces over one pair of tables (`user_group_members`, `resource_grants`), each free to drift from the others, for one object that has exactly two sides: an audience, and a bundle of what that audience can use. **`/admin/access` is now the only one.** Its left column carries what the list table showed — the origin pill, the member count and the grant count on each row, with search matching name, description and Workspace address — and its right pane carries what the detail page owned: the group's name, the Workspace address it is really stored under, its origin, description and created date, plus **Rename** and **Delete** (hidden on system and Google-synced rows, which the API refuses to change; the delete confirmation names the consequence — how many people lose how many things — and uses the app's shared confirm rather than a page-local modal). The audience block gains **Show all N**, the detail page's full roster with each member's source (`added by admin` / `synced from Google` / `system-managed`) and Remove offered only on admin-added rows — a rule the person-search now honours too, instead of showing a button that always 409s. The grant tree gains the **filter** only the detail page had, which opens the sections it matches so a hit inside a collapsed type is never silently hidden. The create drawer is one step again: it names a group and hands it to you selected in the workspace, where the empty audience and the empty grant list teach what its steps 2–4 were built to teach. `/admin/groups` 308s to `/admin/access`, `/admin/groups/{id}` to `/admin/access?group=<id>` (an unknown id still 404s), and `/admin/tables`' *Manage access* now arrives as `?resource=<type>:<id>` with the old `#table:` fragment rewritten to it — so every link, bookmark, `g g`/`g a` shortcut and command-palette entry still lands. What deliberately stays elsewhere is only the transpose: a data package's Share panel (which groups get this package) and a person's memberships on their own page answer different questions. Net: two admin pages, one stylesheet and ~350 lines of duplicated drawer JS removed, with no capability dropped.

  The workspace itself is one panel, not a stack. The group's identity, its People and its Access are three regions of a single card divided by hairlines — a **sticky header** carrying the name, origin, description and one fact strip (which replaces the member count being drawn three separate ways: a sentence, a row of avatars, and a "Show all N" label over the roster), then two collapsible sections built from the same `.dsec` component `/admin/users/{id}` uses for the transpose view. **People is collapsed by default** — its head states the count — and its body is the roster itself. **Searching for someone opens an anchored popover** rather than inserting a block: results used to push the roster, the tier legend and the whole grant tree down the page by their own height, so the row you were reaching for moved while you read it. Access carries its filter and a compact **All / Granted** scope segment on one line, each half labelled with its own count, which answers "what does this group actually have?" without opening ten accordions in turn. The Optional/Automatic key is a **hover tooltip** immediately left of the count it qualifies, rather than the permanent three-line accent panel between the two sections that read as an alert about the members above it. `Admin` and `Everyone` sit under a **System** heading above the editable groups, and the "N groups" count and "Data packages →" button above the cards are gone — the count restated the list directly beneath it and the link is already in the page subtitle. Two layout bugs fixed on the way: the panel no longer sets `overflow: hidden`, which had both clipped the search popover at its bottom edge and silently made the panel the sticky header's scrollport — pinning the header 57px inside the card, on top of the People section.

- **Granting tables works bucket by bucket.** `/api/admin/access-overview` has always grouped each resource type into blocks — buckets for tables, marketplaces for plugins — and the grant editor flattened them into one list with the block name as a suffix on each row. At six tables that is tidy; at six hundred it is why an admin cannot find `in.c-revenue_core`, and granting a whole bucket means ticking every row in it. A type with real blocks now renders them as **collapsed buckets**, each head carrying the two facts that decide whether to open it — how much of the bucket this group already holds, out of how big it is — and a **tri-state checkbox** that grants or revokes the whole bucket in one gesture. Partially-granted buckets render `indeterminate` rather than unchecked, so the control never reads as "grant this" when half of it is already granted; a click from any partial state grants the remainder, and a click from fully-granted revokes. Granted rows carry a tint, so what the group already has survives scrolling past the checkbox column. Search works through the nesting: it narrows to the types and buckets that match, auto-expands them, and labels a narrowed bucket "1 of 4 shown · 3 granted" so it never presents a slice as the whole. Types whose blocks are decorative — one block named after the type itself — stay flat rather than growing a disclosure around their only child. Writes go through the same per-item `/api/admin/grants` calls a single row uses; there is no bulk endpoint and no second write path.

- **A person's admin page is now about that person.** `/admin/users/{id}` opened on a floating gradient hero card titled **"User detail"** under the eyebrow "Users & Access" — the page's most prominent slot spent on the name of a page *type*, a card drawn around a title on a page whose whole body is cards, and an eyebrow restating the sidebar the reader had just used to get there. The head is now the identity, on the page ground with nothing drawn around it: the person's own avatar circle (the same initials and colour their `/admin/users` row draws, from the shared `AgnesIdentity` derivation), their name, their state, and the three account actions. The **back link moved above the heading** — it sat to the *left* of the hero, centred against a 112px card and therefore level with the middle of the title and off the page's own left margin — and it is now the shared `.apg-back` (`css/admin_page.css`), which retires the sixth page-local copy of that same link. The **"Account" section is gone**: it was a bordered card whose entire content was the sentence "*<email> is active*", which the head says twice over, plus the buttons that now live at the identity. Its one piece of real cargo — the consequence of being deactivated — is a page-level condition and now reads as one, an amber context strip above the work; the SSO case gets the same treatment, where previously "this account is managed by Google Workspace" was communicated *only* by two buttons silently not being there. The **five peer sections** (Groups · Effective access · Access tokens · Sessions · Activity), which had been five identical grey-headed cards giving the page no hierarchy at all, are now two named halves — **Access** (the authority, and what it yields) and **Credentials & activity** (what was issued, and what was done with it) — built from the shared `.dsec` section card `/me/profile` and `/me/activity` use, each head carrying its own count so a collapsed section still answers its own question. Groups and Access tokens open; the three read-outs wait to be asked for, and a `#tokens` / `#sessions` / `#activity` deep link opens the section it names instead of landing on a closed drawer. Everything the page used to draw itself now comes from the design system: tables are `.data-table`, the add-to-group control is the shared `.fbar` toolbar rather than a bare `<select>` in a grey footer band, row actions and paginators are `.btn`, and transient outcomes go to the global `appToast` instead of a private toast stack with its own hardcoded near-black — about 240 lines of page-local CSS, almost all of it a private re-derivation of one of those five, replaced by ~90 lines that are only ever this page's own. Three state-pill families (`.ud-status-pill`, `.tok-pill`, `.unprocessed-badge`) collapse into one, and the resource-kind read-out in Effective access picks up the categorical `--ds-kind-*` accents a data package or a plugin already wears everywhere else. Two smaller fixes fall out of it: the group-chip base no longer paints a light-only `--ds-*-soft` tint under theme-flipping ink (the shape that measures ~1:1 in dark mode — the list page's copy still hides that from the guard behind a hex fallback), and the "Download all (.zip)" control appears only once there is something to download. Functionality is unchanged throughout.
- **Fixed: the admin sidebar scrolled away at the bottom of every admin page.** The column is `position: sticky` at a full `100vh - 32px`, so its slide room is whatever its containing block — its grid area in `.admin-split` — has left over. The shared footer was rendered *after* `<main>`, outside that grid, and `.container` added 48px of bottom padding below it: together ~160px of scroll the column had no way to stick through. Over that last stretch it was dragged up with the page, taking its title, the instance name and the Overview row off the top of the screen — on a page long enough to reach the bottom, which is why it looked intermittent. The footer now renders **inside `.admin-main`**, where it also belongs visually (its hairline spans the content it closes instead of running under a full-height rail), and the container's trailing gutter on an admin chrome drops to the same 16px of air the column already leaves below itself, so the split spans every scrollable pixel and the two bottom edges agree. `page_footer` is a new block in `base_ds.html` so a chrome with a sticky column can relocate the partial rather than get a second copy of it. Verified pinned at every scroll offset on both admin bases and on the longest admin surfaces; short admin pages now fit the viewport without scrolling at all.
- **Fixed: a focused section card was ringed around its head alone, which read as the head coming loose from its body.** The `.dsec` collapsible section card (`/me/profile`, `/me/activity`, and now a person's admin page) drew its focus ring on the `<summary>` at `outline-offset: -2px` — a rectangle inscribed just inside the card, around the head and nothing else. On an open section that rectangle runs along the hairline between the head and the content it opens, so one card reads as two. It is easy to hit without meaning to: `<summary>` is a focusable control, so clicking a section head — the ordinary way to open one — leaves it focused; the click alone shows nothing (Chrome withholds `:focus-visible` for pointer input), and then the first arrow or page key pressed **to scroll** flips the heuristic and the box appears with no apparent cause. The ring now belongs to the card the summary controls: `:has()` moves it to the parent at `+2px`, outside the border where every other focus ring in the product sits, with the browser's default outline on the head cleared in the same rule and an `@supports` fallback that keeps a ring (pushed clear of the hairline) on engines without `:has()`. Which element holds focus is unchanged — only where the ring is drawn.
- **A long sentence in an admin context strip no longer wraps below its own glyph.** `.apg-strip` wraps by design, so the trailing links can drop onto a second line on a narrow column — but the sentence itself had an `auto` flex basis, and flexbox decides *wrapping* from an item's max-content width before shrinking is ever considered. Any strip whose text ran past one line therefore broke onto the next, leaving its leading identity mark sitting alone above it: two stacked fragments instead of one line of standing fact. The sentence now takes a zero basis and grows into what the mark and the links leave.
- **The rail has a Chats destination, so collapsing it no longer hides the way to your conversations.** Rail-layout instances only. Every row in the rail carried an icon except the conversation region — two section labels and a list of titles — and the only door out of it was a "View all chats" link *inside* it, itself hidden until the caller had a conversation.
