The rail collapses to a 56px glyph strip, by default on `/admin`, so that link was unreachable exactly where it was needed most: from an admin page the product had **no path to `/chats` at all**, and on a first run it had none anywhere. **Chats** is now an ordinary destination row (`id="nav-chats"`, a speech-bubble glyph at the same weight as Library and Agents) directly under New chat — verb then noun — active on `/chats` and nowhere else; Pinned and Recent are the content beneath it, and the foot-of-the-list link, its reveal logic in `rail_history.js` and its `.rail-history-all` rules are all gone. Two things follow from the same rule, that a rail row must have an icon or it vanishes when the rail narrows: **the conversation lists no longer render on admin pages** (they cannot survive the collapse; the Chats row reaches them in one click from either width, and the invariant that matters — collapsed and expanded holding the same set of destinations — is now true *per page*), and **the onboarding card no longer renders there either** — it measures the analyst's journey (connect your tools, ask your first question) and was the only element in the chrome with a coloured progress arc, so it pulled the eye hardest of anything on screen while an admin registered a table; it stays on every app page, and the checklist is still reachable from the account menu. The admin column's head changes with it, under the rail chrome only: **"← Back to the app" is replaced by a two-segment mode switch** — `Admin` ⇄ the brand, the pressed segment saying which of the two products you are standing in and the other being one click to the app you'd use as an analyst, with the consequence spelled out underneath ("Everything here applies to the whole instance"). The row it replaced was a fifth way to a destination the collapsed rail already carries — New chat · Chats · Library · Agents, all with icons — and it never said anything about the mode you were leaving. The switch deliberately spends no accent (a lifted surface on a sunken track, the theme-toggle idiom): `.is-active` rows below own the column's one blue, and two blue blocks meaning different things is how a column stops saying anything. Above it, the uppercase `ADMIN` micro-label becomes a real heading beside the **instance name** — which deployment a change lands on was previously answerable only from the fixed grey build stamp in the corner. Under `topnav`, still the default layout, the head and the back row are byte-for-byte unchanged. A new guard (`TestRailChatsDestination`) asserts every `.rail-i` row contains an `<svg>`, because the next text-only row would reintroduce this bug somewhere else.

- **People, Data and Access are one page pattern now, and the pattern is the Library's.** The three surfaces an admin actually works in read as three views of one product instead of three products: the same head, the same rhythm below it, the same section head, the same toolbar. Concretely — (1) **no card around the page header.** The head is the canonical `.page-header` primitive in a new `--plain` variant (`page_hero_plain = True`), which is the head `/library`, `/agents` and `/chats` already render by hand: a 24px title, one 15px sentence capped at 68ch, and nothing drawn around them. The hero card stays for pages that have to introduce themselves (`/home`, install); a workspace you stand in and filter is not one of those, and on Access it was a bordered card sitting above a pane made of cards. The eyebrow ("Administration", "Sources", "Admin") went with it — it restated the sidebar row the reader used to get here, one line above a tab strip that names the lens. (2) **The h1 names the SECTION, the tabs name the lens**, on every page of a section: People · Tokens both say "People", Access · Groups both say "Access", and the Data lenses all say "Data" (`/admin/tokens` had been saying "Users & Access", a section that stopped existing when People and Access split). (3) **One shared vocabulary** in `css/admin_page.css`, loaded by both admin bases: `.apg-strip` (the one-line context strip — Workspace identity, semantic-layer status, the vault-key warning), `.apg-sechead` (section name · count · actions, the Library's `.lib-section-head`), `.apg-sec-desc` and `.apg-bar`. It replaces seven page-local copies of the same four objects (`.pp-*`, `.gp-*`, `.ds-section-*`, `.idp-strip`, `.ds-semantic-summary`, `.sl-*`, `.adp-count`), each a few pixels and one type size from the others. Behaviour changes worth knowing: the semantic-layer strip is **neutral when the last sync succeeded** and tinted only on failure (a green band for "nothing is wrong" teaches admins to stop reading the strip); the `{% block toolbar %}` slot renders *above* the tab strip, so the two lone buttons parked there — Access's "Data packages", Semantic's "Sync now" — moved onto their section head, where the page's other controls are; the Data-sources section head drops the amber emoji tile (a status accent on something that was only a heading); and `/admin/tokens`' four count chips move off the retired gradient onto the page surface. `tests/test_web_admin_page_pattern.py` pins all of it.
- **The admin sidebar is organized around the admin's jobs, not the tables underneath.** The seven sections (People & access / Data / Connections / Moderation / Content / Instance / Insights) grouped routes by what the backing table is; the new shape is the redesign's People → Data → Access model: **Overview** (the hub row, renamed from Dashboard to match what the page now is), two intent sections — **People** (Users, Groups, Tokens) and **Data** (sources → tables → packages → sync → semantic layer, in the order the work happens) — then a labelled **Maintain** divider and three upkeep sections: **Library** (the old Moderation + Content merged: curation and moderation are the same job from two directions), **Instance** (config + the old Connections folded in: MCP sources, linked apps and instance secrets are the machine's plumbing), **Activity** (Insights renamed for what it shows). Every one of the 30 routes keeps an entry — nothing became unreachable — and the column gains a **“← Back to the app”** link at the top, because admin is a place you visit and the rail beside it is collapsed to a 56px icon strip there. A dedicated Access section joins the intent half when its surface ships; until then access is edited from a group's Access tab and a package's Share editor. Section keys `connections`/`moderation`/`content`/`insights` are retired in favour of `library`/`instance`/`activity` — a browser's stored open/closed preference for those four sections resets once. The intent/maintain split is part of the pinned IA (`divider_before` in `admin_nav.py`, guarded), not template styling.

### Fixed

- **One failed group load no longer blanks the "Grant all to group" picker for the rest of the visit.** `/admin/data-sources` cached the empty fallback it assigns when the groups request fails, and an empty array is truthy in JavaScript — so the cache short-circuit handed that failure back as a valid group list on every later call, the picker rendered zero options, and each grant attempt answered "Pick a group first" until the page was fully reloaded. Only a successful load is cached now; a failure returns an empty list without remembering it, so the next render retries.
- **A derived chat-tools source now follows its connection's `workspace_schema` in both directions.** Set on an already-enabled connection it used to arrive only after the admin toggled chat tools off and on; removed, it never went away at all — the env merge was `existing | derived`, which cannot delete, so the agent kept running SQL against a workspace the admin had taken away and nothing said so. The keys this module derives are now authoritative (absent means absent) while any key an admin added to the derived source survives untouched, and both the enable path and the unrelated-edit resync go through one shared merge rather than two copies of it.

- **The default chrome's Admin menu had fallen behind the pages it links to.** The admin pages are not theme-gated — they ship to every instance on upgrade — but the topnav chrome's Admin mega-menu is maintained by hand beside the sidebar's inventory (`app/web/admin_nav.py`), and it had drifted a whole redesign behind: **no `/admin/data-packages` row at all**, under a column literally named "Data Packages", for the object the Data section is now built around; `/admin/access` still listed as "Groups", a section this release deletes; and no row for Store lint, Studio suggestions or Contribute a skill. A default instance therefore got the new information architecture behind a menu describing the old one, with the header and the sidebar disagreeing on the same screen — and the data package, the unit an analyst actually receives, unreachable from its nav. The five missing rows are added and the label corrected. The menu keeps its own columns, which are a decision rather than drift: it groups by the job you came to do ("Moderation queues", "Onboarding & messaging") where the sidebar groups by section. What was missing was a guard, and `tests/test_web_admin_nav.py` now has it — every ungated entry in the inventory must have a row in this menu, compared at page granularity (the same granularity `tests/test_admin_nav_parity.py` already compares the reverse direction at), so the next section added to the sidebar cannot silently skip the header.

- **The Add-data wizard reports what actually happened to each table.** Registering tables that were already in the registry is a success — the server answers `409` and the wizard already marks each such row "already registered" and carries it into the Bundle step — but the summary counted only fresh writes, so a step where every selected table was already registered ended on a success-styled "0 table(s) registered.", which reads as a failure that also did nothing. The 409s are counted apart and named ("1 table(s) registered · 1 already registered"), and a genuinely empty step says so rather than reporting a zero.

- **The wizard's "select at least one table" message is no longer written to nowhere.** Step 2's primary button stayed enabled with nothing ticked, and pressing it appeared to do nothing at all: the guard wrote its message into `ds-browse-error-<connection>`, an element only the standalone Browse&register panel renders, so in the wizard it resolved to `null`. It falls back to the wizard's own error line and reveals it, since `.ds-wizard-error` is `display:none` until it carries text.

- **The Tables lens no longer claims Keboola is not connected when it is.** The instance-level "X is not connected — N registered tables … cannot sync" strip was resolved from the legacy single-source `data_source.type` scalar, which names one default type and cannot answer whether a given source has a connection. An instance defaulting to another type while holding connected Keboola projects — listed by name on the adjacent Sources tab — was told its Keboola tables could not sync until a project was connected, sending the admin off to re-enter credentials the instance already had. Connectedness now comes from the source-connection registry (`connected_source_types`).

- **A data package's own page names the door to editing it.** `/admin/data-packages/{id}` could add tables and change sharing but offered no rename, no description and no delete, while stating "No description yet — analysts see this text in their Library" about a field it could not edit; the full editor (name, description, status, category, icon, colour, Delete package) was reachable only by typing `/admin/tables?edit_package=<id>`, and the create drawer's own copy promises the package "stays editable on the package's own page afterwards". The "Appears as" panel — which describes exactly those fields — now links to it.

- **The Tables lens states its sharing note with the icon set, not an emoji.** The line explaining that grants are set on the package carried a literal `📦` as its mark — a font's picture of a parcel, drawn four different ways across platforms, and unable to take the strip's own ink the way every other mark on these surfaces does. It is `ico.icon('package')` from `macros/_icon.html` now, the shared set the no-emoji policy points at (`tests/test_no_ui_emoji.py`, which this line had been failing).

- **Paper theme: static cards no longer lift on hover.** The design system makes the card hover-lift opt-in — `.ds-card[data-clickable]`, with the default theme's own comment reading "cards stay still by default — calm" — and `paper-skin.css` applied it to every `.ds-card` regardless. Any static container under the paper theme (an "At a glance" panel, a form section, a read-out) therefore rose 2px and grew a shadow when the pointer crossed it: elevation promising an interaction the card does not have. Paper now honours the same `[data-clickable]` gate, so cards that ARE clickable still lift and containers stay put. `.stack-card` and `.card` keep the ungated rule deliberately — neither sets that attribute and both are genuinely clickable where they are used, so gating them on it would remove the hover from the cards that have earned it.

- **A filter chip no longer eats a name that ends in a number.** The shared toolbar read a chip's label off its menu option and stripped a trailing number from it, on the theory that the text ended in the option's tally — but every caller puts the tally in a sibling element, so the label held the name alone and the strip took the digits with it: a data package called `Customer 360` chipped as **Customer**, a tag `Q3 2026` as **Q3**. The strip now runs only on the fallback path, where the row's own text really does carry the count. Affects every surface with a chip row (`/library`, `/chats`, `/stack`, the package picker, and now Tables).

### Added

- **`/admin/access` is a real surface again — a cross-group workspace, plus "simulate a person".** The URL has had three lives, and the middle one is why this shape is what it is: it was a standalone grant matrix; it was retired into the group detail page's **Access tab**, correctly, because `resource_grants` keys on `group_id` and the old page was the same editor behind a second group picker; and it returns as the thing that tab structurally cannot be. **Who can use what** puts the groups in a left column and the editor in the right pane — moving between groups is a click instead of a page load, `Everyone` sorts first because a grant to it is company-wide, data packages open first as the redesign's spine, and every other `ResourceType` keeps a section that is merely collapsed (breadth disclosed, never removed). **Simulate a person** answers "why can / can't they see X?" — the question that previously meant joining four pages by hand: it walks memberships → grant → tier from the existing `effective-access` endpoint, names each data package individually, folds every other kind into one row per type with its count and granting groups (listing nine collection rows buried the packages under them), and — the half a grant list cannot show — names the packages that are **not** shared with them, each with a link to share it. Admin god-mode is stated rather than implied ("Admins can always reach everything regardless of grants"), a grant whose target no longer exists or is private to its owner is counted and labelled as such rather than hidden, and the closing line says a shared package still only reaches a machine on the next `agnes pull`. Deliberately **not a fork**: the page reads `/api/admin/access-overview` in one round trip and writes the same `/api/admin/grants` rows as the group tab and the package-side Share editor, so the three entry points cannot disagree — and the group tab stays, because it carries Members beside Access and is where you land from a group. `/admin/grants` 308s here carrying `?group=`, so old deep links still preselect their group. Access joins the sidebar as the **third intent section** (People → Data → Access), the shape the redesign is named after. Fifth slice of the admin-experience redesign.

- **Every source card answers "is this project healthy, and is anyone getting its data?" in one strip.** Each connection on `/admin/data-sources` now carries a four-cell pipeline: **Tables** (registered against this connection) · **Sync** (freshest run, or how many tables are failing) · **Semantic layer** (owner-token state, then metric/glossary counts) · **Feeds** (packages holding this source's tables → the people they reach). That vertical previously took four pages to assemble by hand — Data sources, Tables, Sync, Semantic layer — and the last cell existed nowhere at all, so "this project syncs perfectly and reaches nobody" was invisible. The strip is **per-connector by construction**, not a fixed four: the Metastore is a Keboola API, so a BigQuery source renders no semantic cell rather than an empty one. Each cell links to the page that owns its stage, and every value is worded as a state an admin can act on ("Never synced", "Token not set", "0 packages"). Two honesty details: a grant to the system **Everyone** group reads "→ everyone" instead of a member count it would have to guess, and tables registered before per-connection tracking (or through the CLI) are counted as **"N unlinked"** with an explanation — reporting them as "No tables yet" made an instance with eleven registered tables read as empty on every card. Cells resolve independently and degrade to omission rather than a 500, for the same reason the `/admin` dashboard isolates its resolvers: this is the page an admin opens when a source is *already* broken. Fourth slice of the admin-experience redesign.

- **Adding data is one guided flow: connect → choose tables → bundle → share.** The "+ Add Keboola project" modal (connect + register, then stop) becomes the four-step **Add data** wizard, reachable from the Overview's new "＋ Add data" action (`/admin/data-sources?add=1` auto-opens it). Steps 1–2 are the previous wizard *unchanged* — connection retry-reuse, detected-name adoption, project binding, per-row register statuses all preserved, and "Register only & finish" keeps the old stop-after-registering exit. What's new is everything after: **Connect** now offers the semantic layer at the moment it belongs ("also sync business metrics & glossary" with the owner-token field inline — previously discoverable only on the semantic-layer page's empty state; a refused or missing token degrades to a warning, never blocks the tables). **Bundle** is a composer over the just-registered tables — one pre-made package as the default, "Split by bucket" as a one-click *seed* rather than a mode, tick-and-move between packages, inline rename, "＋ New package", and a warn-styled **Leave out** tray whose tables land in the standing unpackaged tray instead of vanishing — because tables reach analysts only through a package, a rule the flow now states out loud. **Share** renders one card per created package (the same Optional/Automatic tiers as everywhere else, Everyone labeled company-wide) and writes ordinary `/api/admin/grants` rows; it is **skippable**, because an unshared package now warns on the Overview and on Data packages rather than failing silently — which is also what the honest closing summary says, per package ("shared with Everyone (automatic)" next to "created, shared with nobody yet — it waits on the Overview"). Packages are created through `POST /api/admin/data-packages` + `/tables` — the same rows every other surface manages, no parallel store. Step 1 opens on a **connector picker** — only the connect step varies by source; bundling and sharing don't care where data came from. **Keboola** is the full flow above, plus an "Already connected" shortcut so adding more tables from an existing project doesn't read as "new connection only". **BigQuery** is real: the wizard reads the instance service-account status from `/api/admin/datasource-secrets` (routing to Instance secrets when unset, never growing its own credential field) and registers named dataset+table rows as live queries (`query_mode='remote'`, cost-guarded); saved queries and partitioning keep their full editor on `/admin/tables`, stated in the flow. **CSV / files** and **Jira** are deliberately guidance, not forms — there is no CSV connector (files enter through Library Collections, and the card links the Collections-vs-packages trade-off doc) and Jira is configured instance-side with a webhook (the card links the recipe) — pretending otherwise would fail at the last step instead of the first. Third slice of the admin-experience redesign.

- **"Who can use this package?" finally has an answer — sharing is rendered and editable from the package's side.** `/admin/data-packages` was explicitly read-only (its card footer buttons were hidden by CSS) and grants were writable only from a group's Access tab, so the most natural sharing question in the product had no surface at all. Each package card now carries a sharing strip — the groups it is granted to, each with its tier — and a **Share…** editor listing every group with a checkbox and an Optional/Automatic tier control. The tiers are the API's `available`/`required` worded as what they *do* ("Optional shows it in members' Library to add themselves; Automatic puts it in their workspace on the next sync"), with the system word carried in the control's title so the two vocabularies stay connected. The editor writes the same `/api/admin/grants` rows the group-side matrix writes — one storage, two entry points, so the surfaces cannot disagree — and the group-side editor remains the canonical, full-breadth one (every ResourceType). An ungranted package says **"Shared with nobody — invisible to analysts"** on its own card, and the system **Everyone** group is labeled "the whole company — every account, automatically" in the editor, because a grant to it is the one that over-shares by accident. The page also grows the **unpackaged tray**: registered, syncing, distributable tables that belong to no package — the rows `agnes pull` will never deliver — named out loud with a link to the Tables page where assignment happens (`remote` rows are excluded: they answer server-side without a package; blank `query_mode` folds to `local`, the same rule as everywhere else). Second slice of the admin-experience redesign.

- **`/admin` opens with where the instance stands, not just what's queued.** Above the two signal zones, three always-on **gap cards** walk the People → Data → Access chain and lead with the broken link: *N tables are in no package — analysts cannot pull them*, *N packages are shared with nobody — invisible to analysts*, *N people are in no group with access to a data package*. Each is a real count from existing repository reads (no new repo methods, no parity surface) and links to the page where the gap is closed; the healthy state renders as an explicit all-clear line, because the chain being whole is information, not noise. `remote` tables are deliberately not counted as unreachable (they answer server-side without a package), a blank `query_mode` folds to `local` exactly as the manifest and the distribution gate fold it, and a grant to the system **Everyone** group short-circuits the people gap without enumerating a single membership. A fresh instance additionally gets a **setup path** — Connect a source → Add tables → Bundle into packages → Share with people — with live per-step state, one CTA on the first undone step, and each step naming the dependency the product otherwise leaves invisible ("tables reach analysts only through a data package"); it retires itself once all four are done, the same pattern as the rail's onboarding card, because "Nothing needs your attention" is the worst possible first-run signal. Every resolver is isolated: a raising repo degrades that one card to "could not be checked" — shown rather than hidden, since a broken check must never read as a healthy chain — and the rest of the page renders. First slice of the admin-experience redesign (`docs/superpowers/specs/2026-08-12-admin-redesign-exploration.md`).

- **A grouped, collapsible left sidebar for `/admin`.** Every `/admin/*` page carries a persistent nav — People & access (Users, Groups, Tokens), Data (Data sources, Tables, Sync, Data packages, Semantic layer), Connections (MCP sources, Linked apps, Instance secrets), Moderation (Store moderation, Flea submissions, Store lint, Studio suggestions), Content (Marketplaces, Knowledge digests, Corporate memory, News, Contribute a skill), Instance (Server config, Database backend, Initial workspace, Prompts) and Insights (Audit log, Telemetry, Analyst sessions, Adoption) — instead of only being reachable from the topnav's Admin dropdown or the `/admin` hub's card grid. Each section is a disclosure button (chevron, `aria-expanded`/`aria-controls`): only the section containing the current page renders expanded by default, so the ~31-row list a first cut of this nav shipped as collapses to ~12; a caller's own manually opened/closed sections persist per browser (`localStorage`), though the active section can never end up hidden regardless of stored state, and the default/active state is resolved server-side so nothing flashes fully expanded before JS runs. The column itself does NOT collapse. A toggle that shrank it to a ~56px icon strip with per-section hover flyouts shipped and is retired, along with the stored preference behind it: this column is the primary navigation of every page that renders it, and the rail beside it already owns collapse/expand for the window — two collapsible columns side by side turned "how do I get back?" into a two-step puzzle. Two base templates carry the sidebar: `base_admin.html` for pages that own a `content` block outright, `base_admin_page.html` for pages riding `base_page.html`'s hero/toolbar/page convention — both a one-or-two-line `{% extends %}` swap per page, no other template changes. The sidebar hides entirely below ~820px, as before; pages stay fully usable via their existing hero/tabs. `tests/test_web_admin_nav.py` keeps the nav inventory-honest: it parses every `require_admin`-gated, template-rendering GET route in `app/web/router.py` and fails if one has no entry in `app/web/admin_nav.py`, and asserts the server-rendered expand/collapse state per section. On rail-layout instances the new sidebar used to sit beside a SECOND permanent 240px column — the global rail — leaving ~39% of a 1100px viewport as chrome and re-offering the same seven admin areas a second time through the rail's own Admin flyout. The rail now collapses to a ~56px icon strip on `/admin/*` — brand mark, destination rows (New chat, Library, Agents, Admin, the onboarding row), profile avatar — and the admin sidebar becomes the primary nav. The conversation list (Pinned/Recent/View all chats) renders on admin pages too, hidden by CSS while the strip is collapsed — its rows are text and have no icon form — and back in full when the rail is hover-expanded, so an expanded rail on `/admin` is the standard rail. It spent one pass omitted from the admin render entirely, on the rule that the item set must be identical collapsed and expanded so no row below it could shift; the price was a 240px hover-expanded column with no conversations in it, which is the one thing the gesture is for. The shift is accepted and confined instead: expanded, the rail is `position: fixed`, so nothing outside it reflows, and inside it the bottom zone rides the `margin-top: auto` it already had. The onboarding row is now the SAME anatomy as every other rail destination on every rail page, admin or not — an icon plus a label, no card chrome — and its icon is a circular progress ring (steps complete/total, a small checklist glyph centered in it swapping to a checkmark at 5/5) in place of the retired horizontal bar and chevron; the ring is a fixed size in both icon-mode states, so this row's height never differs between collapsed and expanded either. It no longer retires itself entirely at 5/5 — the ring simply reads full — and the label carries the same "N of 5 steps complete" sentence via `aria-label`/`title` for icon mode and screen readers alike. Hovering, tabbing/`:focus-within`, or (on touch, which has neither) tapping the new `#rail-icon-toggle` pin button — CSS-hidden on hover-capable/fine-pointer devices, since a mouse or keyboard already reaches the same expansion for free — widens the rail back to 240px as a floating overlay (`position: fixed`, so it never reflows the admin sidebar or the page under it) and reveals the label text beside each icon; no row's height or position changes between the two states. Escape collapses it again. The rail's Admin entry is now ONE plain link to `/admin`, on every page — not just on admin pages.

**Follow-up:** the collapsed/expanded width above is now a **persisted user preference** (`localStorage agnes.rail.collapsed`) rather than something the request path decides — page-dependent chrome was unlearnable, since the same destination sat at a different place depending on where you stood and walking from `/admin` to `/chat` silently changed modes underneath you. `_admin_page` in `_app_rail.html` now only supplies the STARTING value for a caller who has never toggled (collapsed on `/admin`, expanded everywhere else); the first toggle anywhere overwrites it, and the stored value then wins on every page, `/admin` included. Applied before first paint by a tiny inline script at the top of `<nav>` — the same before-paint technique `_theme_resolve.html` already uses for the colour scheme, just scoped to this element — so there is no flash regardless of which page loads first. The two admin-only tap/hover controls are consolidated into ONE `#rail-toggle`, moved into the logo row (ChatGPT's pattern): expanded, it sits at the row's right end beside the wordmark, persistently visible; collapsed, only the orb shows at rest, and hovering or focusing the row swaps it for the toggle in the orb's own slot (no permanently visible chrome in the 56px strip for a caller who already has a free way in); touch, which has no hover event, sees it there always instead — one control for that job, not a second one bolted on. Clicking it (rather than merely hovering) is what PERSISTS the state; hover/keyboard `:focus-within` still just PEEK the collapsed rail open, unpersisted, exactly as before, now with a ~120ms opening delay (closing on mouse-leave stays instant) so a pointer passing through doesn't trigger a peek. `Cmd/Ctrl+\` toggles the same preference from the keyboard (VS Code/Slack's convention), guarded against firing while typing in a field. The now-redundant admin-only `#rail-icon-toggle` and its `rail_icon_mode.js` are retired in favour of the one `#rail-toggle` / `rail_toggle.js` pair, loaded on every rail page. The hover flyout it used to open (seven "area" rows, each revealing a panel of links beside the column) is gone, and with it a second, hand-written copy of the admin inventory that had already drifted from the real one in `app/web/admin_nav.py`: different labels, different grouping, and three `/documentation` links that are not admin pages at all (that route is gated by `get_current_user`, not `require_admin`). Two IAs for one section is a maintenance trap, and the flyout was the wrong half to keep — it could only ever be a menu, where `/admin` is a page that explains itself, and its card grid is where those Documentation links live on. ~250 lines of flyout CSS and the hover-bridge machinery that kept a diagonal pointer inside it go with it. The column is now drawn as the **secondary variant of that rail** rather than as its own vocabulary. It had three different left margins (title 8px, section labels 10px, rows 10px inside a 8px-padded aside), a section header that filled on hover exactly like a destination row, and a chevron pushed to the far right edge — which read as a second column of controls and left seven collapsed sections looking like seven identical rows. Now: one inset drives the title, all seven labels and every row, so the column has a single optical left edge; section headers are labels that happen to be operable — no fill in any state, ink-only on hover, caret against the word, the rail's own `.rail-chatsec-hd` idiom — so only rows fill and a filled thing here is always somewhere you can go; the open section's label steps one shade darker than the six closed ones, so you can see which group you are standing in from the column's shape before reading it; and proximity does the grouping (2px binding items to their label, 10px/14px lifting the open block out of the index) instead of dividers. Rows are the rail's rows — same 34px ladder, same 14px/500 type, same active tint. They spent a pass one step quieter (32px, 13.5px) on the theory that this is a secondary nav, which is wrong on the surface that matters: the rail defaults to its collapsed icon strip on `/admin`, so this column is the PRIMARY navigation there, and a nav doing the primary job while dressed as a subordinate one is what read as unpolished beside it. The left-edge system is now one figure: the title, the hub row, every section label and the guide all resolve to 16px from the column edge (a 6px aside padding plus each pill's own 10px inset), where the aside's 10px used to stack with the pill's 10px and open a 20px gutter before the first character of a 200px column. Nested rows clear the guide by 8px — as the body's `border-left` the guide had the nested pill starting at the border's outer edge, so every hover and active fill butted straight into the line and the rows read as clipped against a rule rather than indented under a heading. The guide is a pseudo-element now, inset 3px top and bottom so it brackets the rows it belongs to instead of running edge to edge into the labels above and below it. The aside's right padding is 4px against the left's 6px because `.admin-nav__sections` adds 2px of scrollbar room that stacks with it; balanced at the source, a pill clears the hairline by the same 6px it clears the left edge by. Two fixes came out of that: the hover wash was `--ds-surface-dim`, which is a *near-background* token — correct in the rail, where rows are hovered on white, but under the paper theme it is `#f5f7fb` against a `#f3f6fa` page canvas, i.e. lighter than what it was marking, so hovering an admin nav row showed nothing at all; it is now `--ds-surface-sunken`, the token defined to read a shade darker than the canvas (and correctly a shade lighter under dark). And the column is full-height, so its hairline reads as a rail edge instead of stopping in mid-page wherever the seven labels happened to end; on `topnav` instances it now pins below the sticky 57px `.app-header` rather than sliding underneath it on scroll. The hub is now the sidebar's FIRST ROW ("Dashboard"), above the seven sections and in none of them, active on `/admin` exactly so it never competes with the section row that owns an `/admin/*` page; the column's "Admin" title, previously the only way back to the hub, is a plain label again, because a small uppercase column heading is not something anyone reads as a link. And nesting is now DRAWN rather than implied: an item used to sit flush with its section label — borrowed from the rail, where a section holds conversations that are obviously its contents — but here label and row are both navigation words in the same column, so flush left made seven sections and their rows read as one long ladder. Items indent 13px past their label and hang off a hairline guide that spans exactly the open section's rows, stopping at the last one (the gap to the next section lives on the group's margin, not the body's padding, or the line would dangle past its own content). The column's side padding is symmetric again — it was `0` left against `12px` right for a pass, which read as a misalignment rather than a decision and left the pills touching the page's left gutter.

- **`/admin` is a dashboard of what needs an admin, not an index of where things are.** With the sidebar above shipped, the hub's card grid became a second copy of the same inventory rendered beside the first — it answered "where do I go" for a question the column already answered better, and it carried no data at all. The page now opens on two zones of work. **Needs you** is decisions: entities awaiting verification, submissions needing review, corporate-memory items pending, authoring suggestions waiting to be replayed, open store-lint findings. **Needs fixing** is breakage: syncs failed in the last 24h, curated marketplaces with an error or no sync in 48h, tools erroring above 10% over 7d. Every one of these was already computable — the counts come from existing repository methods composed in a service layer, so nothing new landed in `src/repositories` and no DuckDB↔Postgres parity surface moved. Three rules make it stay readable, each pinned by `tests/test_admin_signals.py`. **A clear signal renders nothing** — resolvers return `None`, never a zero — so an instance with nothing pending gets one line saying so rather than a wall of zeros, which is the state you want to be in and the state that trains people to stop reading a dashboard when it is nine of them. **The count and its destination's filter come from one constant**: the submissions row builds its `?status=` from the same tuple its count queried, so the number here can never disagree with the row count on the page it opens — a guard asserts the derivation on the source, because on an empty instance the runtime check passes vacuously forever. And **a row must land somewhere the work can be done**, which is why two candidates are absent. Memory-domain suggestions have a complete admin API (`count-pending`, `approve`, `reject`) and no page that renders the queue. Dead-letter jobs looked like they had one — `/admin/activity` filtered to `job:` — until the filter was checked: those audit rows are admin-*triggered* scheduler runs, a different thing from the work-queue rows that exhaust their retries, and the page reads `resource_prefix` rather than the `resource` the link passed. Either way a row would have shown a number and then sent someone to a page not containing it, which spends the trust the dashboard needs to be worth opening. A guard now checks every filtered link's parameter against what its destination actually reads, since the count being right is exactly what makes a wrong destination hard to notice. The row inventory is a spec list (`app/web/admin_signals.py`) in the same idiom as `admin_nav.py`, not twelve hardcoded cards — new queues surface by adding an entry, and each resolver is individually isolated so one raising repo degrades to a single "could not be checked" row instead of 500-ing the page an admin opens *when something is already wrong*. A failed check is deliberately shown rather than hidden: an empty zone renders as "everything is running normally", and a silently dropped row would mean a broken check reads as all-clear. The **Needs fixing** zone is fetched after first paint from `GET /api/admin/dashboard/signals` and memoised for 60s, because those four signals read `sync_history`, `jobs` and `usage_events` — the tables that grow without bound — and serving them inline would have made `/admin` the slowest page in the product. The sidebar is now the **only** admin navigation, so everything the grid was the sole link to moved into it: Chat sessions (genuinely `require_admin`, but registered in `app/api/admin_chat.py`, which is why the nav's reverse guard had never seen it and now reads that module too), Studio (gated by `studio.enabled`, carried by the one conditional-item mechanism in the nav), and the three API-documentation links as a pinned footer strip — not an eighth section, since they are not `/admin` routes and an eighth section would break the deliberate seven-section IA. `tests/test_web_admin_hub.py` asserts each of those is still linked from `/admin`, because the way this change fails is not visibly: a surface that quietly becomes reachable by typed URL only.

### Changed

- **`/admin` (Overview) is the last admin surface to join the page pattern, and its setup chain now folds away.** The page carried twelve containers for two ideas: a bordered hero card above the content, a bespoke panel around the setup chain, and nine individually bordered signal rows with severity stripes down their left edges — nine tinted blocks reading as nine alarms of equal rank. It now opens on the plain `.page-header--plain` head every other admin page uses (the "ADMINISTRATION" eyebrow goes with the card: the rail says *Admin* two inches to the left), and its two standing verbs sit in a toolbar pinned right, where People puts `+ Invite person`. **The setup chain is the shared collapsible section card** (`.dsec`, the component `/me/profile` and `/me/activity` run), so it collapses on *any* instance rather than only a finished one — an admin who has read it twice can put it away, and the head still answers its own question while closed by carrying the fraction and the progress bar. It opens by default while there is work left and closed once there is not, still graduating to a summary row instead of deleting itself. **A step is one row.** It used to be a five-line block — title, state word, detail, a bordered "why" quote, its counts at 20px, a health line and a button row — so six steps filled two screens to carry six sentences; a finished step is now a single 40px line in a four-column grid (tick · name · the count that proves it · one quiet link), which puts every name, every sentence and every link on its own x and lets six rows read as a table of state without any of a table's rules. Only the step you are being sent to opens, with its *why*, the gap it owns and one filled CTA, so the page has exactly one focal point; `Do this next` is the one state word left on screen, because a tick already says "done" and a numeral already says "later". Dropped as noise: the per-step `ok` health lines (green reassurance under five finished steps teaches the eye to skip the slot where the amber one will appear) and the duplicate "could not be checked" line a failed step rendered twice. The signal zones lose their nine cards — **the list is the panel**, rows inside it are whitespace and a hairline, and severity moved into the element that was already each row's loudest mark, its count; an all-clear zone collapses to one quiet line rather than a green box saying nothing is wrong. The setup panel is 462px where it was over 900, and a fully-set-up instance's whole page now fits one screen. Same data (`resolve_journey`), same destinations, same class names for the rows `admin_dashboard.js` builds client-side; the glyph that replaced each state word is `aria-hidden` with the word kept for screen readers, and the `Do this next` label takes the row's own ink rather than the brand's because `--ds-primary-dark` measures 4.0:1 on the tinted row under navy and 4.3:1 under dark.
- **The user menu's theme control is one row instead of two.** It shipped as a stacked block — a small uppercase "THEME" caption over three full-width text buttons — which spent two rows and the menu's whole width on a three-way choice, and read as a form field dropped into a list of links. It is now a single row in the menu's own vocabulary: the label sits left at the same size and ink as "Logout" beside it, and the three choices sit opposite as an icon-only pill (sun · moon · monitor), each carrying its name as `aria-label` + `title` since the visible text is gone. Same markup contract as before — `id="themeToggle"`, `data-theme-choice`, `role="radiogroup"` with roving arrow keys — so `app.js` and `window.__agnesTheme` are untouched, and the markup now lives in ONE place (`_theme_toggle.html`, included by both chromes) rather than as two hand-kept copies in `_app_header.html` and `_app_rail.html` that could drift. Still built only from tokens that flip under `[data-theme="dark"]`, so the raised active chip inverts correctly in dark instead of needing a dark-specific rule; the icons are inline SVG on `currentColor` and sized from the stylesheet, not on the elements, so a page-level `svg` rule cannot blow the pill apart.

- **Users & Access is one section with three tabs, and a group's resource grants live on the group.** The admin nav carried four sibling destinations — Users, Groups, Resource access, Tokens — modelled on the underlying tables rather than on anything an admin does, so onboarding, offboarding and "why can this person see that?" each spanned three or four pages that linked in circles. The section is now one place: `/admin/users`, `/admin/groups` and `/admin/tokens` share a **People · Groups · Tokens** tab strip under a single "Users & Access" hero, and each tab stays a real URL, so deep links, bookmarks and the back button behave as they did. The change that actually removes a page is the grant editor: `resource_grants` keys on `group_id`, so the standalone matrix at `/admin/access` was the same editor reached through a second group picker, and it is now the group detail page's **Access** tab beside Members. A group is therefore whole on its own page — identity in the header, membership and authority in the two panes — and the old detail page's dead "Resource grants: manage on the dedicated page" panel (a count and a link out) is gone. `/admin/access` and `/admin/grants` 308 to `/admin/groups`, and with `?group=<id>` straight to that group's Access tab; the nav, the admin hub, the `g a` shortcut and the command palette all point at the new home. The tab strip is the shared `ds.tabs` macro, so the section inherits the same secondary-tab treatment as `/library` and `/chats`.

- **The user detail page answers "what do they have?" and "why?" without leaving it.** Offboarding needed three pages — deactivate here, drop group memberships here, then hunt the fleet-wide token list for that person's credentials — so the page grew an **Access tokens** section listing that user's personal access tokens with inline revoke (the same admin endpoint the fleet page uses; `/admin/tokens` keeps the cross-user view for incident response, and the Users row action now jumps to `#tokens` on the detail page rather than a pre-filtered fleet list). Each "granted via" group in Effective access is now a link into that group's Access tab, so the read path ("they can see this because of group X") reaches the write path in one click instead of landing on a different page.

- **`/admin/tables`' Manage-access deep link states which group it is granting to.** It jumped to the grant matrix with a resource filter pre-filled and no group chosen, leaving the operator on a page whose filter had no stated cause. It now lands on the group list with a "Granting access to `<resource>` — pick the group that should get it" banner, and carries the resource through to the chosen group's Access tab. The filter it pre-fills also matches on `resource_id`, which is what makes the deep link work at all: a table projects into the matrix as block `in.c-customer_360` plus name `customer_accounts`, so the registry id the link passes matched neither field and the old page silently rendered an empty result.

### Fixed

- **`instance.copyright` never reached the page, so every footer showed a fallback nobody configured — and the line it showed had no business being there.** The key is documented in `instance.yaml.example` and read by all six footer chromes as `config.INSTANCE_COPYRIGHT`, but `_config_proxy` hardcoded the attribute to `""` — there was no resolver behind it. The `or 'AI Harness'` fallback therefore fired on every page of every instance, printing the OSS default *deployment* name as if it were a copyright holder. There is now a `get_instance_copyright()` (`AGNES_INSTANCE_COPYRIGHT` env > `instance.copyright` YAML > `""`), registered in the `/admin/server-config` inventory. **Empty now means empty**: the footer omits the attribution rather than inventing one, which is what keeps the public distribution vendor-neutral. The six copies of the footer markup collapse into one `_footer.html`, and what it renders changed: `© {year} {name}` — which repeated the header brand and asserted a copyright the deploying org does not hold over software it did not write — becomes two-part attribution, the **product** on the left (`instance.brand`, default "Agnes", plus the running build) and the **operator** on the right ("Deployed by …", only when set). Self-hosted instances need the first far more than they needed the copyright: the build string is the answer to "what am I actually running", and it moves here from `_version_badge.html`, the fixed grey chip that sat at `z-index: 9999` over the content of every page. That chip stays on pre-auth `base_login.html`, which has no footer to carry it; its hover also stops printing `commit_sha` and `schema_version`, two fields `/api/version` has never returned and which read "undefined" for as long as the badge existed. Per-chrome footer CSS is preserved by passing `footer_class`, so `.footer`, `.cloud-chat-empty-foot`, the `.idx > footer` flush treatment and the rail detail-page rule all still land.

- **The rail's collapse/expand animation, in four places — three of them not animation bugs at all but state bugs wearing its clothes.** (1) The width transition was declared only on `.rail.rail-icon-mode`. A transition can only run when the rule carrying it still matches *after* the change, so clicking the toggle to EXPAND — which removes that class — dropped the transition in the same frame the width changed: collapsing glided, expanding snapped 56 → 240px. It now lives on the base `.rail`, with the two states overriding only the delay (0s closing, 120ms peeking open). (2) `body`'s clearance flipped 240px ↔ 56px with no transition of its own, so the page tore away from the column it belongs to — content landed 184px away a full 160ms before the rail arrived. Same duration token on both edges. (3) A collapse could land in a visibly broken state rather than an un-animated one: `#rail-toggle` is inside the rail and Cmd+\ can fire while the pointer rests on it, so `:hover` / `:focus-within` kept the peek open — measured on Cmd+\, `body` padding 56px against a rail still 240px wide, sitting on top of a page that had already reflowed, with nothing looking collapsed until the caller wandered off. Every peek rule is now gated on `:not(.rail-no-peek)`, which `rail_toggle.js` parks on the rail for exactly that window and releases the moment the pointer is genuinely outside it (read from the geometry, not from `mouseleave` alone — a collapse shrinks the rail out from under a stationary pointer) or the caller tabs to another row, where `:focus-within` is the only way they read the labels at all. (4) Peeking restored the conversation region's `display` but not the `opacity` the collapsed rule set alongside it, so the peeked rail laid Pinned/Recent out at full height and painted none of it: a ~500px void between New chat and Library, which is the whole reason to peek. Also retimed the label fade — `display` can't be transitioned, so labels are laid out at t=0 while the column is still 56px, and `.rail` is `overflow: visible` for its popovers, so on the width's own 120ms delay they became legible while the column was ~90px and painted *outside* the rail, over the page. One shared `--rail-peek-text-delay` token now trails the width instead, and keeps the label rules from drifting apart.

- **The peek now opens the column first and reveals its contents inside it — the sequence was inverted.** Delaying the label fade (previous entry) treated a symptom; the cause was that *everything except the width* changed discretely on the frame the pointer arrived. `display: none` held the labels and the conversation region out of flow, so peeking put them back at t=0 — an un-animatable relayout of the whole column, with text laid out in a 40px content box, before a single pixel of width had been gained. `justify-content: center → flex-start` snapped every icon sideways on that same frame. The toggle's `position: absolute → static` teleported it from the middle of the 56px strip to the right end of a column that had not widened yet, and it was already fully opaque when it did, because its reveal carried no delay of its own. The width was the only thing that animated, so content always arrived ahead of the panel meant to contain it. Now nothing discrete flips: hidden content is `visibility: hidden` and stays **in flow**, so hover changes nothing but the rail's width; the icons travel by `padding-left` (one formula — the strip's centre is 27.5px and content starts at 8px, so a row centres its icon at `19.5px - iconWidth/2`, over four icon sizes) instead of by an alignment switch; and the toggle is anchored to the row's right edge in both states, so it rides the widening edge rather than jumping to it. The reveal itself needs no timing trick to stay inside the panel: every label already clips itself (`overflow: hidden` + ellipsis + `nowrap`) and is squeezed to ~zero in the narrow column, so the growing width is what unveils the text, progressively — measured at 56/137/214/240px, the label's right edge tracks the rail's and never crosses it. That let the reveal move back from 220ms to 140ms, just behind the width's own 120ms anti-pass-through delay, so the column is visibly opening before anything appears in it without the reveal feeling held back. Closing reverses it on a shorter undelayed token: content is gone by ~80ms with the column still 69px wide, which is also why `visibility` is stepped *behind* the opacity it guards rather than with it. Two smaller things fell out of it: a keyboard caller skips the reveal delay outright, because to a `visibility: hidden` row 140ms is 140ms of not being focusable and a held Tab would have stepped straight past the conversation list; and `.app-avatar` needed a `flex-shrink: 0` floor in the rail, since keeping the profile label in flow gave the row an avatar + gap + label flex line against a ~38px box and the avatar was the only shrinkable item in it (measured 19px instead of 36px). Both settled states are unchanged to the pixel — every icon still centred at cx 27.5 collapsed, every row at the same y — which is the guard that made the refactor safe to do at all. Touch keeps the centred toggle: that one is visible at rest with no choreography to belong to.

- **A collapsed rail left the bottom-docked toolbar off-centre with its frosted band sliced up the left edge.** `.fbar-dock` (the /library and /chats filter toolbar), `.fbar-dock__veil` (its blur) and `.ch-bulk` (the chats bulk bar) are `position: fixed`, so they cannot inherit the `body` padding that clears the rail — each carried its own `left: 240px` instead. 240px is the EXPANDED rail's width and nothing else, so with the rail collapsed to 56px all three started 184px inside the content they belong to: the toolbar card centred 92px right of the column, and the veil's blur began 184px in, ending in a visible vertical cut across a strip of page it should have been frosting. The same literal also sat under a `max-width: 760px` escape hatch, which left the toolbar inset 240px from nothing across the whole 761–1024px band — where the rail is already a top bar with no left edge at all. rail.css now publishes `--rail-clearance` beside every `padding-left` that encodes that edge (240 / 56 / 0), all three consumers read it with a `0px` default — so a topnav-layout page needs no rail-specific rule and the breakpoint hatches are gone — and they transition on the same token as the rail, so the toolbar travels with a collapse instead of teleporting mid-animation. Guarded from both ends: one test asserts the variable and the padding agree in every block that declares either, another fails any CSS file except rail.css that positions with a literal 240px.

- **The Keboola semantic-layer sync imported one model per project and silently discarded the rest.** `_sync_one_source` took `models[0]`, logged `"Keboola project has N semantic models; using the first"`, and dropped every other model's metrics, glossary terms, datasets, relationships and constraints on the floor — a warning in the server log being the only trace, on a scheduled job nobody watches. One model per project is the assumption that is about to stop holding: Keboola's Data Catalog is moving to make the **semantic model** the unit of sharing (`keboola/ui#7739`), with a `targeted` Metastore scope so a model can be exposed to specific sibling projects (`keboola/go-monorepo#571`) — at which point a consumer project routinely carries its own model plus every linked one, and the linked ones are precisely the shared semantics Agnes exists to surface. All models are now imported. Three things this required beyond the loop: datasets, constraints and relationships resolve per model rather than from a merged pool, so a dataset in one model cannot silently satisfy a metric in another; the prune runs **once** against the union of every model's ids, since a per-model prune would delete the other models' rows on each pass; and every model is fetched before anything is written, so a Metastore failure partway through aborts with the tables untouched instead of letting the models that did load prune the rows of the model that did not. Two models publishing the same metric name (`revenue` in both a local and a linked model — cross-project identity is an open question upstream, not something Agnes can resolve) is counted as `skipped_conflict` and the first model processed keeps the name, matching the sticky-ownership rule already applied across sources; the within-run claim is tracked separately because the existing ownership gate deliberately permits a same-source write under a different id, which is right across runs (the project's model was recreated under a new uuid, and the stale row prunes) and wrong within one, where both rows would survive. Models are processed in sorted-uuid order rather than API order, because that tie-break decides a user-visible outcome and Metastore list order is not a documented guarantee — a flapping order would silently swap what `revenue` means between syncs.

- **The user detail page's Account section no longer sits on "Loading…".** `renderHeader()` writes the Active/Deactivated pill into `#status-pill`, but that element was lost when the page's header became the shared `_page_hero.html` include — so the lookup returned `null`, `renderHeader()` threw, and `renderAccountStatus()` (the very next call) never ran, leaving the section's status line permanently on its placeholder. The pill is back, next to the Account heading rather than in the hero, since Account is the state it describes.

- **Sections on the user detail page no longer race the timestamp helper.** `datetime.js` is loaded `defer`, so `window.AgnesTime` does not exist until parsing finishes, while the page's inline script starts its fetches during parse: a fast endpoint resolving first threw inside `fmtDate` and aborted that section's render mid-loop, leaving a populated header over an empty table with nothing in the console. The page now starts its loads on `DOMContentLoaded` (after deferred scripts run) and `fmtDate` falls back to the raw timestamp rather than taking a section down.

### Added
- **`agnes diagnose` now checks whether the analyst can actually reach their data.** Every check it ran asked the server about itself, so it reported `Overall: healthy` — including `[ok] data` — while a fresh analyst's tables were unreachable: the manifest listed a table, `agnes pull` had 403'd on the download, and nothing on the laptop said so. The analyst who hit this stopped trusting the command and went to raw `curl`. A new `local-data` check compares what the manifest offers against the parquets on disk and names the next step ("run `agnes pull` and read its output; a download that 403s means the table is not in your stack yet"). A workspace with nothing pulled yet stays `info` — a normal first run is not a broken instance — but a genuine shortfall reports `warning`, which is the severity the headline aggregation actually reads (`warn`, the setup command's vocabulary, is inert here and would have left the verdict on `healthy`, the exact failure the check exists to catch).
  Both halves of the comparison are read the way the rest of the CLI reads them, so the answer agrees with what `agnes pull` fetches rather than with what the server lists. **Offered** is the manifest's `tables` **dict** keyed by table id — the shape the server emits and `agnes pull` consumes — filtered through the same download-set rules: `query_mode='remote'` rows answer server-side and have no parquet at all, `server_only` rows have one that is never distributed, and when the manifest carries the typed `direct_tables` / `data_packages[].tables[]` sections those are the stack-scoped truth (the flat dict is gated by a check whose Admin short-circuit bypasses the stack, so for an admin it over-lists tables `agnes pull` deliberately never downloads). **Local** mirrors the DuckDB view rebuild, which is what decides whether `agnes query <table>` resolves: a partitioned table lives as a directory of parts under `server/parquet/<table_id>/` and counts as one table, where a top-level `*.parquet` glob missed it and told analysts to re-fetch data they already had.
### Fixed
- **`agnes diagnose`'s local-data check no longer reports green through a manifest it never read.** A 401/403/500 manifest response returns an ordinary error body with no `tables` key, which read as "the server offers nothing" — empty offered set, empty shortfall, `[ok] local-data` — straight through an auth outage; the fetch now `raise_for_status()`es into the could-not-compare branch, the same way `agnes pull`'s own manifest fetch treats non-2xx. And a relocated server crashed the whole command: `RedirectHardStop` derives from `BaseException` precisely so broad handlers can't eat it, and the manifest fetch was the one call in the command not shielded by name — so `agnes diagnose` exited 2 with empty output on exactly the deployment it exists to describe. The check now declines the comparison with an `info` row; the redirect verdict itself stays the `api` check's business. It also looked in the wrong directory on any machine where the data workspace is not the push anchor: it resolved via the `workspace_root` config key (the anchor `agnes push` and the session upload use), while every data command — `agnes pull`, `agnes query`, `agnes status`, `agnes disk-info` — resolves through `resolve_data_workspace()` (`AGNES_LOCAL_DIR` override → cwd if workspace-shaped → anchor), so with the override set, the analyst standing in another workspace, or a stale/unset anchor it reported a false shortfall — or a false "run `agnes init`" — about parquets sitting exactly where `agnes query` reads them; it now resolves the workspace the same way the data commands do. All three found by Devin Review on this PR.
### Internal
- **`_build_context` now composes `_chrome_ctx` instead of hand-copying its keys.** The two web-template-context builders in `app/web/router.py` each maintained their own list of chrome-level keys (nav, branding, theme, feature toggles) by hand, so every new chrome key gave its author a chance to forget one — the failure was silent because Jinja renders undefined as empty. This bug class had already fired three times (`can_chat`, `can_studio`, and `config`/`can_chat` again in #993/#995). `_chrome_ctx` is now the single owner of every chrome-level key; `_build_context` starts from it and layers only its own heavier, page-specific payloads (the setup-prompt clipboard script, `server_url`). A new chrome key now only needs to be added once. No behavior change: a drift-guard test (`test_build_context_is_a_superset_of_chrome_ctx`) pins that the two stay in lockstep going forward. Closes #996.

## [0.83.15] - 2026-08-14
### Added

- **Connector-catalogued attachments are now fetchable over the authenticated API.** The Jira connector downloads attachment binaries to the server and records where they landed (the `attachments` catalogue's `local_path`), but no client surface could fetch them — the only reader was a human with a shell on the host, neither RBAC-gated nor audited. `GET /api/attachments/{source}/{attachment_id}/download` + `agnes attachment get <source> <id> [-o <path>]` close that: a source declares which table catalogues its files, which columns carry the id and the path, and which directory is the permitted root (`src/attachment_sources.py`; `jira` is the first registered source), so a later connector that stores attachments registers a declaration and gets the route and the CLI command for free. RBAC is read access to the catalogue table (`can_access_table`, same gate as the parquet download), and a catalogue table marked `server_only` refuses with 403 `attachment_table_server_only` — its binaries stay on the server just as its parquet does (Devin Review on this PR); the catalogue's path value is contained under the source's permitted root before serving; misses stay distinguishable from denials (404 `attachment_not_found` / `attachment_not_stored` vs the RBAC 403) so a client can fall back to the upstream system's own API for exactly the rows the server never stored; and every fetch, granted or denied, lands in the audit log as `attachment.download` — refusals written as `denied`, the audit read layer's class for correct policy refusals, so they never inflate the Activity Center's error bucket (Devin Review on this PR). Deliberately a lazy per-id fetch, not manifest sync — nothing lands on an analyst's machine until someone asks for it. The backfill script's attachment downloader now publishes atomically (temp + `os.replace`) like the webhook path, and the streamed response is bounded at the size it advertises, so a concurrent writer can neither expose a torn file nor push the body past the declared Content-Length (Devin Review on this PR). Both publishers also pin the published file's mode to `0o660` explicitly — `os.replace` hands over the temp file's umask-derived mode, which under a restrictive deploy-time umask would leave the attachment unreadable to the serving process, while a world-readable `0o644` would both expose the bytes to every local account and collapse the POSIX-ACL mask on ACL-managed data dirs; `0o660` is the same group-rw pin the connector's issue-JSON writer already uses for exactly that reason; it assumes the connector's documented group/ACL storage setup — a serving process outside the backfill writer's group fails loudly (503 `attachment_unreadable` + a logged path), never silently, and the fix is aligning the groups, not widening the mode (Devin Review on this PR). A transient registry read failure now refuses the download with 503 `registry_unavailable` instead of proceeding with the `server_only` policy check silently skipped — bytes are never released by a gate that did not run, mirroring the parquet route's `distribution_check_unavailable` (Devin Review on this PR). Staging names carry a random component so two concurrent downloads of the same attachment (webhook threadpool, backfill workers) can never publish each other's half-written bytes, and a webhook that actually lands attachment files re-runs the incremental transform afterwards — the transform deliberately runs before the download (worker-timeout rationale), which would otherwise catalogue every freshly attached file with no stored path and 404 exactly the attachments users are most likely to fetch (Devin Review on this PR). That re-transform re-acquires the per-issue lock (the slow download itself stays outside it), so it can never publish a stale snapshot over a concurrent SLA-poll update that holds the same lock across its own write+transform (Devin Review on this PR). And a catalogue that cannot be OPENED or QUERIED refuses with 503 `catalogue_unavailable` instead of masquerading as `attachment_not_found` (or, for a failed open, escaping as an unaudited bare 500): only a genuinely absent view (declared but never synced) reads as a miss — a broken analytics attach or a declaration whose columns drifted from the connector's output must not send the client to the upstream API for rows the server actually has (Devin Review on this PR). The same misses-vs-malfunctions line runs through the filesystem open: a catalogued file the OS refuses to hand over (`EACCES`/`EIO`…, e.g. a serving process outside the `0o660` writer group) answers 503 `attachment_unreadable` with a warning log, never `attachment_not_stored` — only `ENOENT`/`ENOTDIR` reads as "no bytes here", so a misconfigured deployment cannot silently answer every request with "fetch it from the upstream system" while the outage looks like normal behaviour (Devin Review on this PR). The webhook downloader also gained the backfill's already-on-disk short-circuit (Jira attachment ids are immutable, so an existing `<id>_<name>` file is already the right bytes) and reports only NEWLY published files — without it every event re-fetched every attachment of the issue and the post-download re-transform ran on every event for any attachment-bearing issue, doubling webhook processing instead of firing only when a fresh file actually landed (Devin Review on this PR). Both exists-skips additionally require the on-disk size to match the size Jira reports — an existence-only skip would trust a file truncated by the pre-atomic writer (worker SIGKILL mid-write) and serve the short bytes with a self-consistent Content-Length forever; a size mismatch re-fetches and heals (Devin Review on this PR). And both publishers sweep dead `.tmp-*` staging files (older than an hour — the client itself times out at 60s) before staging: a SIGKILLed worker cannot unlink its staging file, the retry mints a fresh random name, and nothing else touches hidden names, so each interrupted download would otherwise leak up to the attachment size cap forever (Devin Review on this PR).

### Fixed

- **Five live pages were unreachable under the rail chrome** (`ui_layout: rail` — the redesign's default). The rail renders *instead of* the topnav header, no fallback, and it shipped without links the topnav carries: **My connections** (`/me/connections` — per-user MCP OAuth self-service; restored to the account menu), **Memory** (`/corporate-memory`; restored as a nav destination — the first rail had it, the redesign dropped it), and **Apps** (`/apps`, same `data_apps.enabled` gate as the topnav). **Marketplace** and **Data Packages** (`/catalog`) were retired from the rail deliberately, onto in-page paths that were never built — the Library "+ Add" menu now really carries both ("Install from the marketplace", "Add shared data & recipes"). With Memory back in the nav, a memory-domain detail's back link under `rail` returns to the `/corporate-memory` browse again (the Library detour existed only because that page was unreachable; `?source=library` arrivals still return to the Library). Guarded from here on: the existing `/me/connections` nav test now runs over both chromes, and a new static parity guard (`tests/test_web_nav_user_parity.py`, sibling of the admin one) fails on any topnav-linked user page the rail cannot reach.
- `agnes admin sessions download` raised `TypeError` before the request ever left: it passed `stream=True` through `api_get` into `httpx.Client.get()`, which has no such argument. The flag is dropped (`api_get` buffers the response body regardless); the new `agnes attachment get` never carried it.

- **The in-chat app preview no longer spins forever after the app is up.** The preview credential was minted as a cookie scoped `Path=/apps/<slug>/`, but the holding page polls `/api/data-apps/<slug>/readiness` — a path that scoping does not cover, so the browser never attached it, the poll 401'd, and the page's `catch` swallowed it. The cookie is now `Path=/` — and because that narrow path was also, silently, the only thing keeping two apps' cookies out of one browser jar slot, the cookie's NAME is now per-app (`adp_preview_<slug>`). Without that, previewing a second app overwrote the first app's credential, and since the slug pin lives in the token scope the survivor authorized nothing for the other app: its poll 401'd forever while the app was healthy — two chat tabs with two previews is the ordinary case, not a corner. Found by Devin Review on this PR. Neither change widens authority: the pin stays in the token's own scope rather than in the cookie, and `HttpOnly` / `SameSite=Lax` are untouched. The proxy still accepts the old bare cookie name, so a preview already open across the upgrade keeps working for the rest of its token's TTL. Also normalises a dotted `data_apps.subdomain_base` before building the CORS origin regex (a value written `.apps.example.com` produced a pattern matching nothing, leaving the poll CORS-blocked on a subdomain the middleware would happily serve) and narrows that regex to a single label, matching what the middleware actually routes.

- **One badly-timed request permanently bricked a healthy hosted app.** The proxy latched `state = "error" / "container unreachable"` on a single refused connection, and nothing ever cleared it: the `error` branch only replays the stored detail and never re-checks, so the only recovery was a redeploy. The window that triggers it is not narrow — a first deploy clones the repo, runs `npm install` and builds before anything listens on 8888 (~90s for a real dashboard), while the row is marked `running` the moment the runner *accepts* the container, not when it serves. Watched end to end on a running instance: the app finished building and answered 200 inside its own container while Agnes returned `app_error` to every caller, and the chat agent that had just built it was told its app was unreachable. The proxy now asks the runner what is actually true before latching. A container that is up but not yet listening is *starting*, and gets the same holding page a sleeping app gets; only a container that is genuinely stopped or gone latches an error, and the detail now names the state the container was actually in. When the runner itself is unreachable the row is left alone — guessing `error` there blames the app for the sidecar's outage, and the guess would stick.

- **On subdomain-served instances the holding page never reloaded itself, and a Library with many apps hid some of your own.** Two more from review. (1) `DataAppSubdomainMiddleware` rewrites *every* path on `<slug>.<base>` to `/apps/<slug>/…` with no `/api` carve-out, so the holding page's relative readiness poll came back as the holding page's own HTML: `r.json()` threw, the `catch` swallowed it, and the page spun forever while the app was already up. The poll is now absolute against the configured public URL when the request arrived on an app subdomain, and stays relative otherwise (no host pinned into the page where none is needed; no configured public URL keeps the previous behaviour rather than guessing an origin). A carve-out in the middleware would have been the wrong fix — an app may serve its own `/api/*`, as the scaffolded dashboard does, so diverting those to Agnes would break the app being hosted. (2) The Library listing took the repository's default `limit=1000`, applied *before* the ownership/grant filter, so on an instance with more apps than that a caller's older apps silently vanished from the one page the rail chrome offers to reach them. Now `limit=100000`, matching every sibling listing in the same function.

- **The holding page's poll was refused for the very credential the page is served to.** `data_app_waking.html` polls `GET /api/data-apps/{slug}/readiness` — which is also what flips a woken app to `running` — but that endpoint resolved its caller through `get_current_user`, which rejects the `data-app-preview:<slug>` scoped token the in-chat preview iframe carries and which the proxy itself accepts. So a preview iframe got a holding page whose poll 401'd forever and never noticed the app come up. Pre-existing for the `sleeping`/`deploying` branches; the starting-app branch added above reaches it far more often, which is what makes serving the page and refusing its only poll half a fix. Readiness now resolves through the proxy's own chain, with the token's scope pinned to the slug being polled — a token minted for another app still gets nothing. Two visible consequences: the endpoint no longer declares an `authorization` header parameter in the API schema (it accepts more than one credential shape now), and because the auth no longer sits in a `Depends` chain the route needs an entry in `tests/test_route_auth_guard.py::_EXEMPT` — added with the reason, alongside the existing entries for handlers that authenticate in their body. Unauthenticated callers still get 401, and the preview token stays pinned to the slug being polled.

- **The Library both listed your apps and told you they were coming.** The Files band carried a "Data apps coming soon" badge whose tooltip said hosted apps "will appear here" and there is "nothing to do yet" — false on both counts once apps got their own section, and a direct contradiction on one page. Retired, which is what the badge was built to do: its own test docstring says it "deletes itself when the kind ships". The mechanism stays for the next kind. Separately, the start-grace window measured from `last_deploy_at`, which only `POST /{slug}/deploy` writes — the auto-wake path never refreshes it, so a woken app's grace was computed from a deploy that could be days old and the first refused connection after a wake would latch instead of holding. It now takes the later of that and `updated_at`, which the wake's own state write moves, rather than recording a deploy that never happened.

- **Two more from review, both in code added by this PR.** The new Apps band was told to use a colour named `app` that the palette never defined — and a missing `--ds-kind-*` does not fall back to a default: `library.html` sets the accent inline as `var(--ds-kind-{{ sec.kind }})`, so an undefined name is invalid at computed-value time and the heading, count, edge stripe and icon tiles all render colourless. The token pair now exists in the default theme and is re-pointed onto `--ds-resource-app-*` in paper (light and dark), like every sibling kind. The hue was picked by measurement, not taste: the first choice was an indigo that sat **dE 19 from plugin and dE 20 from agent**, while the tightest pair the existing eight kinds tolerate is 17 — a fourth entry in the blue-violet region is how a categorical palette stops being categorical. App takes the one hue the family had not spent, forest green, at dE 33 from its nearest neighbour and 6.5:1 on white, which the family's `-ink` contract requires, and a guard asserts every kind in `_SECTION_KINDS` has a **base** colour. The first version of that guard was itself a false green — it matched the paper alias and passed with the token deleted — which is why it is pinned to the literal definition. Separately, the start-grace window read naive DB timestamps as UTC (the codebase's standing convention, and containers run UTC); the comparison is now symmetric so a clock offset in either direction still reads as recent for the same span, rather than only one direction being survivable.
