- **Three follow-ups from review on this change set.** (1) **The Library listing leaked every app in the instance to an admin.** It filtered with `data_apps._can_view`, which short-circuits True for any admin — while `library_page`'s own docstring says the opposite: "Deliberately NOT admin god-mode — an admin still sees their own Library, not every item in the instance". So an admin's Library listed other people's private apps, labelled "Shared with you" with owner "Your workspace", a claim that is false for an app they hold no grant on. Scope is now ownership ∪ grant, with the grant set fetched once instead of two DB lookups per app per render. Reuse was right for the row shape and the draft rule and wrong for the scope: the two surfaces answer different questions. (2) **"Starting" is now time-bounded.** The runner reports `running | paused | stopped | absent`, so a container whose app process died or wedged *without the container exiting* still reads `running` — and the fix above would have served it a holding page forever, trading a permanent latch for a permanent spinner. Past a 7-minute grace measured from the last deploy, a live-but-silent container is recorded as an error that says `container not listening` rather than blaming its state; with no usable timestamp the answer is "not provably still starting", which fails toward the diagnosable outcome. `paused` now triggers a wake instead of latching — it is the pause-mode sleep state, not a fault. (3) The Apps band had no label, hint, glyph or ordering entry, so it fell back to a generic accent, sorted to the end, and `/library?section=data_app` could never open it.

- **A hosted app that fails its first boot can never restart.** Data-app containers run under `restart_policy=unless-stopped`, but the runtime image's entrypoint clones the repo into `/app` on every start, and that clone fails once `/app` is populated. So the first boot's *real* error — in the run that surfaced this, five TypeScript errors from `tsc` — scrolls away behind an endless `fatal: destination path '/app' already exists and is not an empty directory`, exit 128, forever (16 restarts before it was noticed). The restart policy never provided the resilience it promises: because the clone is not idempotent, *no* restart of a data-app container can succeed, whatever killed it. `data_app_logs` — the only debugging surface an agent has for its own app — therefore reports a cause that is never the cause. Left as a known limitation for now rather than silently changing the policy: the honest fix is for the entrypoint to be restart-safe, which lives in the runtime image, and the deploy path already recreates the container from scratch so a redeploy recovers. Recorded here so the next person reading that log knows the clone error is a symptom.

## [0.83.14] - 2026-08-14
### Added
- **`system.duckdb.rolling-snapshot/` — a rolling-refreshed recovery snapshot, refreshed independently of migration transitions.** `system.duckdb.pre-migrate` is captured once per migration and never touched again, so as a recovery aid it goes stale within hours of normal operation — every row written since the last migration is lost on a WAL-recovery restore (#379). `refresh_rolling_snapshot` (`src/db.py`) now maintains a second, rolling-refreshed artifact on a configurable cadence (`backups.rolling_snapshot_interval_hours`, default 6h, `0` disables — see `config/instance.yaml.example`): a `CHECKPOINT` followed by a logical `EXPORT DATABASE (FORMAT PARQUET, COMPRESSION ZSTD)` into a tmp directory, atomically swapped into place only once the export fully succeeds. It runs over the app's own long-lived `system.duckdb` connection on the existing periodic-checkpoint tick (#710) — never a second connection to the file — and is a no-op on a Postgres-state instance. `system.duckdb.pre-migrate` itself is unchanged: it stays the single-file artifact the WAL-recovery auto-restore path (`_try_open_system_db`) reads directly. The rolling snapshot is a manual-recovery aid (`IMPORT DATABASE`) documented as a new "Option A2" in `docs/runbooks/wal-recovery.md` (#380).

  The swap can never leave the instance with *no* snapshot, which is the one outcome a recovery mechanism exists to prevent. The last good copy is moved aside to `.prev` and deleted only once a snapshot is confirmed present under the final name; if the swap fails and the restore that puts the old one back fails too, the copy at `.prev` is preserved — rather than the restore's error escaping past the documented `False` return and the cleanup then destroying it — and the next refresh reclaims it under the documented name before doing anything else, including before its own export (which may itself fail). Option A2 in the runbook names `.prev` as a fallback for an operator who looks during that window. Found by Devin Review on this PR.

  The export is also owner-only, like every other derivative of `system.duckdb`: it is a full logical copy of the state DB — argon2 password hashes, personal-access-token rows, the audit log, vault rows — and `EXPORT DATABASE` would otherwise write it under the process umask (directory `0o755`, files `0o644`), making it the one world-readable copy next to `.broken.*` and the discarded WAL, both already `0o600`. The scratch directory is created `0o700` *before* the export rather than tightened after it, so the parquet is never exposed even for the export's duration, and each exported file is `0o600`. Found by Devin Review on this PR.

  **A shutdown mid-export no longer risks closing `system.duckdb` out from under the refresh's own cursor.** `refresh_rolling_snapshot` now bails out immediately, before touching the filesystem, once the lifespan has called `begin_shutdown()` — checked again right before `EXPORT DATABASE` itself, in case shutdown starts mid-`CHECKPOINT` — and while an export cursor is running, `close_system_db()` interrupts it and waits (bounded) for it to unwind before closing the connection instead of closing straight through it. Previously, a `to_thread_drain_on_cancel` budget exhausted by a multi-second `EXPORT DATABASE` abandoned that thread and let the lifespan proceed straight to `close_system_db()`, which took no lock at all — closing the parent connection while the export's child cursor was still executing, the exact wedge that drain helper exists to prevent. Found by Devin Review on this PR.

  **EXPORT/IMPORT fidelity for the DuckDB FTS index schemas (`fts_main_knowledge_items`, `fts_main_glossary_terms`) is now verified, and the boot-time index rebuild the runbook leans on actually covers both tables it claims to.** A new test builds real FTS artifacts (`PRAGMA create_fts_index` via `src/fts.py`) over `knowledge_items` and `glossary_terms` before running `refresh_rolling_snapshot`, and confirms both that the export succeeds and that the core tables round-trip through a fresh `IMPORT DATABASE`. Restoring those schemas' `match_bm25` macro can trigger DuckDB's extension auto-install, and on a host with no network access to the extension repository that failing statement aborts the *entire* `IMPORT DATABASE` (it replays `schema.sql` as one transaction) — `docs/runbooks/wal-recovery.md` Option A2 now documents a strip-the-FTS-lines workaround alongside the existing recipe. Separately, `app/main.py`'s boot-time FTS rebuild — the safety net the runbook now points operators at — previously only rebuilt the `knowledge_items` index; `glossary_terms` never got the same startup pass and depended entirely on its own next write to recover its ranking. It now rebuilds both. Found by Devin Review on this PR.

  **Four more hardenings from the same review.** A non-finite configured cadence (YAML `.nan`/`.inf` for `backups.rolling_snapshot_interval_hours`) no longer defeats the gates — `.nan` made the full export run on every tick and `.inf` silently disabled the safeguard forever; both now fall back to the 6h default with a warning, matching the sibling checkpoint-interval knob. The refresh is serialized against itself (`try`-acquire, second overlapping call skips) — the export machinery is single-slot (one published cursor, one fixed scratch path), so an overlapping caller could clear the first run's in-flight state and delete its half-written export. An export still executing when shutdown *begins* is now interrupted immediately by `begin_shutdown()` itself rather than only by `close_system_db()` much later — the checkpoint loop is the first task the lifespan cancels, and draining its multi-second export would otherwise consume the whole shared drain budget, leaving the canary/worker drains with none. And `close_singleton_connections()` (the migrator-subprocess handoff, which also closes the singleton) gained the same interrupt-and-wait handshake as `close_system_db()`. The WAL-recovery runbook's restore recipes (Options A and A2) now `CHECKPOINT` and close the recovered file before the single-file `cp`, so imported rows can't be left behind in a companion `.wal` the copy misses. Found by Devin Review on this PR.

- Jira issues with more than 100 comments no longer lose their newest ones. Jira's issue endpoint embeds `fields.comment.comments` capped at 100, oldest-first, so any issue over that count arrived missing its newest comments — and because every later full-refetch re-hits the same cap, the gap never healed, it only widened. The fetch layer now compares the embedded count against `fields.comment.total` and, when short, pages through `GET /issue/{key}/comment` for the remainder before the issue reaches transform. Fixed for both ingestion paths — the batch/full extract and the webhook full-refetch — via one shared completion step. A residual shortfall after completion (comments legitimately added mid-fetch, or a page request failing) is logged as a warning rather than silently swallowed. Two hardenings from Devin Review on this PR: a page request that itself fails mid-pagination (5xx / connection error) now marks the issue `_comments_incomplete` so the incremental transform preserves the previously stored comment thread instead of overwriting it with the known-truncated partial list — the comments upsert is an issue-scoped delete-then-insert, so a transient failure on a refetch could otherwise regress a complete stored thread down to whatever was fetched before the failure. The two paged requests (embed + `GET .../comment`) are also de-duplicated by comment id (first occurrence wins) before storing, so ordering drift or a comment added/removed between the two calls can no longer produce duplicate rows.

- Three more hardenings from Devin Review on the same PR, all about what the `_comments_incomplete` marker means where it is read. **The marker no longer costs an issue all of its comments in a full rebuild**: `transform_all` writes the monthly parquets from scratch, so "skip the write and preserve what is there" preserves nothing — it wrote ZERO comment rows for a marked issue, strictly worse than the partially-fetched list its JSON already carries. The preserve semantics now belong to the incremental delete-then-insert path alone (`preserve_on_incomplete`, defaulting to the safe behaviour); the batch rebuild opts out and keeps the partial thread. The incremental path draws the same line one step finer: it preserves when there are stored rows for that issue and writes the partial list when there are none, because on an issue's first fetch the marker would otherwise mean no comment row is ever written — the marker lives in the raw JSON, so every later re-transform reads it again. **The marker also stopped being permanent**: the backfill skips any issue whose JSON exists, and `--skip-existing` is the default, so a marked issue was never re-fetched and never healed. A marked JSON — or one that cannot be read at all — is now exactly the case that gets re-fetched. **And comment pagination honours `429 Retry-After`** like the issue and remote-link fetchers already did: with four parallel workers and an extra request per >100-comment issue, rate limiting is the batch path's likeliest failure, and without a retry it routinely left issues marked incomplete. Bounded at three retries, the wait capped at 300s (an hours-long `Retry-After`, or an HTTP-date the old `int()` would have crashed on, must not park a worker).

- **A webhook whose refetch fails no longer lets the embedded payload shorten a stored comment thread.** When `fetch_issue` returns None, `process_webhook_event` falls back to the issue payload the webhook carried — which never passes through the pagination-completion step, so its `fields.comment.comments` is whatever Jira chose to embed. The incremental upsert being an issue-scoped delete-then-insert, that shorter list replaced a complete stored thread. The fallback payload is now treated as authoritative for comments only when it demonstrably carries the whole thread (embedded count ≥ `fields.comment.total`); otherwise — including when it carries no comment field at all, which is not evidence that the issue has no comments — it is marked `_comments_incomplete` and the stored rows are preserved. Pre-existing behaviour, fixed here because it is the same failure this PR exists to prevent. Found by Devin Review on this PR.

- **A rate-limited webhook could freeze the entire app for up to 15 minutes — chat, admin, every other request.** The comment-pagination retry added above calls `time.sleep()` on a 429, up to three retries capped at 300s each, and nothing moved that work off the webhook's request handler: it ran straight on the asyncio event loop. `process_webhook_event` is now dispatched via `run_in_threadpool`, and the webhook's own issue refetch passes a zero-retry comment budget of its own — a 429 there marks the issue `_comments_incomplete` immediately instead of sleeping at all, healed later by a backfill run's `_needs_refetch`. The batch path is unaffected and keeps its generous retry budget, since it was never on a request thread. Found by Devin Review on this PR.

- **The batch backfill's per-issue rate-limit retry no longer opens one `httpx.Client` per retry without closing the previous one.** Handing the open client to comment-pagination required moving the success branch inside the `with httpx.Client(...)` block; the 429 branch's retry was left recursing from inside that same block, so N consecutive rate limits held N open clients and stack frames, with no cap. The retry is now a bounded loop (five attempts) that closes each client before sleeping and opening the next. Found by Devin Review on this PR.

- **`--skip-existing` no longer opens and parses every existing issue's full JSON just to decide whether to skip it.** At six-figure issue counts with `fields=*all` payloads running hundreds of KB each, that was tens of GB of reads on every backfill run. A sidecar marker file next to the issue JSON — written and cleared alongside it — now carries the `_comments_incomplete` signal, so the skip check costs a single `stat()` again; `--dry-run`'s "already downloaded" counters use the same decision, where they previously ignored the marker and under-reported what a real run would re-fetch. Found by Devin Review on this PR.

- **A `_comments_incomplete` payload with no parseable `created_at` — realistic via the webhook fallback path — no longer risks writing its partial comment list into the wrong month.** The preserve-vs-write decision probes the monthly comments partition the issue's `created_at` falls in, and a missing `created_at` defaulted that probe to the current month. An issue whose real thread lives in an earlier month would read the (empty) current month as "nothing stored" and write the partial list there, splitting the same issue's comments across two partitions that double-count once views glob `month=*`. The probe now treats an unparseable `created_at` the same as "something is already stored" and preserves the existing rows instead. Found by Devin Review on this PR.

### Fixed

- **Postgres's corporate-memory duplicate/lexical scan now finds items moved between domains by the admin multi-domain editor.** `list_by_domain` (used by the verification detector's lexical-similarity fallback) read a `knowledge_items.domain` scalar column that only ever reflected the domain passed to `create`/`update` — a multi-domain re-assignment through `/api/admin/...` (`domain_ids`, `MemoryDomainsRepositoryPg.replace_domains_for_item`) touches only the `knowledge_item_domains` junction, so a moved item stayed invisible under its new domain and kept surfacing under the one it left. It now resolves the slug through `memory_domains` and joins the junction, matching the DuckDB repo (#1017). `find_duplicate_candidates_by_entities` (the entity-overlap duplicate finder, the detector's other candidate source) had the same scalar-column read and is fixed the same way, so both finders now agree on where a moved item lives (Devin Review on #1290).
- **A one-time Postgres data migration backfills `knowledge_item_domains` for items created before the junction write path existed.** PG's `create`/`update` didn't start writing the junction until #1263 — any row created between the junction table's introduction and that fix carries a scalar `domain` with no junction row, so the two junction-only reads above would otherwise still miss it. DuckDB needs no equivalent step: its own junction-introducing migration (v49, `src/db.py::_v51_to_v52`) backfilled every historical value in the same migration that dropped the scalar column, so no such gap ever existed there (Devin Review on #1290).
- **That backfill files a capitalised legacy domain under the real domain instead of minting a junk one.** Postgres' `regexp_replace` is case-sensitive, so `[^a-z0-9]` matches uppercase letters too — and the slug formula ran it on the RAW value, lower-casing only afterwards. A perfectly ordinary pre-#1263 `domain` of `'Finance'` (that write path did no slug validation at all, so any free-text string is in scope) normalized to `'-inance'`: the migration created a `memory_domains` row for it and filed every such item under that, leaving the item invisible under the domain it actually belongs to while a junk domain nobody asked for showed up in the admin's domain list. `lower()` now runs inside the regexp in all three normalization expressions. Because normalization is many-to-one, the domain-creating step now also groups on the resulting slug rather than the raw value: `'Finance'`/`'finance'` and `'q team'`/`'q-team'` collapse to one row each, where per-raw-value inserts would have pushed rows sharing a primary key through a single statement and aborted the migration. Found by Devin Review on #1290; the existing test used only a lowercase value, which is why it passed.
- **The Postgres admin corporate-memory list, search and counts follow domain moves too.** Third read path of the same divergence class as the two finders above: `list_items`, `search` and `count_items` filtered `domain` on the stale scalar column, so the admin item list, search and pagination counts showed a moved item under the domain it left and never under the one it joined — and an unknown slug matched raw scalar values instead of returning nothing. All three now resolve the slug through `memory_domains` and EXISTS-join the junction, with the DuckDB repo's unknown-slug → empty/zero short-circuit, and cross-engine contract tests pin every path on both backends (Devin Review on #1290, third round).
- **That backfill also survives padded or punctuated legacy values.** The slug formula collapsed non-alphanumeric runs to `-` without trimming the edges, so `' Finance '` normalized to `'-finance'` and `'(Ops)'` to `'-ops-'` — never matching the real domain, minting a junk grantable one instead, and a whitespace-only value (which passes the `<> ''` guard) minted a domain named `'-'`. Both steps now `btrim` the edge separators with one shared expression (they must stay identical or the join misses the row the mint step created), values that normalize to nothing are excluded outright, and the display name is whitespace-trimmed (Devin Review on #1290, third round).
- **That backfill no longer undoes domain moves an admin made in the item editor.** It filed every item under whatever its legacy `domain` scalar said, including items whose memberships an admin had already deliberately re-pointed — and since the admin editor's `domain_ids` chip-input (the only UI path to an item's domains since #1263) writes the junction and deliberately never touches the scalar, an item created under `q-team` and moved to `ops` carries a stale `q-team` forever. So a Postgres upgrade re-filed it under `q-team`: the move silently undone, restoring exactly the listing and grant reach the admin had removed it from, and re-asserting the stale-scalar membership this whole PR exists to stop honouring. The junction is authoritative now — both migration steps touch only items with **no** junction row at all, so an item anyone has spoken for is left exactly as it stands. The domain-minting step is scanned over that same cohort, so a stale scalar naming a domain that no longer exists can no longer conjure it back as a grantable, browsable entity. What remains genuinely undecidable is stated in the migration's own docstring rather than papered over: for an item with a non-empty scalar and zero junction rows, nothing in the data separates "never migrated" (the cohort the migration is for) from "an admin emptied it" or "its only domain was hard-deleted" — the clear path deletes the rows and writes nothing back, so all three end in identical state, and skipping the ambiguous set would not be conservative, it would be deleting the migration. The backfill therefore runs but stamps `added_by`/`created_by` = `migration_0062` on everything it writes, which makes the write attributable and lets `downgrade()` take back exactly its own rows and no others — a one-command undo in place of a silent, permanent clobber. Found by Devin Review on #1290.

### Added

- A sync that actually syncs ≥1 table now publishes a `sync_completed` event to every active user's desktop notification channel (`app.notifications.publish_notification` → the existing `notify:{user}` WebSocket), so a connected desktop client hears about fresh data without polling. The payload follows the existing notification producers' contract — the event kind rides in `kind` (`type` is reserved by the delivery envelope), with a renderable `title`/`message` plus `source`, `table_count`, and the run outcome (`status: "ok" | "partial"` + `error_count`); a run with per-table failures that still synced something announces `partial`, not an unqualified success. The event is scoped to the tables THIS run actually synced, not the orchestrator's full rebuild result (which re-attaches every table from every prior sync) — a scheduled tick where nothing was due sends no notification at all, instead of re-announcing the whole instance's tables on every tick (Devin review). The count is restricted to tables whose data this run actually wrote: a `materialized` or `remote` row named in a scoped `POST /api/sync/trigger?tables=…` is never counted (the extractor skips the former and only creates a view for the latter), and a partial extractor run whose per-table stats could not be recovered claims none of its tables rather than announcing the failed ones as refreshed (Devin review). Partial step toward #412 (`agnes watch`): the CLI side is not shipped — the notifications WebSocket only accepts a `DESKTOP_JWT_SECRET`-signed token from the interactive desktop-app pairing flow, which analyst CLI PATs/JWTs cannot obtain.

## [0.83.13] - 2026-08-13
### Added

- **Jira tickets can be joined to organizations on ids rather than names.** `issues` gained `organization_ids` (a JSON array — the Jira field is multi-valued), and a new current-state `organizations` table maps each id to the organization's current name plus whichever detail fields the operator names in `JIRA_ORG_DETAIL_FIELDS` (e.g. `38:crm_account_id` — detail ids are per-instance, so there are no defaults). Previously only ingest-time name strings were available, so renaming an organization orphaned its old tickets from any exact-name join. The table refreshes daily via a new `jira-org-refresh` job kind (scheduler row at 05:00); a manual run is `python -m connectors.jira.organizations` (`--dry-run`, `--force`). The refresh refuses to publish on states indistinguishable from data loss — failed or empty enumeration over an existing table, an unreadable baseline, a sweep that would remove most existing rows — and a per-organization failure carries the previous row forward; the connector README tabulates the refusal reasons and `--force` clears the two that never self-clear. `extract_init` now supports flat (unpartitioned) tables and upserts `_meta` rows so tables added after an instance's `extract.duckdb` was created still reach the catalog; `migrate_flat_to_hive` only migrates real `YYYY-MM` month files. The profiler catalog gains `jira_organizations` and the `jira_issues.organization_ids` relationship, and the legacy Data Broker `sync_jira.sh` creates the view. On existing installs, partitions written before this change read NULL in `organization_ids` — re-running the batch transform backfills them from the stored raw JSON with no re-fetch (command in the connector README).

### Internal

- **CI now runs the connector test suites.** `pytest tests/` never reached `connectors/`, where every connector keeps its tests beside the code (`connectors/jira/tests/`, ...) — 138 tests that ran only on developer machines, including the whole failure-semantics surface of the Jira connector, so no regression in them could ever fail a build. The shard job now runs `tests/ connectors/`, and the connector tests' measured `.test_durations` entries ship with the change so they shard like any other test. Regeneration command in the workflow comment is updated to match.

## [0.83.12] - 2026-08-13
### Fixed

- **A redirect no longer kills `agnes diagnose` — the command whose whole job is to tell you what is wrong.** Measured against a real relocated deployment: an unreachable server produces exit 0 and the full JSON checklist with an `api: error` row, while a server answering `308` produced exit 2, empty stdout and not a single check. The shared HTTP client refuses a redirect from an httpx *response event hook* and ended the process right there with `sys.exit(2)`, deep inside somebody else's `api_get(...)`. `SystemExit` derives from `BaseException`, so it walks straight through `except Exception` — which is how it voided the two callers built precisely to survive a failed request: `diagnose`, which records a row per failed check, and `agnes update`, whose `_run_step` exists so one bad step cannot abort a convergence run and which therefore died before writing its report. Both now handle it, and it is delivered as `RedirectHardStop` rather than a process exit.

  **Handling is opt-in by name, and that is the design.** `RedirectHardStop` also derives from `BaseException`, so no broad `except Exception` can take it: a command that has not written `except RedirectHardStop` behaves exactly as before — same `error: …` text on stderr, same exit code 2, pinned by a test that drives the real `main()` rather than a copy of its handler. The first version of this change made it an ordinary exception instead, which fixed the two aggregators by exposing the stop to every broad handler in the CLI, and cost more than it bought: `agnes diagnose system` printed `Cannot reach server: <…answered HTTP 308…>`, a heading contradicting its own body and the precise lie this work exists to remove, while `query`, `pull` and `chat` relabelled it and exited 1 instead of 2 — with `chat` keeping the REPL alive so every later turn hit it again. Found by Devin Review on this PR; that list is now a test class. The opt-in is scoped to the reachability probe for the same reason: `diagnose` asks `/api/health` and then, best-effort, `/api/health/detailed`, and a redirect answered by only the second one (a proxy rewriting some paths) would otherwise unwind past that best-effort handler and file a second `api` row saying `error` beside the `ok` one already there — telling the reader both at once.

  The neighbouring **version floor stays an unconditional exit**, deliberately: a redirect means one request went nowhere, while a version floor means the server has refused this CLI outright, and making it catchable had `agnes update` file it as one row and carry on running every remaining convergence step against that server. Hard stops are also still **not** forwarded to telemetry — the old form raised `SystemExit`, which that wrapper never reported, and a structural fix must not quietly open a new reporting stream. Found while verifying the moved-server work end to end, not by the unit tests: the suite asserted that the hook exits, which is the mechanism, and never that a caller could survive it.
- **`agnes self-upgrade` went silent against a moved server — the one command run to repair a stale install.** Measured against the real relocated hostname: the plain form printed nothing and exited 0, so the caller could not tell the upgrade had not happened, and `--force` reported `cannot reach <old>/cli/latest` for a server that answers `308` with a `Location` header. `cli/update_check.py::_fetch_latest` calls `raise_for_status()`, which does not treat 3xx as an error, then `.json()` on a redirect's empty body; the exception is swallowed into `None`, and `_resolve_info` maps that to "probe failed". #1266 taught both HTTP clients and the setup-token exchange to name the new address, but this path reaches the server through neither. A redirect is now its own verdict, diagnosed by a re-probe that runs **only** after the normal probe already came back empty — so the happy path pays nothing — and worded by the same `cli/server_moved.py` the other callers use, so the three cannot drift. Every redirect counts, not only a cross-host move: a same-origin bounce (an SSO proxy answering `302 /login`) is equally a check that did not happen, and `cannot reach` is equally untrue of it — what differs is the remedy, which the shared classifier already picks. `--check-only` reports it too and exits 1, where it swallows every other transport verdict into exit 0; its help text now names that second case rather than promising exit 1 means `outdated` alone.

  `--quiet` stays silent — that is the SessionStart hook, whose non-noisy contract (#601) outranks this diagnosis — but it now records the failure, which the first draft did not. Without that the hook would fail identically on every shell, forever, with nothing ever said: the counter behind the "self-upgrade has failed N times" warning (#478) is the only channel that path has, and the analyst would sit on the stale CLI this command exists to repair. A redirect is counted where an offline server deliberately is not, because it is deterministic rather than a transient blip that would raise a false alarm; the recorded reason names the new address, so the warning arrives useful. `--check-only` reports the redirect but records nothing and touches no workspace — it is read-only intent, and no upgrade was attempted, so counting one as failed would warn about something nobody tried. The counter is symmetric now, too: an unattended run whose probe completes and concludes "already current" records success — a redirect counted while the CLI happened to be current must not keep warning "server moved" after the server is fixed — while offline stays neutral, neither counting nor clearing. Found by Devin Review on this PR (second round). Both halves of that contract already had guards, but each exercised only the outdated path, so a new branch above them stayed green. The workspace hook refresh still runs on the way to the error, because converging the hook layout has nothing to do with where `/cli/latest` now points, and the verdict this case used to reach refreshed on the same path: a relocated server should not quietly freeze an analyst's hooks as well. Found by Devin Review on this PR.

  **`agnes update` carries the same verdict, and that is the one that runs by itself.** `agnes init` installs a detached `agnes update --quiet` as the SessionStart hook — not `agnes self-upgrade` — and its CLI step tested only for an available upgrade, folding a redirect into the report line `already current / offline`. So every claim above about the unattended path was, until this, a claim about a command a person types: on the path that actually repairs stale installs, a relocated server still produced a silent and falsely reassuring no-op, with nothing recorded. That step now reports it as an error naming where the server went, and records the failure, so the counter moves where it was always supposed to. The recorded failure is what this rests on: it is written immediately, so it survives regardless of what the rest of the run does. The report line is best-effort by comparison — on a workspace that has a token, a later step calls the shared HTTP client, whose redirect handling exits the process outright, so the run ends before its report is written at all. That is a separate defect in the client, not in this step, and it is being fixed on its own. Separately, `--force --quiet` exited 0 on a redirect, telling an automation that the upgrade it asked for had worked; `--quiet` suppresses progress, not failures, so a forced upgrade that did not happen now exits non-zero as an unreachable server already did. Both found by Devin Review on this PR. A genuinely unreachable server keeps its existing `cannot reach` message, which is a test in its own right.
- **`agnes chat <slug> --once` no longer prints "(no answer)" on a turn that actually answered.** It assembled the answer only from streamed `TEXT_MESSAGE_CONTENT` deltas, but a turn that answers without incremental streaming — the test/dev fake-agent runner's `echo:` reply, and the real runner's idle-watchdog partial-save — carries its text solely on the trailing `TEXT_MESSAGE_END` event. `_send_turn` now falls back to that event's content (and prints it live) whenever no deltas arrived. Same fix covers the interactive REPL for the same event shape. The stream is now also drained past `RUN_ERROR` rather than stopping at it, so a watchdog partial-save that arrives after the error event is shown instead of discarded.

### Removed

- **The phantom desktop-pairing surface is gone.** `dev_docs/desktop-app.md` documented a browser pairing flow (`/desktop/link` → `data-analyst://` deep link → `POST /api/desktop/refresh`) whose routes were deleted with the legacy webapp and never ported to the FastAPI app; `desktop_link.html` was a template no route ever rendered; and the `desktop:` config section (instance.yaml + `/admin/server-config`, down to the admin page's own section label and sidenav entry) configured nothing — the notifications WebSocket reads `DESKTOP_JWT_SECRET` straight from the environment. All of it is removed rather than left pointing at endpoints that don't exist. A guard now fails the build if the admin page's client-side section lists name a section the API no longer accepts, so the next such removal cannot go half-done. A leftover `desktop:` block in an existing instance.yaml is harmless (it was already unread); the section is simply no longer served or writable via the server-config editor. Note the WS endpoint itself stays and still validates `DESKTOP_JWT_SECRET`-signed tokens — but nothing in-repo mints them; how clients obtain one is the open design question tracked in #412.

### Added

- **A per-instance switch hides the MCP connector surface for VPN/intranet-only deployments.** In-network MCP clients always worked fine on such an instance, but a cloud-side connector client resolved from outside the network can never reach the endpoint — yet users still saw install instructions for a surface that could never work for them. `mcp.connector_ui_enabled: false` (env `AGNES_MCP_CONNECTOR_UI_ENABLED=0`, default `true` — current behavior unchanged) hides the `/me/ai-connector` and `/mcp-connect` pages, the MCP tab of `/how-it-works#connect`, and every nav/command-palette entry pointing at them, on both chrome variants. It is UI only: the MCP protocol endpoints (`/api/mcp/http`, `/api/mcp/sse`) keep serving in-network clients regardless. `docs/DEPLOYMENT.md` documents the two supported postures for a private-network instance — expose the endpoint through an authenticated TLS reverse proxy, or hide the surface with this switch.

  The switch also takes the copy that points at what it removed, which the first pass left behind. Gating the default chrome's MCP-only "AI Connector" row alone left that user menu with an entry to *neither* surface — paper renders "Learn how it works" in the same slot, so the code comment claiming the orientation row survives the switch was true only under paper — and `/how-it-works` carries the CLI setup, the first-session narrative and the privacy content, so hiding MCP quietly took all of it out of the menu. The default chrome now falls back to that row. Inside the page, the plugin-packages note stopped telling the reader to "use the connector above instead" of a block that is no longer rendered, and the two connector-specific troubleshooting entries ("MCP endpoint not found", "Can't add a custom connector on Claude.ai?") follow the surface they troubleshoot; the transport-agnostic entries stay. Found by Devin Review on this PR.

## [0.83.11] - 2026-08-13
### Fixed

- **A scoped sync for an already-deleted table id no longer re-registers the whole source project.** The auto-discovery gate on a `tables=[...]`-scoped sync trigger derived "is the registry empty?" from the requested subset (`repo.get(id)` returning `None` for a deleted id looked like an empty registry), instead of the whole registry like the scheduled-sync branch already did — so triggering a sync for a table id that was deleted while queued or running could re-discover and re-register every table on the source. Both branches now check the whole registry.

## [0.83.8] - 2026-08-13
### Internal

- Deflaked `test_concurrent_deploy_calls_never_overlap_inside_runner_up` (CI-only `[200, 200] != [200, 409]`): the runner stub now holds `up()` open on a latch the test releases only after the second deploy request completes, so the op lease is provably held for that request's whole lifetime. The old fixed 0.5s sleep left ~0.3s of real-time margin for the second request's retry-then-409 window; a loaded CI runner could stretch past it, the first deploy released the lease early, and both requests legitimately succeeded. The lease itself serialized correctly all along (the concurrency assertion never fired).

## [0.83.7] - 2026-08-12
### Fixed

- **Turning chat tools on for a connected project now leaves the agent with tools to call.** As shipped in 0.83.5 the switch created the MCP source and stopped: the agent's passthrough surface is built from `tool_registry`, and those rows are otherwise written only by an admin curating each tool by hand under `/admin/mcp` — `introspect` and `classify` are read-only probes that persist nothing. So a switch that reported success produced a project the agent could not reach, and the surrounding copy sent the admin off to run Introspect themselves, on roughly forty tools, one at a time. Enabling now introspects the upstream and registers its tools as passthrough rows itself. `mutating` is taken from each tool's `readOnlyHint`, and a tool the upstream does **not** annotate is recorded as mutating rather than assumed safe — the absence of a claim is not a claim of safety. Exposed names carry a per-connection prefix, because every Keboola project exposes `query_data` and the agent picks a tool by name alone; without it two connected projects' tools would be indistinguishable at the point of choice. Grants are still not created: registering makes a tool curatable, granting makes it reachable, and only the second is an access-control decision — the UI and CLI now say so, and name the grants page that actually carries it rather than the Access screen, which does not. The two failure domains stay apart: an upstream that will not answer returns 502 with a retry hint, while a failed local config write propagates, because telling an admin to retry an upstream when their database write failed is a worse answer than none.

- Three hardenings of the chat-tools switch, from Devin Review on this PR. **A failed re-run now actually restores the previous state instead of claiming to**: the 502's "nothing was changed" was made true rather than reworded — the source row (including a deliberate "off"), the credential slot, the tool set and its grants all go back, where before only the credential did. **A tool the upstream no longer offers is retired on the next re-run**: registration reconciles the registry against the fresh listing, so a vanished tool — and its grants — stops being served to analysts only to fail at the far end. **Introspection is bounded** (300 s): a stalled first-run download becomes the 502 with its retry hint instead of an admin request that never returns.

- Fifth Devin round on the same switch. **The response and every surface now say how many registered tools stay admin-only** (`tools_admin_only`): a `mutating` tool is refused for non-admins by the passthrough policy gate even when granted, and an unannotated tool is recorded as mutating — so on an upstream that annotates nothing, "grant them and analysts see them" was a false promise; the CLI and the admin page now state the count (and the page calls out the all-of-them case). **Exposed tool names are capped at 64 characters** — the tool-name limit model APIs enforce — shrinking the readable connection slug before anything load-bearing, so one over-long upstream name cannot poison the whole tool list. And the CLI guard test asserts the text the command actually prints, where it had kept passing on a word that survived only in a comment.

- Sixth Devin round, same switch. **A re-sync no longer wipes the admin's per-tool curation**: the re-run upsert was full-row, so pressing "Re-sync token" silently reset PII masking, removed rate limits, re-armed a deliberately disabled tool and reverted a hand-corrected `mutating` — the very correction the CLI text invites. A re-run now re-derives what is this release's (names, schema, description) and keeps what is the admin's (`pii_fields`, `rate_limit_pm`, `enabled`, `mutating`) — with one asymmetry: an upstream that *explicitly* declares a tool not-read-only re-tightens `mutating`, because trusting an explicit claim to restrict is safe while relaxing stays a human decision. **An empty upstream listing no longer mass-revokes**: reconcile trusted any successful listing, so a server that starts but lists nothing (expired token, a runner resolving an older package) would have retired every registered tool and its grants behind a 201 — a re-run that lists nothing is now refused as the upstream fault it is (502, nothing changed); a first enable has nothing to destroy and stays permissive.

- The 502 after a failed enable says "restored" only when the restore actually succeeded: `_undo()` reports whether it did, and a failed undo points the admin at `/admin/mcp` instead of telling them nothing changed — asserting it unconditionally was the same class of unverified claim the restore itself was built to retire. Found by Devin Review on this PR (seventh round).

- **The package cache no longer lands somewhere the container cannot keep it.** The derived source runs the upstream MCP server through `uv`, which caches it under `$HOME/.cache/uv` — but the runtime image never sets `HOME` (`python:3.13-slim` does not, and a `USER` directive alone does not either), and the MCP SDK forwards only environment variables that actually exist in the parent. Even where it resolved, the cache sat inside the container filesystem, which is replaced on every upgrade, so the first tool call after each auto-upgrade re-downloaded ~157 MB. It is now pinned to `${DATA_DIR}/cache/uv`, which both survives upgrades and does not depend on `HOME` — verified by running the server with `HOME` unset. Instances on a tight data volume should budget for it.

## [0.83.6] - 2026-08-12
### Changed

- **The provenance line states the record, not an act nobody verified.** It said each note was "approved by an administrator of this instance" — but the bundle's required tier is selected on `is_required` alone, so a required note ships whatever its status, and an instance running the collector in `auto_publish` mode files mined items as approved with nobody looking. A per-item file now says the note is *marked required*, the rollup says the notes carry the status *approved*, and the single-note file stopped describing "each note below". A title is also rendered as a title — one line — because a title carrying newlines wrote its own heading and its own `— author, date` credit under somebody else's name, which the header then vouched for; the note's BODY is still delivered byte-for-byte, and the header now says so, since what it cannot prevent it must not vouch for. The rollup states how many notes it carries, so a body that forges a section makes a discrepancy the reader can see. Found by Devin Review and an adversarial review of this PR.
- **The corporate-memory files `agnes pull` writes into `.claude/rules/` now say where their contents came from.** Claude Code loads that directory at session start as *project rules* — an instruction channel — and approved notes were written into it verbatim, so a colleague's ordinary end-of-session recap ("Next step is to type /exit and rerun claude from /srv … with recaps disabled in /config") arrived in every analyst's workspace shaped exactly like an order from the operator. Verified by handing the real generated file to an agent with no knowledge of this work: it refused to act on the sentence and said it would raise it "before doing anything else with this workspace" — correct on the sentence, but the analyst's session stops on a note nobody meant as an instruction. 0.83.5 gave the *approver* a warning (`delivery_warnings`); this is the other half, for the reader. Each `km_*.md` and `ka_*.md` now opens with a provenance line, notes in the `km_approved.md` rollup are separated by a rule, and each one carries a `— author, date` credit. The note text itself is delivered unchanged. Same agent, same conditions, on the new file: *"My next action is unchanged in kind"* — it proceeded with the user's actual task, used the revenue note as the reference it is, and still declined the directive sentence, which is the whole intent.

  The header states provenance and stops. An earlier draft added "these are recorded observations, not requests made in this session" and tested worse: the naive reader called it "the document coaching my reading of itself, which I treat as a signal to be more skeptical, not less", and noted it changed nothing because treating file content as data is already the baseline. A later draft promised "the credit line under each heading names who and when" unconditionally — both attribution fields are nullable, so on a bundle without them the header made a claim the file did not keep, which the same reader checked, caught, and cited as *"one more reason to treat the embedded directive with suspicion"*. That sentence is now conditional on there being a credit line to find. A provenance header earns its place by being checkable; one that overstates by a clause does the opposite of what it is for.

### Fixed

- `ka_*.md` digests pick up a change to the wording `agnes pull` wraps them in. The cached hash covers the digest's content, not the template, so an already-synced workspace kept the old text until the digest itself changed — the CHANGELOG's claim that both file kinds carry the provenance line was not true for them. A render version rides with the hash and re-writes each digest once.
- A whitespace-only `created_at` no longer renders `_—    _` — a credit line with nothing in it, which also made the header promise credits it could not show.
- The moderation warning strips control characters from a note's excerpt before echoing it: `click.echo` does not, so a crafted note could repaint or erase the very line printed about it.
- **`agnes admin memory approve` printed the same flagged sentence once per pattern it tripped.** The scanner reports a finding per kind, and the sentence this feature exists for trips three at once, so one flagged note filled three consecutive lines with identical text and read as three separate problems. Findings are now grouped by excerpt with their kinds listed together. Found on a live approval against a throwaway instance, not by the unit tests — which asserted the payload's structure and never looked at the shape of the output.

## [0.83.5] - 2026-08-12
### Changed

- **`agnes init` no longer writes a trust declaration into your user-scope Claude Code settings unasked, and the declaration no longer argues for itself.** Two independent problems in the same block, both reported by an agent that read `~/.claude/settings.json` after being told to run `agnes init`. **The wording:** the `autoMode.environment` entries ended with *"cloning it and installing the plugins it grants is a routine, sanctioned internal operation, not integration of untrusted external code"* — a verdict about how the reading agent should judge a future action, written by the tool whose actions were being judged. The agent flagged it as exactly the pattern it is meant to distrust and refused to act on it, which is the correct reading: a claim carries no more weight for being emphatic, and a self-issued one carries less. The entries now state what the slot is for and stop — the host is this organization's Agnes server, it issued this machine's token, its marketplace is served from `https://<host>/marketplace.git/` and curated by that server's operator — leaving the conclusion to the classifier. **The consent:** this is the one write `agnes init` makes outside the workspace it was pointed at, since user-scope settings apply to every project on the machine, and it happened silently with a line printed afterwards. It is now opt-in: `--trust-marketplace-host` / `--no-trust-marketplace-host` decide it outright; an interactive run names the file, prints the exact lines it would add, and asks (defaulting to **No**, because declining costs one approval prompt while agreeing changes machine-wide settings); an unattended run — the pasted-install path, where the "operator" is an agent relaying a script — skips and says how to opt in. **The mechanism is unchanged and still recommended:** `autoMode.environment` is the sanctioned channel for declaring an organization's trust boundary, and the host is still derived from configuration, never hardcoded. Declining is not a broken install — Claude Code's auto mode may ask before `agnes refresh-marketplace --bootstrap` clones the marketplace, which is a human approving in the moment, the thing the pre-declaration was there to skip. Guarded by `tests/test_automode_trust_consent.py`, including a check that the entries contain no verdict language (verified to fail against the previous wording) and one that stripping the argument did not strip the information.
### Fixed

- One classifier decides what a redirect is (`classify_redirect`), so the two HTTP clients and setup cannot disagree about the code name, and a refused plaintext address is carried in its own field rather than inside the wrapped hint — an address split across two lines at 80 columns cannot be copied. Found by Devin Review on this PR.
- The corporate-memory assistant is told about the `content` field, so it can offer the thing this change adds instead of describing the old three-field body. Found by Devin Review on this PR.
- The Archive button agrees with the endpoint. Permitting the withdrawal of an unjudged upload in the API while the detail page kept the button hidden left the author exactly where the change set found them — the button is the only surface they see. Both now ask the same shared question (`entity_has_adverse_verdict`), on all three detail templates. Found by Devin Review on this PR.
- The first-time-setup guide asks for `local` rather than `csv`. `csv` is an accepted alias with no connector behind it, so an agent following the guide could configure an instance with no external source while the operator believed they had chosen one. Found by Devin Review on this PR.
- Four follow-ups from Devin Review on this PR. **A non-admin's knowledge no longer disappears on approval**: the suggestion-queue replay copied only name/slug/description, so an author who filled in the Corporate Memory builder, saw "Submitted for approval" and waited got an empty domain — the seeding is now one shared function both creation paths call, and the item is attributed to the submitter rather than to the admin who approved it. **A flagged upload can no longer be withdrawn by re-uploading first**: the gate read only the latest submission, so a fresh unjudged row made an adverse verdict stop counting; it scans the whole chain like its sibling `_entity_review_blocked` does, while `pending` and `review_error` remain non-verdicts an author may still withdraw. **A builder-assistant outage no longer reads as a missing permission** — the message branches on 401/403 versus anything else, and the API helper carries the status so it can. And the seeded item's `pending` state is stated in the response and on the page, because authoring is not approving.
- **`docs/DATA_SOURCES.md` offered a `data_source.type` value that has no connector, and never named the canonical one.** Three places name this vocabulary and they had drifted: the admin server-config schema says `keboola | bigquery | local | csv`, `config/instance.yaml.example` says `keboola | bigquery | local`, and the docs said `keboola, bigquery, csv` — offering the alias while omitting `local` entirely. `csv` is an alias for `local` and there is no CSV connector; nothing under `connectors/` handles it. So an admin following the docs picked `csv` expecting a Keboola-style pull and configured an instance with no external source at all — which is what a first-day admin did on a fresh instance during an onboarding pass. The docs now carry a table naming all three canonical values, say plainly that `csv` is an alias and that no connector exists behind it, and a guard fails if the three sources drift apart again or if a `connectors/csv/` ever appears without the docs being revisited.

- **An author could not withdraw their own submission when nothing had objected to it.** Owner-delete on a non-approved entity was refused so an author cannot erase a *flagged* upload before triage — a control worth keeping. But it keyed on `visibility_status`, which cannot tell "flagged" from "not judged yet": the runner writes `hidden` both for a blocked verdict and for a `review_error`, and `pending` while the verdict is still in flight. Submissions nothing had ever objected to were therefore trapped. Seen in production: a skill whose inline checks (content, quality, manifest, static security) all passed sat in `review_error` — the LLM call had crashed — for a month, with Delete and Edit both locked and re-upload answering `409 "delete the existing entity first"`, i.e. instructing the author to do the one thing they could not. The refusal now reads the *verdict*: `blocked_inline` / `blocked_llm` keep it, while "no verdict yet" and "the reviewer crashed" are the author's own not-yet-public upload to withdraw. Editing during an in-flight review stays refused — that one is a race against a reviewer reading the bundle, not an evidence question. The submission row, its sha256 and its size survive a withdrawal either way, so forensic correlation is unchanged.

- **The Corporate Memory Builder had nowhere to put the memory.** `/admin/studio/corporate-memory` posts to `POST /api/admin/memory-domains`, whose request body accepted only name / slug / description / icon / colour / cover / status — so a page whose subtitle reads *"Distill reusable knowledge into a memory domain granted to a group"* produced an empty container every time, and the knowledge itself had to be added later through a different surface. The endpoint now takes an optional `content` (plus `content_title`), seeds it as the domain's first knowledge item through the same repository the regular knowledge endpoint uses, and returns its `item_id`; the builder renders a matching Knowledge textarea. Seeding is opt-in — omit `content` and the endpoint behaves exactly as before — and whitespace-only content creates nothing, so a textarea the author tabbed through does not become an empty memory item. The item carries the domain's slug as its category, since the domain is the categorisation and the form does not ask for one. Both the domain and the seeded item get their own audit row.

- **A user without the cloud-chat grant was told "Access denied to chat 'chat'".** Cloud chat is modelled as a singleton feature gate — resource type `chat` holding one resource whose id is the literal string `chat` (`id_format="chat"`) — so the generic resource-denial text, `Access denied to {type} {id!r}`, collapsed into that. The Studio builders print the API's detail straight into their assistant panel, on a page whose banner reads "AI-ASSISTED", so two independent testers met it and neither could tell whether it was their permissions or a broken instance. Singleton resources now name the feature ("Access denied to Cloud chat — it is not enabled for your account."); multi-instance types keep naming the id, which is the part a reader needs there. A guard walks every registered resource type so a future singleton cannot reintroduce the shape. The Studio panel no longer echoes the raw exception either — it says what the reader can do (fill the form in manually, ask an admin for the grant) and keeps the detail in the browser console.

- **The CLI's second HTTP client answered a moved server with `internal CLI error (JSONDecodeError)`.** #1225 taught `cli/client.py` to stop on a 3xx and name the new address, but the CLI has two HTTP clients: `cli/v2_client.py` calls the module-level `httpx.get`/`httpx.post` directly, so it never sees the other client's event hooks — and each of its helpers only raised on `>= 400`, so a redirect fell through to `r.json()` on a redirect's empty body. Ten command modules route through it (`catalog`, `describe`, `search`, `collections`, `store`, `my_stack`, `marketplace`, …), and the message they printed named neither the status, nor the destination, nor a remedy — strictly worse than the bare `HTTP 308:` that fix set out to replace. Measured against a real moved hostname, not inferred. The wording now lives in one place (`cli/server_moved.py`) that both clients call, the nine open-coded `>= 400` guards in `v2_client` are one shared `_raise_for_status`, and a test fails any client module making httpx calls without consulting the shared guard — a second client is what caused this, so the guard is written against the pair rather than against the file that happened to break.
- …and both HTTP clients say the same thing: a redirect to a plaintext address names that address and explains the refusal, instead of reporting it as a redirect that went nowhere. Found by Devin Review on this PR.
- Setup says which kind of no-move it hit: a redirect pointing at an unencrypted address is named as `insecure_redirect` with the address it refused, rather than reported as "the redirect stays on the same address" — which sent someone whose server really had moved hunting for a proxy with no idea where it went. Found by Devin Review on this PR.
- …and a downgrade is refused whether or not the host changes: `https://old` → `http://new` would otherwise have been handed over as a new plaintext address. Found by Devin Review on this PR.
- **The CLI's second HTTP client answered a moved server with `internal CLI error (JSONDecodeError)`.** #1225 taught `cli/client.py` to stop on a 3xx and name the new address, but the CLI has two HTTP clients: `cli/v2_client.py` calls the module-level `httpx.get`/`httpx.post` directly, so it never sees the other client's event hooks — and each of its helpers only raised on `>= 400`, so a redirect fell through to `r.json()` on a redirect's empty body. Ten command modules route through it (`catalog`, `describe`, `search`, `collections`, `store`, `my_stack`, `marketplace`, …), and the message they printed named neither the status, nor the destination, nor a remedy — strictly worse than the bare `HTTP 308:` that fix set out to replace. Measured against a real moved hostname, not inferred. The wording now lives in one place (`cli/server_moved.py`) that both clients call, the open-coded `>= 400` guards in `v2_client` collapse into one shared `_raise_for_status`, and a test fails any client module making httpx calls without consulting it — a second client is what caused this, so the guard is written against the pair rather than against the file that happened to break. `api_get_stream` needed its own line: its check sits inside a `with httpx.stream(...)` block at a different indent, so the sweep over the plain verbs left it behind, and there a redirect is worse than elsewhere — the 3xx is not an error, so the download loop writes the redirect's empty body to disk and reports success. The guard that found it walks the module's AST and matches each function reaching `httpx` to a guard inside that same function; an earlier version counted call sites against guard calls and passed on a coincidence.

### Added

- **Approving a knowledge item now says what approval publishes.** `agnes pull` writes approved and required corporate-memory items into every analyst's `<workspace>/.claude/rules/km_*.md`, and Claude Code loads that directory at session start as **project rules** — an instruction channel, not a reference one. Nothing on the approval path said so, and the two semantics do not match: an admin is deciding "this is worth remembering" while the delivery channel turns it into "every agent must do this". Observed live, an ordinary end-of-session recap saved as knowledge — *"Next step is to type /exit and rerun claude from /srv so the marketplace and session hooks load, with recaps disabled in /config"* — reached every workspace as a standing directive, where an agent refused to follow it and reported the rules file as untrusted content. It was right to: nothing distinguishes a recorded observation from an order once both arrive as rules. The review queue (`GET /api/memory/admin/pending`), the single-item GET, `POST /admin/approve` and the `POST /admin/batch` endpoint behind `agnes admin memory approve` now carry `delivery_warnings` — the spans that read as instructions to the agent, each with the clause and its line — plus a one-line `delivery_notice` stating what the channel is. `/admin/corporate-memory` renders the notice above the queue and the flagged clauses on the card, and the CLI prints them after the ids it approved, so the batch-of-ids path that never displays the content is covered too. The approve audit row records the count, which makes "who approved a note carrying agent directives" answerable after the fact. **Advisory, never a gate** — the same posture as the store's static scan: every action still does exactly what it was asked, and the annotation informs the human making it. `reject` and `revoke` report nothing, since they take an item *out* of the channel. The scanner (`src/knowledge_directive_scan.py`) is tuned for precision over recall, because a warning that fires on ordinary knowledge is a warning nobody reads: it matches only text aimed at the agent's own harness — its slash commands, restarting or leaving its session, toggling its recaps/hooks/permission-mode/`settings.json`, or asking it not to report — and deliberately leaves ordinary imperative knowledge ("you must exclude test accounts", "run the rebuild first") alone. Paths and URLs are excluded from slash-command matching, and `telemetry`, bare `permissions` and "end the session" are excluded outright because all three are data topics here. Both halves are pinned by tests: the shapes that must flag, and the ordinary notes that must stay silent.

- **An agent can read one file from a Collection instead of guessing search terms** — `collection_file_read` on both MCP servers, `agnes collections cat <collection_id> <file_id>` on the CLI. `GET /api/collections/{cid}/files/{fid}/preview` has always returned the extracted text, and the Library's preview modal uses it, but neither the agent-facing nor the terminal surface could reach it. So "what is in this file?" — a question with no keywords to search for — had no answer path: observed live, an agent tried six `collections_search` phrasings, invented an `agnes collections cat` that did not exist, and concluded it lacked access to a file its owner was looking at. Deliberately a thin wrapper over the existing endpoint rather than a new read path, which is what makes the context guard free: the server already caps the text (~20k chars) and reports `truncated`, so the tool cannot flood a context window, and both docstrings say a truncated read is a PREFIX that must not be summarised as the whole document. They also say when NOT to reach for it — reading many files to answer one question is what retrieval is for, and a read tool that quietly displaces search is the failure mode worth naming up front. Both surfaces key on `text`, not on `kind` — `kind` is the browser modal's switch (draw an image, embed a PDF, print text), and the preview endpoint answered every inline-media extension with `kind: "pdf"`/`"image"` and returned *before* its own extracted-text branch. So a PDF, a primary collection format that usually does have ingested text, came back empty: "what is in this PDF?" — the exact question this exists for — answered "no text preview is available" while the text sat in `corpus_chunks` (Devin Review on this PR). The endpoint now attaches the extracted text to those kinds too, which costs the modal one field it ignores and leaves `kind` untouched. When there genuinely is no text (still ingesting, rejected, nothing extractable) `reason` carries the server's own sentence — for images and PDFs as well, where a bare `text: null` previously gave a non-browser caller nothing to relay — and the CLI prints it to stderr and exits non-zero rather than printing nothing. Registered in **both** MCP servers — the stdio one backs the in-chat agent — with a runtime guard asserting the stdio server really registers it, since a `def` missing its `@tool()` decorator would satisfy a source-level check while the agent still saw nothing.

- **An answer's sources are now checked against what it actually ran.** The tour and the chat greeting both promise Agnes "always" says where an answer came from, and 0.83.3 backed that with a prompt rule asking for a `Sources:` line. A prompt is a request to a model, and prose cannot be checked: a wrong claim and a missing one both looked like an ordinary answer. The rule is now a fenced ` ```sources ` block (`table:` / `metric:` / `assumption:`), the server parses it, and **each `table:` and `metric:` is checked against the turn's own tool calls** — the record of what the agent really did. The chat lifts the block out of the prose and renders it as chips: green where a tool call supports the claim, amber and labelled `UNVERIFIED` where the answer named something nothing ran on, neutral for an assumption (there is nothing to check one against, and flagging honest assumptions would teach the reader to ignore the badge). An answer that claimed nothing renders "none declared" rather than nothing at all — absence was previously invisible, which is what let the promise drift. The prompt says the check exists and what an unsupported claim looks like, because a model told only the format has no reason to be careful about the claim. The verdict is **computed, never stored** (`app/chat/sources.py`): both call sites already hold the content and the tool calls together, so there is no column, no migration step and no DuckDB/Postgres parity surface — and improving the matcher improves history rather than only new answers. The matcher is deliberately crude (substring containment over the serialized calls) and errs toward accepting: a false "verified" leaves the reader where they were, a false "unverified" would train them to ignore it. What this is **not** is a refusal to answer without sources — that needs a second pass over the model on every turn, and would trade a visible gap for an invisible cost. Shape borrowed from kai-agent's `next_actions`, which mandates a fenced trailer and re-renders it as chrome; the deliberate divergence is the clipboard, where kai strips its block and we keep ours — a copied transcript is exactly what someone sends when they doubt a number.

- **Mermaid diagrams render in chat.** A ` ```mermaid ` fence becomes a diagram, which is the right answer for structure — a pipeline, a table relationship, a sequence — where the inline-SVG chart channel added in 0.83.3 is the right answer for quantity. The prompt draws that line explicitly, because mermaid cannot plot values and matplotlib should not be drawing boxes. One decision is load-bearing and easy to undo: **mermaid's output does not go through `renderMarkdownSafe`.** Its SVG carries a `<style>` block that every one of its colours depends on, and `style` is in the sanitizer's tag blocklist — routing it through for consistency would leave a grey skeleton that reads as a mermaid bug rather than ours. The fence survives sanitization as inert text; only afterwards is the *source* handed to mermaid, with `securityLevel: 'strict'` (HTML labels off, click handlers refused, label text escaped) as what actually stands between a hostile diagram and the page. A diagram that fails to parse keeps its source on screen with a note rather than leaving a blank. The bundle is 3.5 MB — an order of magnitude more than every other vendored asset combined — so it is **not** loaded with the page: the script is injected the first time a thread actually contains a diagram, and the promise cached for the session.

- **A skill for a feature the instance does not have is worse than no skill.** With data apps switched off, the bundled workspace still shipped `agnes-data-apps-extras` — nothing in the workspace build consulted the instance's own configuration. Watched live: asked for a chart, the agent loaded that skill, called `data_apps_list`, and got `404 data_apps_disabled`. The wasted round trip is the smaller cost; the larger one is that the skill had already aimed it at *building a hosted dashboard* for what was a one-off plot. Bundled skills can now declare the flag that governs them, and the workspace build prunes the ones whose feature is off. Pruning runs after the template copy rather than filtering it, so convergence stays honest in both directions — turn the feature off and the skill leaves on the next pass, turn it back on and it returns. Two ways that fell short, both found by Devin Review on this PR. The prune sat inside `run_init`, which `ensure_user_workdir` only reaches when the sentinel is missing or `needs_reinit` is true — and `needs_reinit` compares the marketplace SHA and the Agnes version, never a feature flag. So the promise above held for a brand-new workspace and for nobody else: an operator flipping `data_apps.enabled` off on a live instance changed nothing until an unrelated upgrade happened to force a reinit. It now runs from `ensure_user_workdir` on **both** paths, which also brings template-OVERRIDE mode in — an operator's repo can vendor the same bundled skill, and it is exactly as useless there. And the composer's slash menu kept offering the skill after the sandbox lost it: `app/chat/skills_catalog.py` lists the SHIPPED template, not the converged workspace, so invoking the entry did nothing because the files were gone. Both now read one gate (`skill_disabled_on_this_instance`), rather than the menu depending on a filesystem convergence having already run for that user.

- **`chat_upload_file` read as a way to hand a file to the user; it is the opposite.** Its direction is the caller's machine → the workspace, and on the server-hosted MCP surface it is refused outright (naming a path there would let a caller exfiltrate any file the server can read). An agent inside a chat sandbox holding a finished chart reached for it anyway, got `No Agnes token configured` from the local stdio server, and carried on hunting — several tool calls, then SVG→PNG conversion, and finally it told the user to open `/tmp/mrr_over_time.png` on a machine they were not using. Both docstrings now lead with the direction and name the channel that does work (inline `<svg>`, a ```mermaid fence, a markdown table). The tool's behaviour is unchanged; what changes is that the description no longer invites the misuse.

- **The sandbox could not reach its own Agnes instance, so building a data app from chat was impossible.** Two allowlists decide what a sandbox may reach: the VM-level egress policy (`e2b_provider._effective_allow_out`, which derives the Agnes host from `agnes_server_url()`) and `ALLOWED_HOSTS` in the bundled `PreToolUse` hook, checked first, inside the sandbox. The provider's docstring says its default "mirrors the bundled PreToolUse hook's ALLOWED_HOSTS so the VM-level policy and the hook agree" — it did not. The hook's set was four hard-coded entries and *could* not contain the Agnes host, because that host differs per deployment and the file ships verbatim. The stricter layer wins, so every in-sandbox request to Agnes was refused before it reached a network that would have allowed it. Watched on a running instance: asked to build a data app, the agent obtained a git credential from the API and then failed to clone the app's repo by name, by hostname and by IP — including one attempt with the sandbox bypass — because `…/data-apps.git/<slug>` lives on the Agnes host. What made it hard to see is that the MCP tools kept working throughout: they reach the server through the local relay on `127.0.0.1`, which was allowed. The hook now derives the host from `AGNES_SERVER`, which the manager already puts in the sandbox environment. This does not weaken anything: the hook lives on a filesystem the agent can write, so it has always been advisory, and the authoritative control is the VM egress policy (`deny_out=[ALL_TRAFFIC]` plus an allowlist the sandbox cannot touch), which is unchanged. The agreement the comment claimed is now asserted by `tests/test_sandbox_egress_allowlist_agreement.py`.

- **The data-app skill pointed at the scaffold with a relative path, and the agent read it relative to the wrong thing.** "`scaffolds/nodejs-dashboard/` (sibling of this skill's session workspace)" was resolved against the skill's own directory. Watched live on a running instance: three `ls` attempts against `.claude/skills/agnes-data-apps-extras/scaffolds/`, then a `find` (refused by the enumeration guard) and a `Read` (EISDIR) — and never once `/work/scaffolds/`, where the scaffolds actually are, symlinked in by `WORKSPACE_LINK_ENTRIES`. The run stalled there, before writing any app code. The path is now absolute and states where the scaffold is *not*, which is the half that was missing: a relative path in a skill is resolved against whatever the reader takes "here" to be.

- **Hosted data apps could never deploy: the container was handed the wrong credential to clone with.** The deploy path passed the app's `data-app:<slug>` *service* token as the git password. `app/api/data_apps_git.py` is the only caller of `resolve_token_to_user` that passes `allow_data_app_git_scope=True`, and it admits exactly `data-app-git:<slug>` — a service token is refused there like anywhere else. So every hosted app's entrypoint failed its first `git clone` with `remote: authentication required` and crash-looped forever, the row settling in `error`. Nothing in the Agnes log said so: the rejection happens inside the git surface, which does not log a denial, and the visible symptom was a `502 runner_unavailable` from the deploy call timing out while the container thrashed. Found by reading the container's own log. The deploy now mints a separate `data-app-git:` credential for the container, scoped to the **repo's** slug (a draft clones its parent's repository, and the git surface pins the scope's slug to the repo requested) and **unbounded**, because the container re-clones whenever it is recreated — including waking from `sleep_mode: recreate`, where a 24-hour token would leave an app that deployed on Monday unable to wake on Wednesday. A failed deploy revokes it, symmetrically with the service token. Verified end to end on a live instance: create → seed the scaffold → `POST /deploy` → `200 {"state":"running"}` on the first attempt, readiness `true` after 30s, and the app serving `HTTP 200` with its built React bundle; before the fix the identical sequence produced a container restarting every few seconds.

- **An agent could not create a data app at all: the MCP surface had no `create`.** `data_apps_list`, `data_app_get`, `data_app_deploy`, `data_app_logs`, `data_app_create_draft` — but nothing to create the app a draft is a sibling *of*. REST has `POST /api/data-apps` and the CLI has `agnes app create`; this surface did not, so an agent asked to build an app started at `data_app_create_draft` and got `404 data_app_not_found` with no way forward. Added on both MCP surfaces (server-hosted and stdio), and the data-app skill now leads with the ordering — create, then seed, then draft — because the model reaches for the draft call first from habit. The `test_exact_server_side_tool_set` pin and the stdio/HTTP parity guard both had to be updated, which is the coverage ratchet doing its job.

- **The sandbox egress hook read a URL's basic-auth username as its hostname.** `re.findall(r"https?://([^/\s'\"]+)")` then `split(":")[0]` takes the first colon-separated token of the whole authority — so `http://agnes:<jwt>@host/…` yields `agnes`. Wrong in both directions, and the second one is a hole: a data-app clone URL (always `agnes:<token>@`) was refused whatever the allowlist said, and `http://api.github.com:pw@evil.example/` extracted `api.github.com` and was **allowed** while the request went to `evil.example` — an allowlist bypass for anyone who can get a command run in the sandbox. The userinfo is now dropped before the host is read (`rsplit("@", 1)[-1]`), and the refusal names the real host.

- **A remote sandbox was handed a clone URL it could not resolve.** `_mint_git_credential` builds its base from `get_public_url()`, which reads `PUBLIC_URL` / `server.public_url` only — not `SERVER_URL`, which is what a compose deployment sets. On such a box the chain fell through to `AGNES_INTERNAL_URL` (`http://app:8000`), a compose-internal name that a remote E2B microVM cannot resolve; the function's own docstring says the URL exists to work from exactly that caller. `SERVER_URL` now sits between the two, so the internal hostname stays the last resort.

- Two defects that measuring the rendered chips turned up and the eye did not: the `SOURCES` label sat at 3.93:1 against the bubble in `--ds-text-muted` (under WCAG AA at 10px), and the `UNVERIFIED` flag was set to `0.85em` of an already-small `--text-xs` — 8.5px measured, on the one word in the row that has to be legible. Both corrected and guarded.
