Deploy after deploy they accumulated without bound, each granting read/write on the app's repo, and deleting the app left them all valid. The token now carries the app's own slug as well as the repo's in its name, and superseded ones are swept after a successful deploy and on stop/delete. Both halves of that name matter: the *scope* must follow the repo, because a draft clones its parent's repository — but a sweep keyed on the repo alone would make a draft's deploy revoke the credential its parent's container wakes with. Revocation is deliberately placed after `_runner().up` accepts the deploy, mirroring the service token: revoking earlier would strand a previously-deployed container that is still asleep. **Tokens leaked by earlier releases are not swept** — they were minted under the old name and cannot be told apart from a sibling draft's — so an operator upgrading an instance that has deployed data apps should revoke the leftover `data-app-git:… (container)` tokens from the admin tokens page once.

- **A VM only reclaimed Docker disk on a tick that happened to upgrade it, so images and build cache piled up until an operator deleted them by hand.** `docker image prune -f` was the last statement *inside* the drift block of `scripts/ops/agnes-auto-upgrade.sh` — a box already sitting on the current image never reached it, and neither did a tick whose recreate was deferred (sync in flight) or aborted (role-split rollout). Garbage accrues from more than upgrades, too: a manual `docker compose build` on a dev VM leaves BuildKit cache that `image prune` cannot see at all. Nothing else on the host reclaims any of it, and nothing reports it either — `agnes-watchdog.sh` alerts on `/data` at 85%, while images and cache live on the **boot** disk under `/var/lib/docker`, which no probe watches, so the first symptom is a failed pull or a wedged daemon rather than a warning. The prune now runs on **every** tick, ahead of `docker compose pull` — which is what makes it self-healing on an already-full disk: the tick frees the superseded image, then fetches the new one. A `docker builder prune -f --filter until=168h` joins it, keeping a week of warm cache so a local rebuild on a dev VM stays fast. Scope is deliberately unchanged in one respect: `image prune` stays **dangling-only** (no `-a`), so it collects the previous `:stable` that lost its tag when the new digest landed and never a tagged image — including a data app's runtime image that happens to have no container running at that moment. Both calls are best-effort (`|| true`), so a docker hiccup or an older daemon without `builder prune` cannot abort the tick under `set -e` and wedge the upgrade behind it. The image a recreate supersedes is now collected by the next tick's GC (≤5 min) rather than inline. **Operator note:** this lands on running VMs on its own — the script self-updates from `main` at the end of each tick — but only reclaims what is *dangling*; a host already out of space from tagged images or a stopped-container hold still needs a one-off `docker system df -v` and a manual cleanup. Guarded by a new no-drift scenario in `tests/test_auto_upgrade_role_split.sh` that pins both prunes, their position ahead of the pull, and the absence of `-a`.

- **`agnes init --help` justified keeping the token out of the command line by the detector that would otherwise notice it, and an agent stopped rather than pick a flag.** The `--token` help said an inline token "trips Claude Code's auto-classifier … prefer `--token-file` or `AGNES_TOKEN` to dodge that", and `--token-file` promised the token "never appears in the command string this way, which dodges Claude Code's bearer-token classifier". Read literally — which is the only way an agent can read it — that is an instruction to route a secret around the agent's own safety detection, and a hardened Claude Code treated the help output as untrusted content and declined to choose a flag at all. Reported from an onboarding session, where `agnes init --help` sits on the critical path. The mechanism was never in question: keeping a PAT out of `argv` is this repo's own rule (`security.md`, "never put secrets on argv"). Only the justification was written backwards, and it now names the real exposure — shell history and the process table — as does the comment beside the token-resolution ladder. **This was the second copy of that framing.** 0.76.4 removed it from the web install prompt (`app/web/setup_instructions.py`) with a guard pinned to that one function, and the CLI kept saying it for another twenty-odd releases, so the new guard (`tests/test_no_safety_evasion_copy.py`) is surface-agnostic instead: it sweeps `cli/`, the install prompt and the shipped workspace template for any sentence that pairs an evasion verb with an agent's safety machinery. It flattens wrapped prose before matching, because two of the three offending sentences split "classifier" and "dodge" across adjacent source lines and a line-by-line scan matched neither — verified by running the guard against the pre-fix file, where it now reports all three. A companion assertion keeps the *reason* in the help text, so a future rewrite cannot satisfy the ban by deleting the rationale and leaving no argument for `--token-file` at all. `src/_bundled_seed/` is deliberately outside the sweep: it is a snapshot synced from the infra-template repo, where a local edit is reverted by the next sync and trips the provenance check, so its copy of this wording has to be fixed upstream.

- **A stray grey scrollbar floated in the middle of the rail chat landing.** Reported from a live instance: a short rounded thumb sat to the left of the window edge, level with the "Ask … anything" heading, attached to nothing the reader could scroll. It was real chrome, painted for a block 59px tall — `#chat-capabilities`, which under the rail holds exactly two lines (the trust caption and the heading). The base `.cloud-chat-capabilities` rule sets `overflow-y: auto`, which is correct for the topnav empty state, where that panel holds the capability cards inside a bounded `flex: 0 1 auto` column and genuinely scrolls; the rail rules restyled the element into a natural-height two-liner and never cancelled it. What made the leftover visible is sub-pixel: the block's height lands on a fraction (21.375 caption + 5 gap + 32.195 heading = 58.57px once the heading's `clamp(23px, 2vw, 28px)` hits its 28px ceiling), the browser resolves that to ~0.5px of scrollable overflow, and `auto` dutifully paints a scrollbar for half a pixel. Hence the two oddities in the report — it appeared and disappeared with the window width as the clamp moved the fraction around (absent at ~1300–1350px, present at ~1250–1275px and ≥1375px), and it sat ~87px inside the window edge, because the panel is the 1280px centred `--rdb-col` and not the full content width. Cancelled in the rail-scoped rule only, so the topnav panel keeps the scroll it needs. Sub-pixel overflow rounds to zero in `scrollHeight - clientHeight`, so nothing downstream would have caught this: the guard in `tests/test_ui_layout_theme.py` asserts both halves — the rail rule cancels the overflow, the base rule keeps it.

- **Two more on this PR, both found by Devin Review.** A failed sync could be labelled with a reason from one project and a failure **type** from another: `error` and `code` were picked by two independent scans over the per-source results, which is the worst possible pairing when several projects fail and only one is the one the admin is debugging. Both now come from the same source. And the identity bookkeeping on `PUT /{id}/secret` is isolated the same way it already is on `/test` — the token is safely stored before that write, so a vault or DB fault there turned an already-successful save into an error response and sent the admin to retry a store that had worked.

- **Two more on the connection page, both found by Devin Review.** The wizard's retry re-saved only the URL, so a name the admin corrected on the second attempt was thrown away while the success banner claimed that name was used; the retry now sends the name too. And `_record_project_identity` ran inside the same `try/except` that catches the outbound call's network errors, so a vault or DB fault turned a **passing** connectivity check into "connection test failed" with a database message, for a project that is correctly configured — bookkeeping is now isolated and logged.

- **An orphaned semantic-layer row told the admin to add a token that was already there.** `_enumerate_master_sources()` skips a connection for three different reasons — no `stack_url`, a master token the vault can no longer decrypt, no master token at all — and the page reported all three as "master token missing". An admin whose connection was missing its URL re-added a token that was never gone, and the rows still did not refresh. The reason is now computed per connection and the page renders it, including the case where the connection has since been deleted. Found by Devin Review on this PR.

- **A mistyped token in the add-project wizard left a stray connection behind on every attempt.** The wizard creates the connection first, and every step after that can fail — a rejected token being the common one — so it returned with the row already saved and a retry re-ran creation, minting another "Untitled project …" per try. A retry now reuses the connection the wizard already created (falling back to creating one if it was deleted underneath), so the eventual success lands on the row the admin has been looking at. The retry also **applies what they corrected** — reuse without that made a mistyped URL unfixable, since the wizard asked them to fix it and retry and then talked to the original address every time, failing identically with nothing saying the new value was ignored. The token-failure message the token-failure message says so, and offers the same discard link the connectivity-test failure already had. Found by Devin Review on this PR.

- **The Semantic layer page presented a capped list of unregistered tables as the complete set to fix.** `unresolved_tables` is truncated to 20 per project in the sync result, and the page renders it under instructions to go and register them — so on a project with more, an admin could register everything shown, sync again, and still lose metrics with nothing naming the rest. The sync result now carries `unresolved_tables_total` alongside the truncated list, and the page says the list is a subset — deliberately WITHOUT a number. The first attempt summed the per-project totals against a list that is de-duplicated across projects, so a table two projects both report counted twice and the page warned that tables were hidden when none were; and a true union total is not computable here, because each project's list is already capped before it arrives. The page therefore carries no count at all: it says at least one project has more than the list shows, and that the cap is per project. (A first attempt printed the de-duplicated list's own length as "the first N", which is a number matching no real limit — the cap applies per project, the list does not.) An entry written before the total was recorded falls back to the listed length, so an older result reads as complete rather than as an error. Found by Devin Review on this PR.

- **An ordinary edit of a connection silently removed the wrong-token safeguard this change set adds.** `PUT /api/admin/source-connections/{id}` REPLACES the stored config, and the admin form posts only the fields it renders — `project_id`/`project_name` are recorded by the connection itself, never typed, so they were never in the payload. A rename, a `token_env` change, or simply re-saving the form therefore dropped the binding, after which a master token for a completely different project was accepted again. Both keys are now carried forward from the stored row unless the caller supplies them — **on Keboola connections only**, since there they are recorded from the token's own owner block rather than typed; on a BigQuery connection `project_id` is an ordinary field the admin fills in, and carrying it forward made it unclearable (emptying it brought it straight back). an explicit `null` still clears one, which is how a mis-recorded binding is reset from the UI. The deliberate clear on a stack move is unchanged and still the only automatic one — a project id means nothing on a different stack. Found by Devin Review on this PR. Making the binding survive an edit turned it into a one-way door, so the page gains the release it was missing: an **unbind** control next to the recorded project, which sends the two keys as explicit `null`. Without it, re-pointing an existing connection at another project on the same stack was impossible from the UI — every token for the new project is refused by `_reject_project_mismatch`, which is the point of the lock, and nothing could clear it. The next token stored after unbinding re-binds the connection to whichever project that token opens. The Test button also gains a `data-role="test"` handle: `testConn` disabled `card.querySelector("button")`, the first button in the card, which stopped being Test once the unbind control landed above it — so the link greyed out, Test stayed live, and repeated presses fired duplicate requests with no sign of progress. Both halves found by Devin Review on this PR.

- **The Semantic layer admin page was unreachable under the `rail` layout, and when reached it misnamed every problem it had.** Five defects from one live report where connecting a Keboola semantic layer looked like an Agnes outage for a day. (1) `/admin/semantic-layer` was linked only from `_app_header.html`; `data-ui-layout` renders exactly one chrome and never falls back, so on a `rail` instance the page existed with no link to it anywhere — found only because someone was handed the URL. It joins the rail's Sources group (with `/admin/linked-apps`, missing the same way), and `tests/test_admin_nav_parity.py` now guards topnav → rail with a reasoned exception list. (2) **BREAKING (status codes)**: `PUT /api/admin/source-connections/{id}/secret` (`kind=master`) answered **502** when the Storage API *refused* the pasted token, and `POST /api/admin/run-keboola-semantic-layer-refresh` answered **502** for "no Keboola credentials configured" — a wrong token and an empty config both reported as Bad Gateway, which reads as "the server is down" and sends operators hunting infrastructure. Both now answer **400**; 502 is reserved for an upstream that is unreachable or returns 5xx, classified by `is_upstream_client_error()` (duck-typed on `.status`, so a transport error with no status stays a 502) and carried out of the sync as an error `code`. An error dict without a `code` still maps to 502, so an unknown shape never silently becomes a 4xx. (3) The empty state said "No Keboola projects have a master (owner) token configured yet" — to an admin looking at a working, table-syncing connection that reads as "your project isn't connected", and it is the state *every* wizard-connected instance starts in, since the master token is a separate vault slot the wizard never fills. It now names the connected projects that lack one. (4) An orphaned row whose `source_ref` still matches a live connection showed a bare UUID; it now shows that connection's name and "master token missing". (5) `skipped_unresolved_table` reached nobody: a sync reporting "9 glossary terms, 0 metrics" gave no hint that 50 metrics died on 12 datasets pointing at unregistered tables — the count existed only in the API response and the skip was not even logged. The page now reports the count, names the tables, and points at *Browse & register tables*; the sync logs them too. Failure toasts on both admin pages also stop auto-hiding after 3.5 s — the reason they were reported as a bare status code with the cause lost.

- **A Keboola connection didn't record which project it opens, so a master token for the *wrong* project stored happily and badged "SET".** On an instance with several Keboola projects the connections were indistinguishable — same stack host, an identical "master token: SET" badge — and nothing anywhere said which project any token actually unlocked. A mis-pasted master token was accepted without complaint, and the semantic-layer sync then imported that other project's metrics under this connection's name and inside its prune scope, so the next sync of the right project deleted them again. Silent in both directions. A connection is now *bound* to a project: `config.project_id`/`project_name` are recorded from the token's own `owner` block at every point a token verifies — the wizard's `/test` probe (which already fetched the project name and threw it away), and both vault slots — and a token that opens a different project is refused with **400 `project_mismatch`** naming both projects. The same check runs at sync time, where the preflight has already fetched the owner so it costs nothing, and fails that source before the Metastore is touched rather than importing across projects. Both admin pages now show the project name and id, since the stack host alone renders identically for every project on a stack. **Behaviour change**: storing a Keboola *storage* token now preflights it upstream (that is where a connection's project identity comes from), so a Storage API outage blocks storing one instead of accepting a token nobody has checked; and the `AGNES_VAULT_KEY` 409 is now raised *before* any upstream call, so an instance that cannot store secrets says so instead of spending a round-trip and reporting a token error it never had. Identity is only ever recorded from a payload that actually carries an `owner.id` — an unreadable identity must not be persisted as a known one, or the mismatch check compares against a hole and passes anything. Two more the same review caught: **Test connection** reports a disagreement as a failed test instead of re-binding the connection (the token it resolves is not necessarily the one that established the binding — `_resolve_token` falls back to `token_env` — so overwriting there would leave the stored master token failing a mismatch nobody caused), and a stored master token that is later *downgraded* upstream now answers **400** whether or not other Keboola connections exist: the multi-source loop captures `MasterTokenRequiredError` per connection instead of letting it propagate, so without a code the aggregate fell back to 502 and the identical misconfiguration reported differently depending on how many projects were connected.

- **"Test" on a Keboola data source reported OK for any token, including a wrong one.** It probed `GET /v2/storage?exclude=components`, which measured live is the *unauthenticated* stack index: it answers **200 with no token at all** and carries no `owner` block. So the button only ever proved the host was reachable, and the `project_name` it returned to the wizard was always the empty string — the reason the "Add Keboola project" flow could never name the project it had just connected. It now calls `GET /v2/storage/tokens/verify`, which rejects a bad token with 401 and returns the real project name and id. Found while wiring project identity into that handler: the identity code read an `owner` block the old endpoint never returns, so it was dead code whose tests passed only because they mocked a payload the API does not produce.
- **BREAKING** **The new storage-token read bypassed the `token_env` allowlist the other read paths enforce.** An admin can set `token_env` to any name, so an ungated `os.environ.get(token_env)` turns a connection row into a way to read an arbitrary host environment variable — the value is then sent to the configured stack as a Storage token, and on this page its resolved project identity is rendered back to the admin. `/test` and `/tables` gate exactly this read behind `is_token_env_allowed` with an explicit SECURITY comment; both places this module resolves a token from the environment now go through ONE gated reader, and a disallowed name is logged and skipped. The sibling read in `_resolve_keboola_credentials_slot` was ungated too — pre-existing rather than introduced here, but leaving one of two reads in a module gated is the shape that gets the gate removed later as "inconsistent". **This is a behaviour change for the sync**, stated rather than slipped in: an instance whose `token_env` names something outside `AGNES_REMOTE_ATTACH_TOKEN_ENVS` (default `KBC_TOKEN`, `KBC_STORAGE_TOKEN`, `KEBOOLA_STORAGE_TOKEN`, …) stops syncing on upgrade until the name is added to that list. The trade is deliberate — the ungated read let an admin point a connection at any host environment variable and have its value sent to the stack as a Storage token — and the refusal logs the name it rejected, so the remedy is visible rather than guessed. Found by Devin Review on this PR.

- **A sync that imported glossary terms but no metrics read as "ran, imported nothing".** The last-sync cell judged the run on `created_or_updated` alone, and a project that publishes terms and no metrics is a normal shape the sync itself documents — so admins were sent looking for a fault that was not there. Glossary writes now count, and the success line names them. A genuinely empty run still says so. Found by Devin Review on this PR.

- **Three more coverage-report defects, all found by Devin Review on this PR.** (1) **A metric blocked only by an unregistered table was filed as an unfixable definition defect.** Two Agnes-side failures — the joined table is not registered here, or is registered without its columns — fell back to the generic `foreign_alias_reference`, which the report classifies as "blocked by their own definition", so the admin was told registering a table would not help when that is exactly the fix. Those two now carry `unresolved_joined_table`, deliberately a new REASON and not a new counter: it folds into `skipped_foreign_alias`, so the published per-source counters are unchanged. (2) **Coverage judged name ownership differently from the sync on the default project.** It passed `adopt_null=False` while the sync passes `adopt_null=(connection_id == default_id)`, so a legacy unattributed row the sync would adopt was reported as a conflict — telling the admin a metric will not import when it will, which is the direction that costs them the most. (3) **An empty orange warning strip rendered under every Keboola connection card**: `display: flex` beats the UA sheet's `[hidden] { display: none }`, so the token-mismatch box showed even with nothing to warn about.

- **The coverage report's empty-state hint printed a command that cannot be run.** It told the operator to run `agnes admin connection secret --id <connection> --kind master`, but `connection_id` is a positional argument there — copying the line fails with "No such option: --id", and an admin with no configured project concludes the feature is broken. Guarded structurally rather than by string match: every `agnes …` command this module prints is resolved against the real Typer app, and each `--flag` must be a real option of the command it targets. Found by Devin Review on this PR.
- The search advice no longer tells people and agents to avoid the query this change makes work. Every surface said "filenames are not indexed" — the two hint texts and both MCP tool descriptions — so an agent was instructed away from the exact search that now succeeds. They describe the fallback instead, including the `matched_on: "filename"` / low-confidence label a name hit carries. That label also caps the damage a weak name match can do: `_minmax` maps any bucket's top hit to 1.0, so a name-only chunk bucket would have arrived looking as strong as a document that really contains the words and could fill every slot of a combined answer — it now takes the same proportional share the semantic buckets get. And `agnes search --local` / the stdio MCP fallback run the same fallback offline, so the same query no longer answers differently depending on whether the server is reachable. Found by Devin Review on this PR.

- **Every brokered clone silently negotiated the v0 git protocol.** Modern git sends `Git-Protocol: version=2` on the initial `info/refs` GET and the git surface turns it into `GIT_PROTOCOL` for `git http-backend`; the proxy forwarded only `Authorization` and `Content-Type`, so the header never arrived and every clone through the relay fell back to v0 — correct output, but the entire ref advertisement on each call rather than the filtered v2 one. Forwarded verbatim; it carries no credential, and the header set stays an allowlist rather than becoming a passthrough (guarded). Found by Devin Review on this PR.

- **Two more on the relay path, both found by Devin Review.** Cloning a **draft** through the relay could not work: a draft shares its PARENT's repository — `create_draft` never gives it one of its own — so a token minted for the draft slug is refused by the git surface (whose scope pins the slug to the repo being requested) and `repo_path(<draft_slug>)` has no HEAD. Both the token and the proxy target now resolve to the parent, while ownership is still checked against the app the caller named. That is the path the data-apps skill actually walks. And the skill told the assistant to copy the scaffold "into the app's managed repo" **before** the section explaining how to obtain that repo, so a run following it in order reached the copy step with nothing to copy into; the cloning section now comes first.

- **Two defects in the git-over-relay path itself, both found by Devin Review.** (1) **A push bigger than a few kilobytes arrived empty.** The relay read a request body only when the sender declared a `Content-Length`, and git switches to `Transfer-Encoding: chunked` past a small threshold — so a chunked request was forwarded with no content at all. Small pushes, being sized, worked, which made it look like a size limit rather than a missing code path. The relay now reassembles chunked bodies (tolerating chunk extensions, and consuming trailers so a kept-alive connection does not desynchronise). (2) **`$AGNES_SERVER_BASE` existed only in the skill's prose.** The data-apps skill tells the in-sandbox assistant to clone from `$AGNES_SERVER_BASE/data-apps.git/<slug>`, nothing set it, and the command expanded to an empty base. It is now set next to `AGNES_SERVER` — the relay's origin without the `/agnes-api` path, since `data-apps.git` is served off the relay root.
- **Two follow-ups on this PR's own fixes, both found by Devin Review.** The warning about a saved authentication method Agnes no longer supports vanished the SECOND time the edit form was opened: the notice fires when the stored value has no matching `<option>`, and the first open inserts one for it, so the check poisoned itself. The injected option is now marked and cleared before the check, which re-evaluates against the real list every time. And the "Chat tools" switch read "on" for a derived source that is **disabled** — it was computed from row existence alone, while enable and the edit re-sync both deliberately carry a previously-set `enabled=False` over, so toggling the switch off and on (the obvious remedy) did nothing because the row was there all along.

- **Editing an MCP server saved under the removed "custom header" method silently set its auth to none.** A `<select>` handed a value with no matching `<option>` selects the FIRST one, so opening such a server and saving an unrelated field rewrote its stored authentication — the very setting this PR removed the option for because it never worked. The stale value is now surfaced as a disabled option with a warning naming it, so the admin has to choose a real method rather than having one chosen for them. Found by Devin Review on this PR.

- **Three interactions between this PR's own fixes, all found by Devin Review.** (1) **Clear-then-store left the agent with no credential while the switch still read "on".** Clearing deletes the agent's copy and storing propagated only when a copy already existed, so the two fixes cancelled each other out; propagation is now keyed on the derived SOURCE, which is what says chat tools are on. (2) **An unrelated edit switched a deliberately-disabled server back on.** `build_stdio_spec` always describes an *enabled* source — it is written for the enable path — and the re-sync upserted it wholesale. The flag is state the admin owns, not something derived from the connection, so the EDIT path carries it over. The **enable** endpoint deliberately does not: it is what the page's switch calls to turn chat tools on, so a stored "off" must not survive it — an earlier revision preserved it there too and the switch could then never turn a disabled server back on, reporting success while leaving it off. Re-running enable is no longer needed to refresh a rotated token either, since storing one propagates on its own path. (3) **A rename onto a name another MCP source already holds is skipped with a warning** naming the clash, rather than letting the unique-constraint violation raise into the broad handler, which logged it as an unexpected failure and told the admin nothing.

- **Editing a connection left the chat agent pointed at the old address.** `build_stdio_spec` bakes the connection's name and `stack_url` into the derived MCP source, and nothing rebuilt it on edit — so after an admin moved a project to a new stack the agent kept querying the previous one, under the previous label. Worse in combination with the token propagation above: a freshly rotated credential was being copied to a source still aimed at the old address. The spec is now rebuilt from the connection row after every update. Only an existing derived source is touched, so this never enables chat tools, and the credential slot is not written on this path at all. Found by Devin Review on this PR.

- **Four more on the chat-tools pair, all found by Devin Review on this PR.** (1) **Clearing a project's stored token left the agent holding a working copy.** Enabling copies the storage token into the MCP vault, and clearing the connection's token — the obvious way to cut a project off — did not touch that copy, so the agent kept querying the project with a credential the admin believed they had removed. `DELETE /{id}/secret` now clears the derived copy too (storage kind only; the master token is a different slot). The source and its tools stay, so the admin still sees the switch is on and turns it off deliberately — what goes is the credential, which is what "cleared" has to mean. **Storing one propagates the same way**, for the same reason: the two halves of one admin intent behaved differently, so rotating a leaked token left the leaked value live in the MCP vault while clearing cut it off, and the agent kept authenticating with a credential that may already have been revoked upstream. Only an existing copy is updated, so this is not a back door to enabling chat tools. (2) **A failed removal of the tools no longer deletes the source.** `list_passthrough_for_groups` joins `tool_registry` to `tool_grants` and never to `mcp_sources`, so a tool whose parent source is gone is **still served** to any granted group — continuing past that failure left the access live while removing the row an admin would use to clean it up from `/admin/mcp`. Failures further down (the credential, per-user rows) still continue, because those leave nothing addressable. (3) **A derived name already taken answers `409` with what clashed** instead of an opaque `500`: `mcp_sources.name` is unique, and a hand-registered source can already hold the name derived from the connection. (4) The CLI's next-step line pointed at `agnes admin grant`, which cannot grant MCP tools, to grant tools that enabling does not create — the same wrong instruction the admin page carried, on the surface that was missed when the page was fixed. Both now name Introspect.

- **A connection's `stack_url` was never checked on the way in.** `_validate_stack_url`'s `required=False` branch was written for `create_connection` and `update_connection` and wired into neither, so the branch had no caller anywhere and an admin-supplied URL was stored without even a scheme check — while the chat-tools enable path skipped validation on the stated premise that the stored URL had already been validated there. Both handlers now call it with `resolve=False`: the **scheme** is enforced at store time, and the private/reserved-range half stays at use (`/test`, `/tables`, `/secret`), which is where it belongs — it needs DNS, and refusing to *save* a stack that does not resolve from the Agnes host yet (a fresh deployment, split-horizon DNS, a momentary outage) would fail configuration for a reason unrelated to the connection. Validate-at-use is also the only placement that closes DNS rebinding, and it is unchanged. Found by Devin Review on this PR, which correctly flagged the enable path's comment as citing a guard that did not run.

- **Three follow-ups on this PR, all found by Devin Review.** (1) **Turning chat tools off could report success while nothing was removed.** Each teardown step sat under `except Exception: logger.debug(…)`, which cannot tell "there was nothing to delete" from "the delete did not work" — so an admin cutting access could be answered `204` with the tools, the grants and the copied credential all still live. Only the **tools and grants** step is fatal — it is the one that is access, it outlives its source row, and nothing has been removed yet, so the caller can retry and the message can honestly name a source that still exists. It reports `500 chat_tools_not_fully_removed`, naming what is still present and where to remove it by hand; a failure past that point leaves ORPHANED MATERIAL rather than access — the grants are already gone — so it is logged with exactly what to clean up and does not block the operation. Raising there made `delete_connection`, which runs the teardown before dropping the row, permanently unfinishable on a persistent vault fault: the retry re-ran the same failing step forever and the connection could never be deleted. The broad catch was never load-bearing for idempotency — each repository's `delete` is a `DELETE … WHERE id = ?`, a no-op on a row that is not there — and a clean disable is still `204` and still repeatable. (2) **The "custom header" authentication method is removed from both MCP admin screens.** Choosing it produced a source that connected with **no** credential at all and said nothing: `connectors/mcp/client.py::_build_http_headers` has no branch for `auth_method='header'`. The option is gone rather than implemented, and `tests/test_keboola_chat_tools.py` now fails the build if either template offers an auth method the client cannot build credentials for. An operator who had selected it was already running without authentication; the source keeps its stored value and must be moved to `bearer`, `basic` or `oauth`. (3) **The enabled-state hint promised tools that enabling does not create.** It read "Tools are registered. Grant them to a group under Access", but enabling writes only the `mcp_sources` row and the vault secret — the `tool_registry` rows the Access screen grants from come from the separate Introspect step on the source detail page, so the admin arrived at a grant screen with nothing on it. The hint now names Introspect as the next step. Two more, on the fix itself: raising a structured `500` made **ordering** matter in `delete_connection`, which tore the chat tools down *after* deleting the row — so a hiccup answered "delete failed" for a connection that was already gone, the retry 404'd, and the leftover tools had no obvious route to removal. The teardown now runs first, which makes the failure honest and the operation repeatable. And the admin page rendered that structured detail as `[object Object]`, throwing away the list of what was still live; a FastAPI `detail` is a string on some paths and an object on others, so all five toasts on the page now go through one `detailMessage()` reader that renders `message`/`error` plus whichever list the path carries (`tables`, `still_present`).

- **Turning a project's chat tools off left its tools and their group permissions behind, and a failed re-sync wiped a working project's credential.** Two defects in the enable/disable pair, both found by Devin Review on this PR. (1) `_remove_chat_tools` deleted the `mcp_sources` row and the vault secret, but the tools discovered under that source live in `tool_registry` keyed by source id and their per-group permissions live in `tool_grants` keyed by tool — neither is reached by deleting the source row. Because `derived_source_id()` is a pure function of the connection id, re-enabling lands on the *same* source id and adopts whatever was left, so an admin who turned chat tools off to revoke access and later turned them back on silently restored the exact grants they had revoked; deleting the connection entirely left the same rows orphaned forever. It now mirrors `admin_mcp.delete_mcp_source` — `delete_for_source` drops the grants per tool before the registry rows, and per-user secrets go the same way, for the same "no orphaned credential material" reason that path already cites. The OAuth trio is deliberately not touched: the derived source is stdio. (2) Enabling is idempotent by design — re-running is how a rotated token is propagated — so on a re-sync the vault slot being written is the credential the existing, still-live setup authenticates with. The rollback for a failed config write deleted that slot unconditionally, turning a working project's every tool call into an auth failure: strictly worse than the failed re-sync the admin came to fix. The previous value is now read before the write and put back on failure; a *first* enable still deletes, so the original guarantee (never leave a token under a source id that does not exist) is unchanged and pinned by its own test.

### Internal

- **`test_drain_budget_is_shared_across_the_whole_shutdown` was flaky under parallel CI load, and too loose to test what it claimed.** It slept 0.3s and asserted the remaining shutdown-drain budget was `9.7 ± 0.5`; with 8 shards on one runner the sleep overshoots (an observed failure measured ~1.3s of real time for it, leaving 8.71s), failing PRs whose diffs never touched the shutdown path. The measurement was also weaker than it looked: `± 0.5` spans `[9.2, 10.2]`, so the reverted behaviour — every drain getting a *fresh* full timeout, i.e. `10.0` — sat inside the accepted window, and only the separate `second < first` assertion caught it at all. The test now advances a fake monotonic clock instead of sleeping and asserts exact remaining values (`10.0`, `9.75`, `9.25`) across three reads. The clock is patched into `health_probes`' own module namespace rather than onto stdlib `time`, which is process-global and also times the event loop and pytest's own bookkeeping; only `monotonic` is provided, so a future `time.*` call added to the module fails loudly rather than silently mixing a real clock into a frozen one. Mutation-checked both ways: a per-call budget now fails on the value (`10.0 != 9.75`), and a subtler regression that charges each drain only the time since the *previous* drain — rather than since `begin_shutdown` — fails the third read (`9.5 != 9.25`) where the old two-measurement version passed it clean.

- **`test_each_shutdown_gets_its_own_budget` could not see the regression it was written for.** It asserted a second `begin_shutdown` produced a deadline `>= first` and a budget of `10.0 ± 0.5` — but on real time the two shutdowns are microseconds apart, so a `begin_shutdown` that re-armed from the *first* start instead of from now satisfied both: the stale deadline is trivially `>= first`, and the budget it yields is still ~`10.0` because no measurable time has passed. The test now advances the same fake clock by 4s between the two shutdowns, which is what makes "fresh" checkable, and pins exact values: the deadline must be `first + 4.0` (re-armed from now, not from the first start) and the budget a whole `10.0` (not the first budget's remains). Verified against two mutants — re-arming from the original start (`1010.0 != 1014.0`, which the old version passed clean) and the arm-once-per-process bug the docstring names (`None != 1014.0`).

- **The last `± 0.5` window in the drain-budget tests tolerated a drift that cannot occur.** `test_routine_cancellation_does_not_arm_the_shutdown_budget` asserted the unshared budget was `10.0 ± 0.5`, but with no deadline armed `_drain_budget_s` returns the configured timeout outright without reading the clock — so there was never anything to tolerate, and the tolerance instead concealed any margin applied to that path: a 2% headroom shaved off the timeout yields `9.8`, which sits inside the window. Now asserted exactly, and confirmed by mutation (`9.8 != 10.0`, where the window returned true). No `pytest.approx` remains in the module's budget assertions.

## [0.83.4] - 2026-08-10
### Added

- **`agnes admin metrics import --prune` — the metric registry can finally shrink** (#1219). The import was upsert-only, so a metric deleted upstream stayed forever and a rename left both ids behind, indistinguishable from a hand-authored one; the practical effect was that an instance whose semantic layer is generated from an external catalog could never be re-synced, only added to. `--prune` reconciles the registry against the directory, and what it may delete is keyed on the **writer**, never on the id: the scope is `source='yaml_import'`, so a metric an admin wrote in the UI (`manual`) or a connector created (`keboola_semantic_layer`) is out of reach by construction rather than by luck. `--source-ref <label>` **partitions** it further and stamps the rows as it imports — two YAML exports into one instance otherwise share `source='yaml_import'`, and the second import would delete the first's metrics. Each label owns its own rows and the unlabeled import owns the unlabeled ones, so labelling an export protects it from every other import rather than only from other labelled ones. `--dry-run` reports the same added/updated/deleted breakdown and writes nothing, which is the recommended first run because a rename reads as delete + create at the id level. Two prune shapes are refused outright rather than obeyed, because both are nearly always a mistyped or half-written path and both would empty the scope: pointing `--prune` at a single **file**, and any input from which no metric parses — a directory one level too shallow globs to nothing (the layout is `<dir>/<category>/<name>.yml`) and a truncated export has files that yield nothing, both of which asked prune to delete everything. A **partial** failure is refused too, and it is the likeliest of the three: in a half-written export the files that did not parse look exactly like metrics the source dropped, so the error names them instead. Every refusal is decided from the parsed input before any row is written, so a refused run leaves the registry exactly as it found it rather than half-applying the readable files. **`POST /api/admin/metrics/import` now stamps `source='web_upload'` instead of `yaml_import`**, because it shared the CLI import's scope and a metric uploaded through the admin page is in no directory — so the next prune run took it as deleted upstream. Rows uploaded that way *before* this release are indistinguishable from CLI-imported ones and stay in scope; `--dry-run` lists them, and re-uploading re-stamps them. Each deletion writes an audit row (`metrics.prune`) **before** the row goes, not after and with `result="attempted"` rather than a success it cannot yet vouch for — this is the only destructive metric path and it runs direct against the repository with no API request behind it, so an interruption between the two would leave a metric deleted with nothing saying so. The report also distinguishes **adopted** from added: an incoming id that already belongs to another writer is overwritten and re-stamped by the upsert, which moves it into this importer's prune scope — calling that an addition told the operator a new metric would appear while a hand-authored one was being taken over. The default is unchanged — without `--prune` the command still only adds, and now says so in its output instead of letting a clean import read as "everything is in sync". A file the importer cannot read is skipped rather than aborting the directory, but the skip is now listed on stderr — silence let a partial import read as a complete one. The import also reads `.yaml` as well as `.yml`, which was merely incomplete before and became destructive once prune read "not in the directory" as "deleted upstream". Implemented on the shared `MetricYamlMixin`, so DuckDB and Postgres get identical behaviour, pinned by `tests/db_pg/test_ported_methods_contract.py`.

- **Native `<select>` dropdowns replaced with a custom design-system component, across most of the app (#1055)**: a `ds.dropdown()` macro (`_components.html`) + `ds_dropdown.css` + `js/components/ds_dropdown.js`, generalizing the chat composer's "+" upload menu (button + `role="menu"` popover, arrow-key nav, Enter/Space, Esc, outside-click) into an accessible select-replacement — items are `role="menuitemradio"` rather than the upload menu's plain `menuitem`, since these choices are mutually exclusive like a `<select>`. On every conversion the real `<select>` stays in the DOM unchanged for existing `change`-event wiring — the macro pairs a dropdown to it via `target`, and on selection the JS sets `.value` on the select and dispatches `change` so callers don't need to change. Which UI is visible is a CSS/theme decision, not a template one: a paired dropdown defers to its native `<select>` by default (zero visual change under the default theme), and `paper-skin.css` claims the control visually under `[data-theme="paper"]`. **Converted** (28 selects across 15 templates): My Stack sort + visibility filter, Activity Center's window/result/resource filters, admin usage/sessions time-range + group-by, admin MCP sources/source-detail transport-scope-auth pickers, profile's token-TTL, contribute-skill's group picker, store-upload's category, first-time-setup's data-source picker, Library's and Workspace's sort controls, admin store-submissions' type/per-page filters, admin users' group filter, and admin Studio's select-type domain fields. **Deliberately left native** where a paired dropdown would either regress behavior or need the shared component itself extended (each documented in its template with a `#1055:` comment): selects whose options are rebuilt by JS at runtime with no re-init hook (facet filters on admin usage/sessions/activity-center, admin linked-apps wizard, admin prompts' git-path picker, admin user-detail's add-group, marketplace's sort, skills' category), a `multiple` select (admin knowledge-digests' sources — the component is single-choice only), a select gated `disabled` while a submission is under review (store-edit's category, where a dropdown would bypass the lock), already-hidden legacy shims kept only for back-compat (`_profile_tokens.html` / admin-tokens' old filter pair), Catalog's recipe-status pickers (`catalog_legacy.html` is a frozen legacy copy — no new features land on the legacy path), and `admin_server_config.html` in full (flagged bespoke/risky by #497; its two selects are JS-templated after load). `admin_corporate_memory.html` (25 selects, its own 3,951-line template) is out of scope here — left for a dedicated follow-up, per the same precedent #497 set for that file.

### Changed

- **/home install guide, steps 1 and 4 slimmed down to what the user actually runs.** Step 1's copy-box is now just the official Claude Code installer per OS (`irm https://claude.ai/install.ps1 | iex` on Windows, `curl -fsSL https://claude.ai/install.sh | bash` on macOS/Linux) — one command on one dark box; the previous self-healing one-liner (already-installed check, in-session PATH fix, trailing version check in one line) read as a wall of shell to the non-technical audience the page serves, and the installer is idempotent anyway. Verify (`claude --version`), the one-time OAuth sign-in with `claude` plus the `/exit` return to the terminal, and the command-not-found remedy ("close and reopen the terminal" — which also covers the lost in-session PATH fix) live as inline text under the box, not a second copy-box. Step 4's sign-in sentence adapts: first launch opens the browser sign-in only for users who skipped it in step 1. Step 4's launch command drops the `command -v claude` guard and its "CLI not found" else-branch: it now only writes the token file and launches Claude with the auto-mode flags. Accepted trade-off: when the CLI is missing, the 0600 token file now stays on disk while the launch fails with "command not found" (the copy routes that to reopen-terminal / re-run step 1; a retry paste overwrites the file and `agnes init` deletes it after use).

- **Publishing surfaces say so when automated review cannot run.** With guardrails enabled and no LLM provider configured, a submission parks at `pending_llm` — hidden from everyone — until an admin retries it. The server has always logged this at boot; the person about to publish had no way to know, and the surrounding copy promises "a few seconds" in three separate places. `/store/new` and the Builder now carry a warning when the provider is missing.

- A failure to load the static `CONFIG_DIR/instance.yaml` is logged at ERROR rather than WARNING, and says what the consequence is: the app keeps serving, on built-in defaults, for every section the writable overlay does not cover. One mistyped key is enough — the instance then runs under the wrong name, the wrong data source and the wrong auth domain, with a single log line as the only evidence. `app.instance_config.get_static_config_error()` now exposes the reason, for a future admin UI to consume — nothing renders it yet. That accessor could itself raise on precisely the instance it exists to explain: it calls `load_instance_config()` before reading the cached reason, and on a process where the writable overlay is unreadable and nothing good has ever loaded, that call raises `InstanceConfigUnreadable` instead of falling back. It now catches that and returns the reason as a string, like any other diagnostic.

### Fixed

- **A Jira webhook updated the raw JSON but never the parquet, so an edit to an already-ingested issue silently never reached the data.** `trigger_incremental_transform` called `transform_single_issue` with no paths, leaving it to resolve its own defaults — and its raw-directory default is derived from `DATA_DIR` (`$DATA_DIR/extracts/<source>/raw`), which bears no relation to `JIRA_DATA_DIR`, the variable the writing half (`save_issue`) actually uses. On any deployment where the two do not coincide — including the **default** one, where `JIRA_DATA_DIR` is unset and the writer lands on the legacy raw path — every webhook transform failed with `Issue JSON not found` while the endpoint still answered Jira `200`. Jira recorded a successful delivery, nothing retried, and the only trace was one ERROR line per event. What made the connector look healthy is that *new* issues kept arriving anyway: the consistency check backfills issues missing from the parquet **by key**, so row counts grew and `max(created_at)` tracked reality while the contents of existing rows — comments, status, changelog, refreshed fields — stayed frozen at whatever their first backfill captured. The raw directory is now passed explicitly, off the same `Config` the writer reads, as `scripts/consistency_check.py` has always done. The **SLA poller carried the identical bug** — `scripts/poll_sla.py` wrote the refreshed JSON under `JIRA_DATA_DIR` and then called the transform with no paths at all, so refreshed field values never reached the data either — and is anchored the same way. `output_dir` is deliberately left unset at every call site: its default is the extract.duckdb-contract location the orchestrator serves, whereas `JIRA_PARQUET_DIR` — the obvious variable to forward — denotes the **legacy Data Broker root** everywhere else in this connector (`jira.env.example.txt`, `scripts/consistency_check.py`, `scripts/poll_sla.py`), which nothing serves. Forwarding it would have pushed webhook writes off the served layout on exactly the installs that set it, reintroducing this bug from the other side, and would additionally have broken `update_meta`, which derives the extract dir as `output_dir.parent` and assumes the `<source>/data` shape. Guarded by `tests/test_jira_webhook_transform_paths.py` in two layers: the webhook path asserted against `JiraService().data_dir` itself rather than a literal, plus a source-level sweep that fails if **any** call site in the connector omits `raw_dir`, so a future caller cannot reintroduce it silently. The detection gap is **not** closed by this change: the consistency check compares issue keys, not freshness, so it reports zero discrepancies while every row is stale — which is why this went unnoticed rather than being caught the first time a comment failed to land.

- **Streaming agent replies arrived as `delta: null`, so a client assembling the answer from deltas saw nothing.** The AG-UI mapper read a `token` frame's text off `frame["content"]`, but the runner emits `{"type": "token", "text": piece}` — `content` is the *`assistant_message`* field, one branch further down the same function. Every `TEXT_MESSAGE_CONTENT` event on `POST /api/v1/sessions/{id}/messages` therefore carried a null delta, and only the trailing `TEXT_MESSAGE_END` (which reads the right field) held the text. The visible symptom was `agnes chat <slug> --once "…"` printing `(no answer)` on a turn that had in fact answered — the CLI accumulates deltas, finds an empty string, and says so; `--json` showed the full reply sitting in the terminal event, which is what made the bug look like a CLI problem rather than a server one. Nothing caught it because the unit and wire-contract fixtures were hand-written to match the mapper (`{"type": "token", "content": …}`), a frame shape the runner has never emitted — the suite was green against a frame that does not exist. `tests/test_agent_sse.py::TestMapperFieldsMatchRealEmitters` now derives what the mapper reads from its OWN ast (the `frame.get("…")` calls per `if ftype == …` branch) and diffs that against the fields real emitters in `app/chat/` write, so neither side can drift alone; its companion test pins that both extractors actually matched something, since a drift check that silently parses nothing asserts nothing. The `tool_call` branch already carried a comment warning about exactly this trap for `tool`/`args` — the guard now enforces for every branch what that comment asked reviewers to remember.

- **The CLI answered a moved server with a bare `HTTP 308:` and no destination.** A deployment that changes hostname typically leaves the old name answering a permanent redirect; httpx does not follow redirects, so every `api_*` helper handed its caller the 3xx and the shared renderer printed the status with the empty body of a redirect — no new address, no remedy, on every command the user ran. `cli/client.py` now stops on any 3xx with an actionable message naming the destination and how to re-point (`AGNES_SERVER=…` for one call, or the `server:` key in the config file). Deliberately *not* fixed by following the redirect: httpx strips `Authorization` on a cross-origin hop, so the retry would land unauthenticated and report `401 Not authenticated` — the same failure under a more confusing name, and a credential-scope change for anyone whose old hostname is no longer theirs. A same-origin or relative redirect gets a different message, since telling that user to re-point at the host they already use is noise.

- **An agent named in the builder kept the placeholder slug `agent`.** `/agents` creates the row when "New agent" is clicked — before a name exists — so `create_agent` falls back to the literal slug `agent` (then `agent-2`, …), and `update_agent` wrote every field the builder sent except the slug. That slug is the public address (`POST /api/v1/agents/{slug}/responses`, `agnes chat <slug>`), and the builder displays it nowhere, so an agent shown as "Revenue Analyst" answered on `/agent` and the only way to discover that was to enumerate the API. Renaming a draft now re-derives the slug through the same per-owner uniqueness search, so the address matches what the agent is called. Bounded on purpose, since a slug is an address: it follows the name only while the agent is a `draft` AND its slug still tracks that name, so marking it ready freezes the address and a slug set by any other means is left alone; a rename to something unsluggable can't push the agent onto `agent-2` either. Re-deriving on every draft rename — rather than once, off the placeholder — is what the builder's save behaviour requires: it PATCHes each field edit behind a debounce, so pausing mid-word flushes a partial name, and a once-only rule would latch onto that fragment and hand the finished agent the address `rev`, uncorrectable from the UI. The uniqueness search is scoped to the agent's **owner**, not the caller: an admin may PATCH someone else's agent, and scoping to the admin would report a slug free that the owner already holds, turning the rename into a `(owner_user_id, slug)` UNIQUE violation. Two more bounds the same review found on the rule itself: the seeded **default agent is exempt** — it holds the reserved `default` slug that `POST /api/v1/agents/default/responses` and every web chat's attribution resolve through, and it is seeded with no status (so it is a *permanent* draft the builder will happily rename), which would have relocated that address with nothing to ever freeze it again; and a slug that **already tracks the new name, suffix included, is left alone** — the builder re-sends the unchanged name on every field edit, and the uniqueness search has no notion of the row being updated, so an agent legitimately sitting on `revenue-analyst-2` (a sibling holds the base) was counted as occupying its own slug and walked up to `-3`, then `-4`, on each ordinary save, up to the 999 cap. All four caught by Devin Review on this PR. Required whitelisting `slug` in the agents repository — in **both** backends, plus a contract test asserting the two `_UPDATABLE` sets are identical: nothing compared them before, so widening one would have left the other raising `ValueError` on the very write this depends on, a one-backend outage the per-backend tests cannot see.

- **`agnes agent list` / `show` refused with a sentence that read like a CLI bug.** `/api/v1/agents` management routes require interactive owner auth by design — a PAT must not be able to mint another PAT or re-scope an agent — but those subcommands authenticate with the PAT `agnes auth login` stores, so they can never succeed, and the CLI printed the server's `This endpoint requires an interactive session, not a PAT` verbatim with no way forward. The shared error renderer now appends where to go (the instance's `/agents` page) and which agent commands *do* work from a terminal (`agnes agent ask`, `agnes chat`). The boundary itself is unchanged.

- **`test_labelling_a_long_query_stays_linear` was both flaky and, more importantly, not testing what it says.** It failed a shard with `small=1.4ms large=912ms` — a 656x ratio on 8x the input, which reads as catastrophically superlinear but was one stalled sample on a loaded runner; both sides are best-of-5 now, since descheduling and GC pauses only ever add time. Investigating that surfaced the real problem: the assertion `large < max(small * 20, 0.5)` never reached its ratio. The parser handles 3200 joins in ~9 ms and a deliberately quadratic stand-in takes ~54 ms, so BOTH cleared the 0.5 s floor — the quadratic regression the test is named for could have landed green. The floor is 5 ms now (just above honest linear cost, which is all a noise guard needs to be) and the inputs moved to 400/3200 so `small` sits far enough above timer resolution for the ratio to mean something. Verified by mutation against a quadratic implementation: linear 8.3x passes, quadratic 57x fails.

- **The agent builder's Preview looked like a chat box and swallowed what you typed.** The preview card renders the app's real composer pill — placeholder text plus a filled send button — but it is a static mock with no input element behind it, so clicking and typing did nothing and read as a broken chat. It stays a mock (the builder cannot run a turn), but stops advertising itself as one: `aria-hidden` keeps a fake textbox out of the accessibility tree, `cursor: default` + `user-select: none` withdraw the cues that invite typing, and the card carries a "Preview only — not a live chat" note, since the `Preview` heading sits outside the card and can be scrolled off on a narrow column.

- **Renaming an agent in the builder could silently move the public address of an agent created through the governance API.** `POST /api/v1/agents` requires an explicit, caller-chosen slug and refuses to change it afterwards (`PUT` 400s `slug_immutable`) — the agent is published by definition the moment it exists. But that route never set a `status`, and both repositories COALESCE a missing one to `'draft'` — the same state a `/agents` builder placeholder sits in before it is named. The builder's draft-rename rule (above, `_draft_slug_rename`) only freezes a slug once the agent is `'ready'`, so a governance-created agent's deliberately-chosen slug — the one a PAT may already be minted against — stayed renameable forever through an ordinary `/agents` field-edit save: create with `slug='my-bot'`, PATCH the name from the builder, and the agent answers on `my-bot` no longer. `create_agent` now sets `status='ready'`, an API-visible change to that route's create response. A one-time migration (schema v115, `src/db.py::_v114_to_v115` / Alembic `0061_agent_status_backfill_v115`) closes the gap retroactively: it promotes every pre-existing `draft` row to `ready` UNLESS its `id` carries the builder's own `agt_` prefix (`POST /api/agents` mints one on every row it creates, named or not) or it is the seeded default agent (a *permanent* draft by design). A first version of this discriminator matched on the *slug* instead — the builder's placeholder lineage (`agent`, `agent-2`, …) versus anything else — and that was wrong: a builder draft the user had already named (e.g. `finance-bot`) is *also* still unpublished, but its slug no longer looks like a placeholder, so the slug check froze an address for an agent nobody had ever marked ready. The `id` prefix has no such gap — it is fixed at create time and never depends on how (or whether) the agent has been named since. The DuckDB step guards on `agents` already having `status`/`is_default` before it writes: a database still in the pre-merge paper-theme `agents` shape (`created_by`/`instructions`, no `is_default`) reaches this step stamped past it, and without the guard the `UPDATE` raised a DuckDB `Binder Error` and aborted startup before `_heal_legacy_agents_table` — which alone rebuilds that shape, and runs only after the migration ladder — ever got a chance to run.

- **Deleted Flea Market entities stayed on the admin's Browse shelf.** `agnes store delete` (and the UI's Delete) is a soft-delete: it flips the entity to `visibility_status='archived'`. Non-admins never see those — not even their own — but the admin branch of both the listing and the category counts passed *no* visibility filter, so every entity anyone had ever deleted stayed on the admin's shelf, badged **Quarantined** (which means blocked / under review, not deleted) and counted in the Browse tab total. Reproduced end to end on a live instance: a skill deleted seconds earlier was still on the shelf and the counter had gone up by one. Admin browse now shows every state *except* `archived`; deleted rows keep their own home on the Archived tab of `/admin/store/submissions`.

- **`agnes store delete` gave a non-interactive caller no way forward.** Without a terminal, the confirmation prompt reads EOF and aborts with a bare `Aborted.` and exit 1, naming no remedy — the shape hit from a chat sandbox, a CI step, or any agent context. The `--yes` flag existed but the failure never mentioned it. The command now detects the missing terminal and says which flag to re-run with. A review before merge found that guard was stricter than the prompt it replaced: it checked `sys.stdin.isatty()` *before* ever prompting, so a piped answer (`echo y | agnes store delete <id>`) aborted too, even though `typer.confirm` would have read it fine — breaking existing automation and one-liners that worked before this change. The command now attempts the confirmation first and only substitutes the actionable message when that confirmation itself hits true EOF (`typer.Abort`), so a pipe carrying a real "y" or "n" answer still works.

- **A chat message that opened with "add", "enable" or "install" never reached the model.** The in-chat Catalog shortcut matched `/^(?:add|enable|install)\s+(.+)/i` and claimed the whole turn, so *"Add the sales package to my stack. Then explain our churn definition"* was taken as a request for an item literally named *"the sales package to my stack. Then explain our churn definition"* — everything after the first clause was discarded, and the user got back a "couldn't find anything called …" quoting their own sentence. Worse, the matcher behind it awards 12 points per word found anywhere in an item's name, id **or description**, and any score above zero was enough to `subscribe()` with no confirmation: one incidental word shared with a long description could add something to the user's Stack that they never named. The shortcut now claims a message only when it is a short single clause (no sentence break, no newline, at most eight words) **and** the match is confident — an exact name or a substring hit. A lone weak candidate no longer counts as confident either: the confidence bar used to also accept a bag-of-words score `> 0` whenever exactly one addable item matched, so a single 12-point incidental-word hit could `subscribe()` on a fresh instance with only one package available — exactly the first-run case this shortcut targets. Anything below the bar now falls through to the model, which can ask what was meant, regardless of how many candidates matched. Found by driving the chat on a live instance. A review before merge found one more gap in the same shortcut: the word-count guard tolerates a trailing sentence terminator (`subject.replace(/[.!?]+$/, "")`), so a short imperative ending in punctuation isn't mistaken for prose, but the search query built right after it was still read off the raw capture — the dot rode along into `q` and broke the exact-name match, the substring match, and the per-token fallback alike, so `add sales-package.` silently failed to resolve while the identical message without the full stop worked. Both normalizations now read from the same stripped subject.

- **A chat could be titled with a refusal it never made.** Auto-titling asks Haiku for a 2–6 word title from the first user message; when that message reads as a direct question, Haiku sometimes answers it instead, and the sanitizer stored the answer verbatim — truncated at 60 characters, so it even looked like a title. Observed in production: a conversation that read the user's Stack and removed a plugin from it was listed in the sidebar as *"I don't have access to information about your stack or the…"*. The sidebar reported an outcome opposite to what happened, on a turn that had performed a write. Answer-shaped replies (leading first-person/assistant openers, or more than ten words) are now discarded in favour of the honest `Untitled chat` default, and the discard is logged.

- **A review that crashed had its bundle deleted 30 days later, silently making the documented retry impossible.** `review_error` is not a verdict — it means the LLM call timed out or crashed, so the submission was never judged, and `store_guardrails/llm_review.py` describes it as the state that "exposes a retry path" with "a retry button" in the admin queue. It was nevertheless listed in `TERMINAL_BLOCKED_STATUSES`, so the daily TTL sweep purged its bytes alongside genuinely rejected content. Found on a live instance: a skill whose inline checks (content, quality, manifest, static security) had all passed sat in `review_error` for a month, lost its bundle to the sweep, and can now never be reviewed or recovered — with nothing surfaced to its author. Un-judged submissions are no longer swept; an admin who wants the bytes gone can still Delete by hand. `docs/STORE_GUARDRAILS.md`'s retention-model section still said the TTL job purged `{blocked_inline, blocked_llm, review_error}`, which would have told an operator to expect bytes gone that are now deliberately retained — updated to match, and pinned by a test so the two cannot drift apart again.

- **Every query after the first one 500'd on a fresh instance.** `get_analytics_db_readonly()` opened `analytics/server.duckdb` **read-write** when the file did not exist yet and handed that connection to the caller. The file then existed, so every later call took the read-only branch — and DuckDB refuses to open a file read-only while a read-write connection to it is alive in the same process (`Can't open a connection to same database file with a different configuration than existing connections`). `app/api/query.py` never closes the handle, so on a fresh install the first request touching the query path poisoned every subsequent query in that process until restart, `SELECT 1` included. The branch now materializes the empty database and closes the write handle immediately, then falls through to the normal read-only open — which also means the first caller gets the same ATTACHed extracts and the same read-only guarantee as every caller after it, instead of a silently writable connection. A second door onto the same DuckDB restriction is fixed below: `app/api/mcp_per_table.py` held the read-write `get_analytics_db()` singleton, and once that was open the read-only factory failed the same way. That first fix left a narrower window open: the existence-check, the materialization, and the read-only open that follows it took no lock, so a thread already inside the create branch (its read-write handle still alive) could still lose a race to a second thread that observed the file already existing and reached its own read-only open first — the same `ConnectionException`, now bounded to the first-ever call(s) on a fresh install instead of every call thereafter. Both now run under the module's existing `_analytics_db_lock` (the same lock `get_analytics_db()` and `close_singleton_connections()` already serialize on), so every thread's open happens strictly after any other thread's transient read-write handle has closed; once the file exists permanently the section is a cheap no-op check plus a normal read-only open, so this costs nothing in steady state.

- **Any authenticated user could permanently break every `/api/query` and `/api/query/hybrid` request in the process.** `app/api/mcp_per_table.py`'s `POST /api/mcp/query-table/{table_id}` — gated only by authentication, since internal tables are auto-granted to everyone — read through `get_analytics_db()`, the process-wide read-write singleton, and nothing ever closed it. DuckDB refuses to open a file read-only while a read-write connection to it is alive in the same process, so the very next `get_analytics_db_readonly()` call (the path `/api/query` and `/api/query/hybrid` use) raised `ConnectionException: Can't open a connection to same database file with a different configuration than existing connections` — deterministically, for every request, until restart. Unlike the fresh-instance case above this wasn't a narrow startup race: the singleton stayed open for the rest of the process's life the moment anyone called the endpoint once. The endpoint now opens the same transient, per-call read-only connection `/api/query` and `/api/query/hybrid` already use instead of the long-lived writer — closed after each call, so it can never poison the read-only path. A smaller-looking fix — making the read-only factory degrade to a read-write-capable handle when it finds the singleton already open — was rejected: `/api/query` executes arbitrary caller-supplied SQL behind an app-level keyword blocklist, and the DuckDB-enforced read-only mode is the backstop for whatever that blocklist misses, so silently trading it away for one endpoint's convenience was the wrong side of that trade. A sibling leak in the same fresh-instance materialization step is fixed alongside it: `_open_duckdb()` (`src/duckdb_conn.py`) opens the connection before pinning its session timezone to UTC, and with `AGNES_DUCKDB_TZ_STRICT=1` a pin that didn't take raises `RuntimeError` from inside that helper — after the connection already exists, so the chained `_open_duckdb(...).close()` in the fresh-instance branch never reaches `.close()` and the write handle leaks for the life of the process, poisoning the very read-only open that follows it the same way. `_open_duckdb()` now closes the connection itself before raising. That fix closed the last production call site of `get_analytics_db()`; the invariant it existed to protect — nothing under `app/`, `cli/`, `services/`, or `connectors/` may hold that singleton open — is now spelled out on the function's own docstring and enforced by a static guard, so a future request-path caller reintroducing it fails the build instead of the process.

- **A table created from an uploaded file could not be reached through the Data Package that contained it.** `can_access_table` short-circuited on `source_type='collection'` and returned the *collection's* ACL, so package membership was a no-op for anything that arrived as a file upload. The admin-facing denial told the analyst to "ask an admin to add it to a Data Package you have access to"; doing exactly that changed nothing, while `/catalog` — which resolves through packages — showed the same table as in-stack and badged LOCAL. Catalog said yes, `agnes pull` said 403. Collection sharing is now an *additional* path rather than a replacement: owner-or-share still grants access, and a table that fails that check falls through to the data-package stack like any other table.

- **Signing in with a correct password dropped you on an unexplained "Reset Your Password" screen.** A password set by someone else (the seeded admin, or any admin-set password) forces a rotation before a session is issued — correct — but the web redirect carried no reason, so the page was indistinguishable from "you forgot your password" and a successful sign-in read as a rejected one. Every persona who met it spent extra requests proving their credentials were valid, one by deliberately signing in with a wrong password to compare the two responses. The redirect now carries `reason=must_change` and the page says what happened: "You signed in with a one-time password that was set for you." The JSON path already returned an explicit `403 password_change_required` and is unchanged. The explanation itself turned out to be just as fragile: the form posts back only `email`/`token`/`password`/`confirm_password`, so a mistyped confirmation or a too-short password re-rendered the form with no `reason` at all, silently swapping the forced-rotation copy back for the generic one on the very screen meant to prevent that confusion. `reset_confirm` now re-derives the reason from the account's own `must_change_password` flag on every error path it renders — the true state of the account, not something the client can carry (or forge) across the POST. That fix introduced an account-enumeration oracle of its own: the reason was derived by looking the account up **before** the reset token was validated at all, so an unauthenticated caller could post an arbitrary email with two deliberately mismatched passwords and read the rendered heading back to learn both whether the account exists and whether it's flagged for forced rotation — the same information `reset_request`/`setup_request`/`setup_page` are all careful never to leak, now leaking through the one surface the previous fix touched. `reset_confirm` now validates the token first — a non-consuming check, so a legitimate user who mistypes their confirmation still holds their token and doesn't burn it — and only derives the forced-rotation copy once that check passes; an invalid, expired, or absent token gets the generic "Invalid or expired reset link." regardless of whether the account behind the email exists or is flagged.

- **The only sign-in page on a password-only instance was headed "External User Access — For partners, investors, and other external users."** With no Google OAuth configured, `/login/password` is the single door for every employee and for the instance administrator, and it told them they were in the wrong place. The heading now follows what the instance actually offers: the external-user framing stays when SSO is available (where it is accurate), and an instance without it gets "Sign In".

- `.claude-plugin/marketplace-metadata.json`'s worked example in `docs/curated-marketplace-format.md` used `"Data analysis"` and `"Reporting"` as categories — neither is in `STORE_CATEGORIES`, which the same page documents four rows above. Copying the example the page says to copy produced an invalid category.

## [0.83.3] - 2026-08-10
### Added

- **Charts reach the user.** Asked for a metric over time, the chat agent had no way to show one: the sandbox images shipped pandas and numpy but not matplotlib, and `pip install matplotlib` inside a sandbox does not reach PyPI (E2B's per-hostname egress allowlist; `chat.docker_egress_mode: none` on the Docker sibling). It improvised — an SVG written to `/tmp` and a user told to open a path that does not exist on their machine. Both images now bake `matplotlib` in, and the workspace prompt carries the delivery half, because the library alone would not have been enough: **there is no file-delivery channel out of an interactive chat session at all.** Artifact harvest (`app/chat/artifact_harvest.py`) is wired only into the one-shot agent API, and files written under `/work` flow back to the per-user workspace *on the server*, which the browser never shows. The one channel that does work is inline `<svg>` in the reply — not a feature anyone built, but a standing property of two existing decisions (marked passes raw HTML through; `svg` is not in `renderMarkdownSafe`'s tag blocklist, and its `on*` handlers are stripped attribute-by-attribute). The prompt now names it, along with `svg.fonttype: none` so a figure stays text-sized rather than shipping every glyph as an outline, and refuses the two plausible-looking alternatives explicitly: a file path (unreachable) and a `data:` image URI (stripped by the URL-scheme allowlist, so the reader gets a broken image). The bubble constrains a chart to its column: a chart carries its own absolute size (matplotlib in `pt`, a hand-authored one in `px`) and `.msg-bubble` is a shrink-to-fit flex item, so nothing capped it — measured with the rule removed, a `figsize=(7, 3.2)` figure overflows by 242px in a 420px column and a hand-written 900×300 chart overflows by 197px even at 860px.
