Scoped to `.msg-body > svg` and `.msg-body > p > svg`, since the third `svg` in a bubble is the code-block copy button's icon, which a blanket rule would stretch to full width. All of it is guarded by `tests/test_chat_answer_provenance_and_charts.py`, which runs the markdown parser and the URL-scheme allowlist under `node` rather than asserting on a comment: the day `svg` is added to the blocklist for a good security reason, that file says out loud that the only chart channel is closing with it. Verified end-to-end against a real matplotlib figure rendered through the shipped sanitizer — 15 KB with `svg.fonttype: none` against 29 KB without, axes and labels intact, `<style>` inside `<defs>` stripped with no visual effect (it only restates SVG's own `stroke-linecap` defaults). Two loose ends from the docs written alongside this: the Docker provider's egress-off value is `docker_egress_mode: none`, not `closed` as first written — `closed` is not a value `_parse_docker_egress_mode` accepts, so an operator who copied it would have gotten `open`, the opposite of what the doc told them to expect, with one warning line as the only trace (now guarded — a test fails if any shipped doc or Dockerfile names an egress mode the parser does not recognize). And baking matplotlib into the Docker image *is* a filesystem-contract change — a pre-upgrade image cannot draw a chart — so `agnes.chat-sandbox.contract` bumps from `1` to `2`; the operator note below that tells the reader to check the label now says which value to expect, and a test pins the two together so they cannot drift apart silently the way they just did. A gap found after merge: the rule above lived only in the bundled sandbox-fallback `CLAUDE.md` (`app/initial_workspace_default/CLAUDE.md`) — `WorkdirManager.run_init` overwrites that file with the server-rendered default (`config/claude_md_template.txt`) on the common path (no admin Workspace Prompt override, no Initial Workspace Template repo), and that file carried no chart guidance at all, so the agent an analyst actually talks to never saw it. The same section now lives in both files, and a test renders `compute_default_claude_md` and pins the two copies equal so they cannot drift apart silently again. A second gap found after that: `config/claude_md_template.txt` is not sandbox-only — the same render also backs `agnes init` on an analyst's own laptop via `GET /api/welcome` — and there "you have matplotlib preinstalled", "this sandbox's filesystem is not their computer" and "the chat renders it" are simply false; a saved file is the natural way to hand over a chart on the user's own machine, and a terminal Claude Code session has no chat renderer for inline SVG at all. The template now takes an `is_sandbox` context flag (`True` from the one chat-sandbox call site in `app/main.py`, `False` — the default — from `GET /api/welcome`) and the Charts section branches on it: the sandbox wording is unchanged, a laptop workspace is told the code is identical, a file path is fine on a terminal, and inline SVG is required only inside an actual chat surface — the `data:` URI refusal is the one rule that still holds everywhere. The drift guard between the bundled sandbox-only file and the template now compares the bundled file against the template rendered with `is_sandbox=True`, not the raw template source, since the two are no longer meant to be byte-identical as files — only the sandbox-facing wording still is.

- **"Copy transcript"** in the conversation header — the answer to "can I report this session?", which until now had none. A chat session is owner-only by design (`GET /api/chat/sessions/{id}/messages` 404s for everyone else, admins included) and `/admin/sessions` browses the JSONLs collected from the CLI, not web chat, so a user who hit a wrong answer had nothing to hand to whoever could look at it. The button puts the whole thread on the clipboard as markdown, read back from the API rather than scraped off the rendered bubbles. Two problems in the first cut, both fixed here rather than shipped: reading the transcript back is a `fetch`, and `await`ing it before calling `navigator.clipboard.writeText` drops the click's transient user-activation on WebKit, so the button reported "Couldn't copy to clipboard" even though the fetch and the copy would both have worked — fixed by handing the clipboard a `ClipboardItem` whose value is a promise, so the *write* is issued synchronously in the click handler while the text itself resolves after the fetch, with the old fetch-then-copy path kept as a fallback where `ClipboardItem` is unavailable. And the endpoint's `tool_calls` — described here as carrying the tool calls "in order, as stored" — do not, on the live agent path: the runner streams tool calls as separate frames the manager never re-attaches to the persisted assistant message, so the only `tool_calls` a message ever actually carries are the manager's own cancelled/interrupted markers, which have no `tool` name at all. Rendered unconditionally that produced the literal text `tool: undefined` and an empty ` ```json ``` ` fence in both the exported transcript and the live thread — `JSON.stringify(undefined, …)` is itself `undefined`. Both render paths now go through one `formatToolCall()` that skips a row with no `tool` name instead of stringifying it, and the comment above the export function says what is actually stored rather than promising provenance nothing currently populates. Adding a second item to the header exposed a latent bug in the title beside it: the title is the header's only flexible item and the action's `margin-left:auto` consumes the free space *before* flex shrinking runs, so a title long enough to fill the row kept its full width and the button was painted over its last ~109px, hiding the ellipsis. Measured on the rendered page rather than reasoned about — `min-width:0` does not help and dropping the auto margin is worse — the title now reserves the action's width outright. A regression in the `ClipboardItem` fix itself surfaced after that: any rejection inside that branch — a `NotAllowedError` from the permission gate, or an implementation that refuses a promise-valued entry outright — escaped straight to the outer catch, which unconditionally blamed the fetch ("Couldn't read this conversation") even when the fetch had succeeded, and the working `copyTextToClipboard` fallback was never reached. A write failure and a fetch failure are now told apart: a rejected write retries through the fallback with the already-resolved markdown and reports its own outcome ("Transcript copied" or "Couldn't copy to clipboard"), while a fetch failure alone still gets the original message. The derived promise handed to `ClipboardItem` also carries an unconditional no-op `.catch` now, so a constructor or `write()` call that throws synchronously — before ever consuming that promise — can no longer leave it to surface as an unhandled rejection if the fetch it wraps later fails. Two more gaps found in review, both fixed here: `fetchTranscriptMarkdown` read the header title off the live DOM only after its two `await`s (`fetch(...)` then `res.json()`), so opening a different conversation during that round-trip repainted `#chat-thread-title` before the read happened, and the exported markdown paired the new conversation's title with the old conversation's messages and session id. The title is now snapshotted synchronously in the click handler, alongside `chatId`, and handed into `fetchTranscriptMarkdown` rather than read back out of the DOM — guarded by a `node`-executed test that simulates exactly that race. Separately, the button itself was not gated behind the rail layout the way every other redesign addition to this template is, so it shipped into the default topnav chrome too — a change to the default chat header no default-chrome instance asked for. **It is rail-only**, wrapped in `{% if ui_layout == 'rail' %}` like the composer's "+" menu and the row menu beside it; `.cloud-chat-thread-title`'s 130px reserve for the button's width moved with it, out of the base rule and into the existing rail-scoped override, so a topnav title is no longer squeezed for a button that never renders there. `TestDefaultContentParity`'s topnav chat test now also asserts the shared `cloud-chat-thread-action` class is absent, not only this one button's id, so a *future* header action that ships ungated fails the guard even if nobody thinks to add its id to the hand-list.
- Customer-instance Terraform module: per-VM `experience` field on
  `prod_instance` / `dev_instances` — the deploy-time twin of the app's
  `instance.experience` preset (>= 0.83.1). Set `"redesign"` to write
  `AGNES_INSTANCE_EXPERIENCE=redesign` into the VM's `.env`, flipping the
  app-side defaults of the coupled knobs (ui_layout → rail, theme → paper,
  `features.stack_auto_membership` → on) in one line; any per-knob setting
  (the module's `ui_layout`/`theme` fields, or `instance.yaml`) still wins.
  Empty (the default) writes no env line, keeping the preset
  operator-settable at runtime via `/admin/server-config`. Invalid values
  fail at plan time — the app resolves an unrecognised preset to `classic`
  silently, so a typo would otherwise strip the redesign from a fresh VM
  with nothing anywhere saying why. Like every startup-script value it
  reaches a VM on creation/recreate only (`metadata_startup_script` is in
  `ignore_changes`); live instances switch at runtime instead.

### Changed

- **The onboarding tour's provenance promise is now backed by the agent's instructions.** The newcomer walkthrough tells a first-time user, on the first card, that Agnes "always shows where the answer came from", and on the upload card that she will "cite it in my answers". Nothing *asked* for it: the chat agent's system prompt is the `claude_code` preset plus the workspace `CLAUDE.md`, and that file said nothing about naming a source. Checked against a live instance, the agent often volunteers one anyway — a canonical-metric question came back with a "source notes" section naming the table and the metric id, unprompted — so this is a reliability change rather than the addition of something absent: the promise is worded as *always*, and what backed it was a habit that holds when the agent happens to consult the metric catalogue and lapses when it does not. The one guaranteed provenance on screen is the inline tool-call blocks — a log of `agnes query "SELECT …"`, not a citation, and collapsed by default. The workspace prompt now requires an answer reporting a figure to end with a `Sources:` line naming the table(s) queried and, where the figure is a business metric, the canonical definition adapted — plus the assumptions behind it (date range, filter, de-duplication) where the number depends on a choice the agent made — kept on the `Sources:` line itself, because the reply renders as markdown and a second line written without a blank line before it silently joins the first (seen in the rendered bubble, not in any assertion). Narrower than #1134, which cites the semantic layer specifically and stays open: this is the general "which table, and under what assumptions" that a reader doubting a number asks first. A gap found after merge: that rule was only added to the bundled sandbox-fallback `CLAUDE.md`, which `WorkdirManager.run_init` overwrites with the server-rendered default (`config/claude_md_template.txt`) on the common path — no admin Workspace Prompt override, no Initial Workspace Template repo — so an analyst on a default instance, and `agnes init` on a laptop, never received the rule at all. The `Sources:` section now lives in `config/claude_md_template.txt` too, worded identically to the bundled copy, with a test that renders the actual default and pins both copies equal against future drift. An admin who has fully overridden the Workspace Prompt still opts out of this (and every other default rule) by design — overriding was already "replace, not extend" before this fix, for every section, not only these two.

### Fixed

- **Four stored fields of a metric definition never reached the semantic-layer detail.** `expression`, `time_column`, `filters` and `sql_variants` are columns on `metric_definitions` that the importers and the bundled YAML pack populate — the Keboola semantic-layer import writes an `expression` on every metric it creates, and eleven of the starter-pack metrics carry `expression` plus `time_column` — but `/catalog/semantics` rendered none of them. The detail therefore showed a metric's *generated* SQL while hiding the upstream expression it was composed from, which is the thing an analyst opens the detail to read. All four now render: `time_column` joins the meta line, `expression` gets its own labelled code block above the SQL, `filters` a list, and `sql_variants` one labelled block per variant. The last of those needed a fix in the route as well: the repository serializes that column on write but does not deserialize on read, so it arrived as a JSON *string* on which Jinja's `.items()` silently yields nothing — parsed in the route rather than in the repository, since changing the read shape there would ripple through both backends and their contract tests.

- **`/catalog/semantics` was a dead end — the browser's Back button was the only way out.** The page is reached by link only (the Library's Definitions block, the Catalog's Semantic layer card, a chat citation, a global-search hit) and is a nav destination in neither chrome, so clicking "45 metrics" on `/library` dropped the reader on a page with no way back to where they came from. It now carries a back link resolved per layout by `detail_back`, exactly as the resource detail pages do: topnav returns to `/catalog` — the entry that links here, and the nav item its own `/catalog/*` path already highlights — while the rail, which has no key for this kind, falls through to `/library`, both the rail's one browse surface and the block the reader clicked. Under the rail the chrome was silent about it too: `/catalog/semantics` matched no rail entry, so nothing lit up and the whole nav read as "nowhere" — the same strand the rail already avoids for the surfaces it retired. The Library item now reads active while this page is open, since under the rail the Definitions block is the only way in.

- That back link now returns to the **block** the reader left, not just the page. The rail fallback handed back a bare `/library`, which is the top of the page — and the Definitions block closes `/library` *below* the whole inventory, so on a stocked library the reader landed with everything they own between them and where they had been. `semantics` gets its own `_RAIL_DETAIL_BACK` entry pointing at `/library#lib-defs` rather than inheriting the fallback. It is not a `type_key` like the other entries and has no `?section=` band to open — the block is an adjacent destination under the inventory, not one of the bands — so an anchor is what it gets. `#lib-defs` exists exactly when that block rendered (`library.html` emits it under `if definitions_footer`, set only when the caller can see at least one metric or glossary term), and when it did not the anchor is inert and the browser stays at the top, which is what the bare `/library` did anyway. A test pins the two ends together, because a back link into an id no page emits degrades silently into exactly the link it replaced.

- **The chat sanitizer admitted SMIL, which sets attributes it cannot inspect.** `renderMarkdownSafe` strips `on*` handlers and constrains URL-bearing attributes, but both checks read the attributes an element *has* — and SMIL exists to set one it does not. Measured against the shipped sanitizer, all three of these survived it completely intact, element and payload: `<a href="#x"><animate attributeName="href" values="javascript:…">`, the same via `xlink:href`, and `<set attributeName="onload" to="…">`. The scheme allowlist never sees the first two, because `values`/`to` are not URL-bearing attribute *names*; the `on*` strip never sees the third, because there the handler name is an attribute *value*. `animate`, `animateTransform`, `animateMotion`, `set` and `foreignObject` join the blocklist. The vector predates the chart work — `<svg>` was always admitted — but that work makes inline SVG a routine, actively-instructed output shape, and the threat model is not the chart author: a co-presence peer's message renders through the same path and no prompt rule binds them, which is why "matplotlib never emits SMIL" is not a defence. It is why the fix is free, though — measured on real matplotlib output, a figure contains zero SMIL elements and no `foreignObject`, and the rendered chart is byte-identical before and after. Not fixed here and left as-is deliberately: an external `<use href="https://…">` reference still survives, which browsers already refuse cross-origin.

- **A plugin's self-declared `name` is validated before it is served.** `resolve_manifest_name` read `.claude-plugin/plugin.json` `name` and returned whatever string was there, and that value is emitted verbatim as the `name` of the synth `marketplace.json` entry and the synth bundle `plugin.json`, then rendered in the `/plugin` UI. Its sibling `original_name` — the value that becomes the `plugins/<name>` directory segment — has cleared `is_safe_plugin_name` at ingest since the marketplace endpoints existed, so the two halves of the same identity were held to different bars: a curator-controlled `plugin.json` could declare a name with separators, control characters, or no length limit at all, and it went straight into the served JSON. It now clears the same charset gate plus a 64-character cap (`MAX_MANIFEST_NAME_LEN`), falling back to the already-gated upstream name and logging which plugin tripped it. This is hygiene rather than a traversal fix — `manifest_name` never builds a path, paths are built from the validated slug and `original_name` — and the cap is the part that matters, since `is_safe_plugin_name` constrains the charset but not the length. A conformant plugin is unaffected; surrounding whitespace is still stripped before the check, so a trailing newline is trimmed rather than rejected. Rejecting a name is only half the job: Claude Code matches a loaded plugin back to its catalog entry by name, and a curated plugin's `plugin.json` is served as the curator's own file rather than synthesized, so the rejected name stayed inside the bundle while the entry carried the fallback — the "Plugin &lt;X&gt; not found in marketplace" failure this resolution exists to prevent. Both serving channels now force the served `plugin.json` `name` to the resolved one, which the bundle path already did. A third channel had the same gap: Cowork's single-plugin zip export (`cowork_packager.transform_plugin_json`, for Claude Desktop's "upload a custom plugin file") preferred the plugin's own declared `name` over the resolved `manifest_name`, so a rejected name still shipped there too — kebab-ified by `coerce_plugin_name`, which is charset-safe by construction (so this was never a validation hole for Cowork), but still a different identity than the one the other two channels settled on for the same plugin. It now derives `name` from `manifest_name` as well. That reconciliation had its own gap: the sanitizer resolves `plugin_dir` to scope the component-key pruning pass, and an `OSError` there (a broken symlink, a permission error) returned the file unmodified — discarding the name correction along with the pruning it was actually guarding, so a rejected name could still reach the wire on exactly the plugin whose directory Agnes could least vouch for. The two edits are now independent: an unresolvable `plugin_dir` only skips pruning, never the name fix. Shipping that fix needed a second half: the marketplace ETag is content-addressed over the plugin files on disk, so a change to how those files are *packaged* leaves every hashed byte identical — the ZIP channel would answer `If-None-Match` with a 304 and the git channel would keep its `<etag>.v<N>.git` bare repo, so only users whose plugins happened to change afterwards would ever receive the fix. A `SERVED_FORMAT_VERSION` constant now folds into the ETag, so a packaging change reaches clients that already hold a copy. **Operator note:** a plugin whose declared name is rejected is now served under the upstream name everywhere, so anyone who had already enabled it under the old name in their local `.claude/settings.json` sees a dangling entry and must re-enable it once. Only non-conformant names are affected — and before this they were served under a name their catalog entry disagreed with, which did not load at all.

- **An MCP server's transport is no longer guessed when the author declared it.** The plugin detail page inferred transport purely from config shape — `command` → `stdio`, `url` → `sse` — and ignored the `type` key, which is how both Claude Code's `.mcp.json` and the Agent Plugins `mcp.json` schema actually spell it. Two consequences: a server declaring `streamable-http` was displayed as `sse`, and since HTTP+SSE is the deprecated predecessor transport, *every* URL-based server was mislabelled as legacy. A declared `type` is now authoritative and an unrecognized value is shown as written rather than coerced; inference runs only when the key is absent, and a bare `url` infers `http`.

## [0.83.2] - 2026-08-10
### Fixed

- **A metric or glossary description laid out with `<div>` lost its line breaks in the expanded detail.** 0.83.1 taught the renderer to read an imported description as HTML rather than as markdown, and gave the plain-text projection a word boundary where a stripped block tag had been. The rendered detail needed the same care from the other side: there a stripped `<div>` cannot be replaced by a space, it has to keep its structure — so a description stored as `<div>…</div><div>…</div>` rendered as one fused line (`Share of qualified sales.Excludes refunds and test orders.`) in the expanded metric detail on `/catalog/semantics` — the one surface that renders the description as markup. The one-line previews, the Glossary tab, `agnes catalog --metrics --show` and search hits all read the plain-text projection, which 0.83.1 already fixed, and are unaffected. The `html_source` path now additionally allows the structural block containers (`div`, `section`, `article`, `dl`/`dt`/`dd`, `figure`/`figcaption`, and the `h1`/`h5`/`h6` the narrow allowlist omits) — the same set the plain-text projection already treats as word boundaries, now guarded by a test so the two lists cannot drift apart again. The narrow allowlist keeps only `h2`-`h4` so a curator cannot outrank the page's own headings; an imported description is not authored against this page at all, and dropping its `<h1>` fused the sections it separated. That projection also learned to count **opening** tags, not just closing ones: nested structure separates text with an opening tag and no closing tag in between (`<figure>A<figcaption>B`), which a close-only pattern fused. Its attribute run skips over quoted values, since a `>` inside one does not close the tag — `<div title="a>b">` was cut in half and left `b">` as visible characters — and it is bounded on hostile input in two directions: the three alternatives are mutually exclusive on their first character, so there is no exponential backtracking, and the bare branch excludes `<`, so an unterminated tag stops at the next tag start instead of rescanning the remainder — without which N unclosed tags made the substitution quadratic (20 KB of `<div ` took 620 ms, enough for one malformed description to stall the page rendering it). It also matches case-insensitively: it runs on the rendered HTML, before nh3 — and nh3 is what normalizes tag case — so `<DIV>` arrives exactly as the upstream catalog wrote it. They get no entry in the attribute allowlist, so every attribute including `on*` handlers is still stripped — these carry layout, never behaviour — and curator-authored marketplace content keeps the narrow allowlist unchanged, where a pasted `<div>` staying visible text is the intended tell. Found running the fix against a live instance rather than in a test.

- The metric detail sizes every heading level it now admits. Preserving `h1`/`h5`/`h6` on the `html_source` path is what stops an imported description's sections fusing, but `.sl-detail__desc` styled only `h2`/`h3` — so a preserved `<h1>` fell back to the browser default and rendered at ~2em with large margins inside a compact metric row, out-shouting the page's own heading. `h4` had been in that position since before this change. Structure is preserved by the allowlist; how large it looks is the row's decision, and a guard now fails if the two drift apart.

## [0.83.1] - 2026-08-08
### Added
- **An MCP source's own `url` is validated when it is configured** (#1154). Every forward to an `http`/`sse` source dials that url with a credential attached — the shared vault secret, an analyst's per-user secret, or an OAuth access token — but only the OAuth *endpoints* were ever checked, so an admin could register `http://169.254.169.254/mcp` and Agnes would post user credentials to the cloud metadata endpoint in cleartext. Refused now, at create and at update. The check deliberately is **not** the OAuth endpoints' `resolve_safe(https_only=True)`: that guard rejects every private and loopback address, and an organization running its own MCP server on `http://mcp.internal:8080` is an ordinary deployment rather than an attack. So the line falls where "nobody legitimately wants this" actually falls — link-local/metadata, multicast, reserved and unspecified addresses are refused, as is cleartext http to a *public* address and a hostname resolving to both public and internal addresses (the rebinding shape); an internal address is accepted and recorded in the audit row instead. A host that does not resolve right now is likewise recorded rather than refused, because this runs over the merged row and a DNS blip would otherwise block edits that never touched the url. Operators wanting the fail-closed posture set `mcp.source_url_strict` (`AGNES_MCP_SOURCE_URL_STRICT`), which demands https to a public, resolvable address and honours the existing `security.ssrf_allowed_hosts` allowlist — so a single on-prem source does not stop an instance from adopting it. `stdio` sources are exempt: there the secret rides the subprocess environment and `url` is never dialed. A **disabled** source is exempt on update, because enforcing there traps the operator: a source registered before this guard (or before `source_url_strict` was turned on) would otherwise 400 on every update including the one that turns it OFF, the single action that reduces the risk. Disabling buys the two runtime forwards, which re-fetch the row and refuse — it is not "never dialed", because neither the admin probes (`introspect`, `classify`, `test`) nor the analyst's own `POST /api/mcp/sources/{id}/my-secret/test` consult `enabled`. Those carry the check themselves rather than leaning on the flag — the analyst-facing one also now refuses a disabled source, since it dials with the caller's own credential. `materialize` — the fourth connector helper, and the one the module's own header names alongside the other three — takes it as well. `test` is the exception that proves the shape: its contract is HTTP 200 with a diagnostic, so a refused url is REPORTED as the diagnostic rather than turned into a 400 that would withhold the answer the button exists to give. On the analyst-facing probe the refusal is deliberately generic — the policy reason embeds the source's literal address, and an analyst is not an admin, so the cause goes to the log and the caller gets a sentence naming the source, matching what every other failure branch there already does. Remediation is disable → fix the url → re-enable, and re-enabling validates, so nothing reaches a live state unchecked. The switch is declared in `app.switches.SWITCHES` with a row in `docs/feature-flags.md`, as the registry introduced in #1209 now requires.

- A deployment can now state which chrome it runs: `ui_layout` and `theme` are per-VM fields on the `customer-instance` module (`prod_instance` / `dev_instances`), written to the app `.env` as `AGNES_UI_LAYOUT` / `AGNES_INSTANCE_THEME`. Until now the only way to set them on a provisioned VM was `instance.ui_layout` / `instance.theme` in `/data/state/instance.yaml` — which does survive a VM recreate, since it lives on the data disk, but is invisible to Terraform, so the infrastructure config could not say what the instance looks like and an operator reading it could not tell. Per-VM rather than module-wide, like `dispatcher_enabled` and `data_apps_enabled`, because the redesign is rolled out dev-first and promoted to prod only once it looks right. Both default to empty, which writes **no** env line at all and leaves any existing `instance.yaml` value (or the app default) untouched — an empty `AGNES_UI_LAYOUT=` would resolve to an empty string and, unlike an absent variable, shadow the YAML. Guarded by `tests/test_startup_ui_layout_theme_toggle.py`.
- Per-instance feature flag for Agent profiles (`agent_profiles.enabled` / `AGNES_AGENT_PROFILES_ENABLED`), same mechanism as the Studio flag. Grandfathered on by default; disabling closes the `/agents` builder page, the `/api/v1/agents*` management + runtime API (and its `agnes agent`/`agnes chat` CLI clients) with a 403 `agent_profiles_disabled`, and hides every inbound link to it — the "My agents" nav entry in both chromes, the command-palette row, and the three `/agents` links on `/how-it-works` (which would otherwise be dead ends that bounce the user home). Default-agent seeding, chat attribution, and the broker's agent policy are internal mechanisms and keep working regardless.
- `agnes admin register-table --server-only` — CLI surface for the `server_only` distribution flag (#607). The flag keeps a `local`/`materialized` table synced and queryable server-side while excluding its parquet from `agnes pull`, which is the answer for data that may be queried but must not be copied onto laptops. It has existed as a REST field since schema v74 but had no CLI flag and no documentation, so the only documented way to set it was a raw API call. Pairing it with `--query-mode remote` fails client-side with the same rationale the API validator gives, before the round-trip.
- `docs/admin/collections-vs-data-packages.md` — when to upload files versus register a live source. Both surface under Library, which makes them look like alternatives; the deciding question is who updates the content when it changes.
- `agnes global enable|disable|status` — user-scope (all-repositories) layer: stack plugins installed with `claude plugin install --scope user`, an `agnes` user-scope stdio MCP entry, a marker-fenced rails block in `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md`, and (by default; `--no-hook` opts out) a user-level SessionStart hook running the detached `agnes update`. `agnes update` re-converges the layer via a new `global` step, and `agnes refresh-marketplace` gains `--target user|project` (the `user` target performs no per-repository writes). New docs page: `docs/global-distribution.md`. Three details that only bite once the layer is live in every repository: the `claude mcp get` probe is **bounded by a timeout** — it connects to the server rather than only reading config, and it runs from the user-level SessionStart hook inside `agnes update` while that holds the convergence lock, so an unbounded wait would stall every later convergence; a probe that does not answer is reported as `unknown` rather than as "no entry", so `disable` refuses to write the off-flag while an entry it merely failed to see may still be registered (the flag-last ordering is only as good as what feeds it, and the plugin path already drew this line with `installed is None`); and the MCP entry is removed before it is re-added on every arm that reaches the add, not only when the existing entry is foreign, so convergence stays idempotent on a `claude` that refuses to add a name that already exists instead of reporting an error on every session start. `agnes global status` gained a matching `unknown` state and no longer indexes a dict that a new state could turn into a traceback. Two more states the probe used to collapse into one: an entry whose scope this `claude` does not report reads as `unclassified` rather than `absent` — the probe exited 0, so *something* is registered under that name, and calling it absent sent convergence into the remove-and-replace arm, destroying a user's own `agnes` entry without the `--force` that exists to gate exactly that. `unclassified` and `unknown` are both treated like `foreign` everywhere they surface — convergence, `status`, and `disable`: left alone, reported, replaced only when forced — and `--force` genuinely reaches all three, including `unknown`, which an entry whose server will not start produces deterministically and is therefore exactly the state an operator reaches for `--force` to repair. `disable` is the one that matters most, since a state falling through to its "no entry" branch writes the off-flag while a registered entry keeps loading in every repository the user opens, with the layer marked off so nothing converges or removes it again. And the six-hour freshness interval is now measured with a marker the layer stamps after each drift check, not with `FETCH_HEAD` — git writes that only on a real `git fetch`, and the drift check uses `git ls-remote`, so on a clone that was simply up to date the mtime never moved, the clone read as stale forever, and "at most once every six hours" degraded into a remote probe at every session start in every repository. Separately, `claude plugin update` is now passed the same `--scope` as install and uninstall: its own default is `user`, so running it bare aimed workspace version bumps at the wrong scope entirely — `tests/test_cli_refresh_marketplace.py::test_update_argv_carries_the_scope_for_both_targets` pins the argv, which nothing did before.

- **`instance.experience` preset** (`classic` | `redesign`, env
  `AGNES_INSTANCE_EXPERIENCE`) — the one-line adoption switch for the
  redesign: `redesign` flips the DEFAULTS of the coupled knobs
  (`instance.ui_layout` → `rail`, `instance.theme` → `paper`,
  `features.stack_auto_membership` → `true`); any per-knob env/yaml setting
  still wins, and `classic` (or an absent key) is byte-for-byte the
  pre-redesign experience. The `/admin/server-config` flag inventory leads
  with the preset's resolved value and labels preset-sourced flag defaults
  with a `preset` badge. (`docs/feature-flags.md`, spec
  `docs/superpowers/specs/2026-08-07-default-chrome-ux-parity.md`)

### Changed
- **Topnav content parity extended to the detail pages**: the seven detail templates the redesign restructured in place (`catalog_table_detail`, `catalog_package_detail`, `catalog_recipe_detail`, `marketplace_plugin_detail`, `marketplace_item_detail`, `library_detail`, `memory_domain_detail`) now follow the `/catalog` pattern — rail renders the redesigned kind-coloured detail anatomy, a default topnav instance keeps the pre-redesign page byte-for-byte as a frozen `*_legacy.html` copy. All twelve render sites resolve through a single `_detail_template()` switch (handlers are shared — they pass a superset of the legacy context), and a closed-set guard fails on any bare detail-template literal that would bypass it. Guarded by `tests/test_ui_layout_theme.py::TestDetailPageParity`.
- **Every operator switch is declared in one registry, and says why it is or is not editable.** Gating was spread across the `FEATURE_FLAGS` registry, the `_EDITABLE_SECTIONS` write allowlist in `app/api/admin.py`, the `_KNOWN_FIELDS` form metadata beside it, and — for the reason a registered flag was *not* writable — a dict inside `tests/test_admin_configure_api.py`. Four homes for one switch's metadata, and the one an operator most needed (why can I see this and not change it?) was in a test file they will never read. `app/switches.py` now holds a `Switch` per toggle: its config key, env var, type, default, effect class (`live` / `restart` / `deploy`), whether it is editable, and `lock_reason` when it is not. `_EDITABLE_SECTIONS` is derived from it, so adding an editable switch can no longer leave its section rejecting saves — the omission that shipped `mcp.allow_query_param_token` env-var-only. `data_apps` keeps its existing, deliberate restriction (the flag is read per request, but the apps_runner sidecar sits behind the `apps` Compose profile, so a live flip would surface a backend-less feature) — now stated on the switch and returned by `GET /api/admin/server-config`, which gains `effect`, `editable` and `lock_reason` per row. `FEATURE_FLAGS` remains importable from `app.instance_config` and resolves to the same registry; `feature_enabled` is unchanged, and the editable section set is identical (same 20 sections, just derived instead of hand-listed). Two operator-visible cosmetics did change: `_EDITABLE_SECTIONS` is now alphabetical, which reorders the section list in the settings sidenav and in the `POST /api/admin/server-config` 400 error text, and the `library_show_unverified_trust` description shown in the Feature flags panel is shorter than before (deliberate trim, not a regression). `agent_profiles`, registered on `main` while this branch was open, is carried across as a locked switch: its lock_reason states the owner's decision from #1186 verbatim — a deliberately env-var-only kill switch with no runtime-toggle use case — so the reason now travels with the flag instead of living in the test dict this PR removes. `tests/test_feature_flags.py` passes with only the new inventory-metadata test class appended; no existing test was altered.

- **Default-chrome instances get their remaining pre-redesign surfaces back**
  (spec `docs/superpowers/specs/2026-08-07-default-chrome-ux-parity.md`,
  wave 2). On the default topnav chrome: `/me/profile`, `/me/activity` and
  `/agents` render frozen pre-redesign copies (`*_legacy.html`;
  `/agents` restores the pre-redesign "My agents" management page with its
  original handler logic); `/me/ai-connector` is a real page again (the
  frozen standalone connector page with the `/mcp-connect` token fallback,
  with `/me/mcp` + `/me/cowork` aliases redirecting to it) instead of a
  redirect; the user menu's "AI Connector" row returns; the pre-redesign
  guided tour ships again (frozen `_tour_legacy.html` + `js/tour_legacy.js`
  + `css/tour_legacy.css`, restored `app/web/onboarding.py` steps, and the
  header "?" launcher); and the chat welcome cards keep their pre-redesign
  copy and icons byte-for-byte (`_chat_welcome_cards_legacy.html`). The
  page swaps key on the chrome layout, like every earlier legacy surface
  (library, marketplace, catalog): the rail chrome keeps all redesigned
  pages, while paper-on-topnav — a per-knob combination, not the preset —
  renders the classic pages in paper colors. The two surfaces whose NAV
  affordance is paper-dependent key on the full opt-in expression (rail or
  paper) instead: the legacy tour and the standalone connector page, so a
  paper-on-topnav instance gets neither an orphaned tour pop-up (its "?"
  launcher is hidden there) nor a page its menu no longer links. The
  admin "Moderation & Trust" menu entry stays ungated (an accepted
  additive admin link): the hub hosts the submission-review count and
  curation jump-offs even with Store verification off, and the page
  itself already hides only its verification section then.

- **BREAKING-revert: stack auto-membership is now opt-in**
  (`features.stack_auto_membership`, env `AGNES_STACK_AUTO_MEMBERSHIP`,
  default **off**). **Operators of instances that already adopted
  auto-membership: keep it with one line — `instance.experience: redesign`
  (or the flag itself) — ideally set before upgrading.** Until it is set,
  granted-but-unsubscribed resources leave users' stacks, `agnes pull`
  manifests and query authorization; nothing is lost meanwhile
  (`user_stack_subscriptions` rows are interpreted, never rewritten, so
  flipping the flag restores the exact previous state). The auto-membership
  stack model the redesign shipped as a breaking change reverts to the
  classic pre-redesign subscribe model on default instances: membership = required ∪ subscribed grants (all
  downloaded by `agnes pull`), Catalog Browse lists every granted resource
  with its add-to-stack state, admin god-mode Browse returns to the
  user-facing catalog, and a `required → available` grant downgrade again
  eagerly fans out subscriptions so group members keep the resource. Turning
  the flag on restores the redesign semantics exactly (auto-membership,
  addable-only Browse reshape, `server_only` manifest overlay, no downgrade
  fan-out). The flag flips behavior instantly — `user_stack_subscriptions`
  rows are interpreted, never rewritten. Topnav instances also render the
  frozen pre-redesign `/catalog` and `/corporate-memory` pages
  (`catalog_legacy.html`, `corporate_memory_legacy.html`; rail keeps the
  unified/redesigned pages).

- **The Skill Builder's Category dropdown looks like the rest of the app.** It carried the field border and background but kept the platform's own `<select>` rendering — OS chevron, OS metrics, OS colours in dark theme — so it read as a foreign widget beside Agnes's own menus. Same treatment as the filter toolbar's selects (`appearance: none` plus a drawn chevron), anchored to the bottom of the field rather than its middle so a label that wraps on a narrow column can't push the chevron off the control. Closes #1174.
- **Softened the "check `PLATFORM_SETUP.md` first" banner** on QUICKSTART / DEPLOYMENT / ONBOARDING / HEADLESS_USAGE. `PLATFORM_SETUP.md` is a ~170-line day-2 playbook (marketplaces, scheduler cadence, telemetry, privacy posture, daily routine), not a superset of the docs pointing at it — sending a first-time reader there ahead of the quick start pointed them away from what they needed. Part of #1192.

- **Newline preservation in modal copy is opt-in.** `white-space: pre-wrap` on `.modal-card` headings and sub-lines exists so a message handed to `alertModal` / `confirmModal` / `promptModal` keeps its `\n` line breaks, the way the native dialogs they replace did. Applied to every `.modal-card` on the instance, it also reformatted **static** copy in templates, where newlines and indentation are source formatting — the Add-user helper paragraph, written across three template lines for readability, rendered as three jaggedly-indented lines instead of one wrapped paragraph. `modal.js` now stamps `data-preserve-newlines` on the cards it builds and the rule is scoped to that attribute, so the dialogs that need the behaviour keep it and authored markup is free to wrap however it reads best. Closes #1171.
- CLI data commands (`query --local`, `pull`, `snapshot`, `status`, `disk-info`, `explore`, `statusline`, `mark-private`) and the stdio MCP server (`query_local`, `pull`) now fall back to the workspace anchored by `agnes init` when run outside a workspace directory — Agnes data access works from any repository. `AGNES_LOCAL_DIR` still overrides; behavior inside a workspace is unchanged. `agnes pull` gains `--workspace <dir>`.

### Fixed

- **The local-copy card wording is gated on the membership mode, not hardcoded.** #1206 re-pointed `in_stack` at the local-download state and had the card macro say so through an `in_stack_is_local` flag the projections set unconditionally. That is correct under auto-membership and actively harmful under the classic subscribe model this change restores as the default: there `in_stack` means membership again, so a card would offer **Remove local copy** for a control that unsubscribes — the user gives up access believing they are freeing disk. Both projections now resolve the flag from `stack_auto_membership` instead, and a literal `True` fails a guard. The frozen `corporate_memory_legacy.html` picked up the #1206 client-side fixes as well: freezing forks a page permanently, and without them a classic-chrome instance running auto-membership — a supported combination — would render the old wording beside a live twin rendering the new one. Carrying them costs nothing in classic, because the projection omits the flag there and every one of those behaviours is keyed off it.

- **The Catalog no longer shows three contradictory numbers for one concept.** After the auto-membership reshape `in_stack` carries the local-download state, not stack membership — every granted package is in the stack by definition. The key name still said the old thing, so the card macro read it that way: a package sat under **My Stack** while its own button invited you to "Add to stack", and the "In stack" filter chip reported 3 beside a tab badge reading 29. The projections that re-point the key now say so (`in_stack_is_local`), the card macro switches its wording on that flag rather than guessing from the key name, the chip reads **Downloaded**, and the client-side re-label after an add/remove was updated in lockstep — left alone it would have undone the fix on the first click. Both pages the projection feeds are covered, Catalog and Curated Memory: they carry byte-identical copies of the same re-label routine, so fixing only the one the issue was filed against would have left the other contradicting itself, and each page's clone-into-My-Stack branch — which writes its own label after the re-label loop has already run — is included. The flag also decides what a **removal means**, not just what the button says: where `in_stack` is the local-copy state, dropping the copy leaves the resource in the stack — the server's My Stack grid comes from `resolver.stack()`, whose effective set is `required ∪ available ∪ materialized` — so the card now stays put and re-labels itself instead of being deleted, and the My Stack tab count, which counts membership, no longer moves. Left as it was, removing a local copy made the item vanish and the badge drop, and both came back on the next page load: the very contradiction this change removes, relocated into the optimistic path. The macro exposes the flag as `data-in-stack-is-local` so the click handler can tell the two meanings apart rather than implementing one of them — and the last two strings that still spoke membership follow it as well. The confirmation toast reads **Local copy queued** / **Local copy removed** under the local meaning ("queued", not "downloaded": the request that succeeds is a subscribe and the bytes arrive with the next `agnes pull`); keeping the card in My Stack is what made the old "Removed from stack" actively wrong rather than merely off-vocabulary, since the user watches the item stay put while being told it left. And the active filter is re-applied after any change: the Downloaded chip hides cards on `data-in-stack`, which only ever ran from the chip and search handlers — fine while a removal deleted the card, wrong once the card survives and only flips the attribute, because an item that is no longer downloaded would sit in plain sight under a filter that claims to exclude it. Consumers that never re-pointed `in_stack` omit the flag and keep both the old wording and the old removal behaviour. The `/admin/data-packages` audit grid shares the projection and so picks the new wording up as well, including for a package the admin's own groups hold no grant on — deliberately, because that button posts a subscribe and a subscribe is precisely what puts the local copy on the laptop. Closes #1206.

- **Metric descriptions imported verbatim from an external catalog rendered their own tags as visible text — on the semantic-layer page, in `agnes catalog --metrics --show`, and in unified search hits.** `metric_definitions.description` holds two dialects: markdown for metrics hand-authored in `docs/metrics/*.yaml`, and whatever the upstream catalog stored for metrics written by an import that passes the value through with no normalization (`connectors/keboola/semantic_layer.py`) — routinely rich HTML. Every surface rendered it as pure markdown, and the markdown renderer is deliberately configured to escape raw HTML rather than execute it, so a blob became entities; the plain-text projection's tag-strip then found no tags left to remove, and its closing `unescape` handed them back as the characters `<p><strong>`. `render_safe` / `render_plain` take an `html_source` flag selecting a renderer that passes raw HTML through to the *same* nh3 allowlist, so a blob renders as bold text and flattens to clean plain text, while script tags, event handlers and `javascript:` URLs are stripped exactly as before. It widens what is displayed, never what is allowed, and only for callers that opt in — curator-authored marketplace content keeps its stricter posture, where pasted HTML showing up as literal text is the intended tell. Which renderer applies is decided **per row**, keyed on the writer recorded in `metric_definitions.source` rather than on what the text looks like: a markdown description is free to contain `List<int>` or `orders <shipped>`, and the permissive renderer would delete those (markdown-it reads them as unknown tags, the allowlist rejects them, and a pseudo-tag carries no child text — `<int>.` takes the rest of the line with it). The trade-off does not vanish, it lands on the row class where HTML is the documented dialect instead of on every hand-authored definition. `glossary_terms.definition` gets the same treatment: it is the sibling column, written by the same importer in the same pass and rendered through `esc()` on the Glossary tab, so HTML definitions showed their tags there too — `/api/glossary`, its search and detail routes now carry `definition_text`, and the tab plus `agnes glossary` render that. Unified search flattens both kinds of hit: metric rows are caller-supplied so they are projected before scoring (tag names also stop being tokenized as search terms), while glossary rows are fetched inside the searcher and are projected where the hit is built — before the 280-character truncation, so the cut cannot land mid-tag. The plain-text projection also inserts its word boundaries into the rendered HTML now rather than into the sanitized output: a `<div>` is not on the render allowlist, so by then it was already gone and the two lines it separated had fused into `First line.Second line.`. Stripping every tag afterwards with an empty allowlist is stricter than the render allowlist, so nothing survives the reorder that would not have survived before — the strict (default) path is byte-identical. The metrics API carries the flattened text as a new additive `description_text` field (the stored column travels unchanged beside it) and the CLI prints that, which keeps the markdown/sanitizer dependencies out of the CLI wheel; unified search flattens before scoring, so tag names also stop being ranked as search terms. The CLI and search paths matter beyond cosmetics: `CLAUDE.md`'s agent rails send agents to `agnes catalog --metrics --show <id>` for the canonical business definition before computing any metric, so the tags were being read as part of the definition rather than merely looked at.
- **A Required knowledge item could be hidden from a user on Postgres by a dismissal that predated it.** The `hide_dismissed` subquery exempts Required items so a stale opt-out cannot suppress governance content — but the Postgres repository spelled that exemption `status != 'mandatory'`, a literal the v49 migration retired when it split the overload into the orthogonal `is_required` boolean and rewrote every legacy row. Nothing matches `'mandatory'` any more, so the guard was dead: always true, protecting nothing. A user who dismissed an item before an admin marked it Required then lost it from `list_items`, `search`, and — the part that matters — the agent context bundle, which is where the Required tier does its work. DuckDB used the live column and was correct, so this was a silent one-backend divergence. Both spellings are now the column, and `tests/db_pg/test_knowledge_contract.py` asserts the rule on both backends: the previous coverage was a DuckDB-only unit test plus a static check that matched `status IN (...)` clauses, which this guard is not.
- `instance.yaml` is written owner-only (0600). It carries the Postgres URL with its password inline, plus whatever an operator put in a connector overlay, and it lives on the data volume that several non-root containers mount — yet several of its writers left it at the umask default, typically 0644, while the equivalent `.env` is 0600 — which is why a deployment's mode depended on which surface had last saved it. Every writer is covered now, not just the ones that prompted the change: the `/admin/server-config` editor, the narrow overlay writer beside it, and the initial-workspace save and clear endpoints had no chmod at all, and `write_backend_state` plus the state applier had one but applied it to the destination *after* the rename. Both shapes matter, and the first is the worse of the two: `os.replace` carries the temp file's mode onto the destination, so a writer missing the chmod does not leak one save — it relaxes the file permanently, including on an instance a previous save or the startup script had already repaired. The chmod now lands on the temp file **before** the atomic rename everywhere, so the final path is never observable world-readable rather than merely observable briefly, and the applier's two job-file writers got the same treatment (their error messages can quote a database url). The module's startup script chmods outside the create branch, so a boot also repairs a file written before this existed — but **conditionally**, and this is the part that decides whether the change is safe to roll to a fleet. 0600 makes the file's owner load-bearing, and the owner is decided by `chown -R agnes-applier /data/state` plus the applier re-creating the file under its own uid on every rewrite. That user was created with `useradd --system`, which *allocates* the top free id in the system range — landing on 999, the app container's uid, by coincidence rather than intent. The uid is pinned now; and where the pin cannot take because 999 was already occupied at provisioning time, the mode is left alone and the reason goes to the console, because a 0600 file the app does not own is one it cannot read, which combined with the fail-closed read below is a refusal to start — a full outage traded for a leak. The hardening applies exactly where its precondition holds. Guarded by `tests/test_startup_instance_yaml_perms.py`. `tests/test_startup_instance_yaml_perms.py::test_every_overlay_writer_chmods_the_temp_before_the_rename` enumerates the writers rather than naming the ones a review happened to catch — it is what found the two job-file writers. Making the mode restrictive makes the *owner* load-bearing, so the state applier's merge step was hardened to match: it reads the existing file to carry the operator's non-database sections across a backend switch, and it did so under a blanket `except Exception: existing = {}`. At 0644 that read always succeeded; at 0600 a uid mismatch would have turned it into a rewrite containing only `database:` — silently destroying every operator-set section, which is exactly the destruction the merge was introduced to prevent. A read error now aborts the rewrite and leaves the file alone (a *malformed* file still falls back to the empty base, since that one is recoverable), the refusal propagates to the caller instead of being discarded by a bare `return`, and the post-migration path no longer logs a backend flip that never reached disk. Because the applier runs under `set -euo pipefail` with an `ERR` trap, making the writer able to fail also meant every call site had to consume that failure: an unguarded call would have aborted the run in place, and on the failed-migration rollback path that sits *above* the step which brings app and scheduler back up — so a failed migration on such a host would have left the instance offline, with no later tick able to recover it (the stuck-job sweep only repairs jobs still `running`, and that job is already `failed`). Both migration call sites now consume the status; when the rollback write is the one refused, the lifecycle flag is deliberately left alone — clearing it would assert a lifecycle `instance.yaml` does not agree with — the job is marked failed with that stated, and the restart still runs. `tests/test_startup_instance_yaml_perms.py::test_every_write_instance_yaml_call_site_is_guarded` fails on any bare call. The post-migration write is deliberately NOT allowed to fail the job: the migrator flips the backend itself (`write_backend_state` immediately before `mark_success`), so what the applier runs afterwards normalizes `database.url` from the migrator's pinned-IP form to the canonical hostname — losing it leaves a working instance on the right backend, and marking the job failed there would report a migration that moved every row as a failure. The app's own read of the overlay got the same separation: `app/instance_config.py` caught every exception and fell back to the static base config, logging the file as "corrupt". `database.backend` lives in that overlay, so a PermissionError landing there would boot an instance whose data is on Postgres onto the DuckDB default and start writing to the wrong store — reachable through a plain uid mismatch once the file is 0600, where at 0644 it was not. An unreadable overlay refuses to start and says why; a malformed one — including one whose bytes are not valid UTF-8, which is a `ValueError` rather than an `OSError` and so needs naming — keeps the lenient fallback, since that is visible and repairable through the editor. The refusal is **boot-only**, declared by the caller (`load_instance_config(strict=True)` from the startup block, which drops the parse-once cache first so it actually reads the file) rather than inferred from process history — an earlier attempt gated it on a "have we loaded once" module flag, and importing `app.main` sets that, so the guard was permanently defused before startup ever ran. Otherwise: `load_instance_config` is reached from `get_value()` on essentially every request path and re-runs on a live instance after each admin save, so a file that goes unreadable *after* a good boot logs loudly and keeps serving the config already in hand. Raising there would turn every request into a 500 to prevent a wrong-backend start that a running process is not about to make. What it serves in that case is the last config it built successfully, held in its own module global — `reset_cache()` (which every admin save calls) is precisely the path that reaches this branch, and by then the parse-once cache is empty, so leaning on it would hand back the static base with every operator-set section missing while the log claimed they were kept. The fallback is cached, too, or each request would redo the whole load and emit another error line. The applier's own writer needed the same UTF-8 arm: without it a byte-corrupt overlay made the rewrite exit non-zero, which the caller reads as a refused rollback, which leaves app and scheduler down with nothing to bring them back. The refusal carries its own exception type, because the boot path wraps that load in `except Exception` on purpose — a soft config problem must not stop an instance serving — and that arm would otherwise have swallowed this one too, leaving a process that looks healthy and returns 500 from every `get_value()` consumer, which is the harder failure to diagnose of the two. The split had to cover a third shape as well: `Path.read_text()` raises `UnicodeDecodeError` — a `ValueError`, not an `OSError` — for bytes that are not valid UTF-8, which is precisely the partial-write case the lenient path was written for, so undecodable content degrades to the base config rather than escaping both arms and 500ing every later lookup. On the applier side, a refused *rollback* no longer restarts app and scheduler: `use_pg()` counts `side_car_in_progress` and `cloud_in_progress` as Postgres, so an overlay left naming the transient points a duckdb-source instance at a Postgres the failed migration never filled — an empty database that accepts writes is not something an operator can tell apart from a healthy one, so the containers stay down and the job and the log both say why — on BOTH restart paths, the post-migration one and the stuck-job recovery's own, which is a separate `dc up` that inherits nothing — and each on its own flag, since shell variables have no function scope and a shared one leaked the recovery's refusal into the rest of the tick, blocking the restart after a *later* migration in the same run that had completed perfectly. And the applier's licence to shrug off its own post-migration write is now enforced where it is earned rather than inferred across files: the migrator re-reads the overlay and refuses to report success unless the backend it just wrote is actually there — inside the same `MigrationLock` as the cancel re-check and the write, because a cancel landing between the write and an outside read-back reverts the file and the mismatch would be reported as a *failure* rather than a cancellation, losing the distinction the host applier uses to tell those apart. A verification failure also gets its own exception type, handled ahead of the generic one: the rows are already on the target by then, so the generic handler's revert-to-source would write a config that disagrees with where the data is — the split the whole mechanism exists to prevent, arriving through the guard meant to catch it. The applier honours that decision too: its failure branch fires for every non-success status, so it reads the class the migrator recorded and skips the rollback for this one — otherwise it would undo one layer down and point the app at the old store while every row lives in the new one. Relatedly, a job whose migration failed and whose rollback then also failed keeps BOTH messages: `update_job` gained an append mode, because it overwrites `error.message` by default and the second write was destroying the migrator's account of why the migration failed at all. Ownership itself is unchanged — uid 999, which the app container runs as — but note that the recursive `chown -R agnes-applier:agnes-applier /data/state` in provisioning is what actually decides it, and `useradd --system` gives the applier that uid by allocation rather than by pin; pinning it is a fleet provisioning change tracked on its own.

- The frozen pre-redesign marketplace detail pages carry the Private-entity fixes. Freezing a copy forks the page permanently, and these copies were snapshotted before #1177/#1178 landed — so on a DEFAULT instance (which is exactly what renders them) the author of a Private plugin, skill or agent lost both the Archive control and the install button again, while redesigned instances kept them. Both gates are carried over, and `tests/test_ui_layout_theme.py::TestDetailPageParity` now pins the load-bearing predicates on both halves of each pair, so a fix that reaches only the redesigned template fails rather than silently reverting itself.
- **The chat runner token is signed through the canonical, fail-closed key resolver.** `mint_session_jwt` read `os.environ.get("JWT_SECRET_KEY", "<dev constant>")` directly instead of going through `app.auth.jwt`, the module that decides what a signing key may be: production without `JWT_SECRET_KEY` refuses to boot (lifespan calls `validate_jwt_secret_or_raise`), local dev signs with an auto-generated per-instance key persisted in `${DATA_DIR}/state/.jwt_secret`, and the committed dev constant is reachable only under `TESTING=1`. No deployment ever signed with that constant — the boot guard means a serving process always has the variable set, so the fallback could not win — and the one environment where the resolved key and the environment variable genuinely diverge (local dev, auto-generated key, never exported to the environment) is also the one where `get_current_user` short-circuits to the seeded dev user without verifying a token at all. So this is defense in depth, not a live hole: it removes the last occurrence of the constant outside `TESTING`-gated code, and it removes a mint/verify key mismatch that was invisible only because two unrelated guards happened to cover it. Both siblings (`mint_co_session_jwt`, `mint_agent_session_jwt`) already routed through `app.auth.jwt`; this one had never been converted. A ratchet (`tests/auth/test_jwt_secret_single_source.py`) now fails on any hardcoded `JWT_SECRET_KEY` fallback outside the resolver, so the next such read is caught in review rather than by a secret scanner.
- The frozen pre-redesign data-package page keeps its original badge order. The page a default instance now serves renders `badges` in list order, and recomputing that list appended `Curated` after `New` where the page it freezes had always appended it before — so a recently created organization package rendered "New Curated" instead of "Curated New" on a page this change set otherwise leaves byte-identical.
- The warning that logs a BigQuery-rejected query now shows the clause BigQuery
  actually refused. The preview was anchored at the head and capped at 200
  characters, but the rejection this hint was written for reports its position at
  `[1:657]` — so the `GROUP BY ROLLUP(...)` the operator needed to see sat past
  the cut, and the log line could not support the diagnosis it was added for. The
  window now centers on the offset parsed out of the BigQuery message, falling
  back to the head preview when the message carries no position. The cap is
  unchanged, so the sensitive-value bound the truncation exists for still holds —
  the window moves rather than grows. Whitespace is collapsed after windowing,
  since the offset indexes the raw SQL the engine parsed.

- `/api/query` now returns an accurate hint when BigQuery rejects a query for combining `ROLLUP` with other grouping elements in a `GROUP BY`. DuckDB accepts `GROUP BY a, ROLLUP(b)` and BigQuery does not, so a query that runs fine locally is rejected during cost estimation with a `remote_estimate_failed` 400. The hint previously fell through to the generic branch, which sent analysts hunting through columns, aliases and table paths, none of which were the cause. It now names the dialect divergence and gives the faithful `GROUPING SETS` rewrite, explicitly noting that `GROUP BY ROLLUP(a, b)` is *not* an equivalent query (it adds a grand-total row).

- **The semantic layer's category sidebar could render blank on instances with a populated semantic layer.** A bare `nav { display: flex; … }` rule in `style-custom.css`, written for the header's primary nav, applied to every `<nav>` in the app — including the metric-category list, whose buttons were built to stack vertically. Turned into a horizontal row, the buttons were centred inside a tall, unbounded sidebar column and clipped by its `overflow: hidden` parent, so the categories were present in the DOM and the API response but invisible on screen. The bare rule was dead weight — every current header nav already carries its own explicit `display` — so it is now removed, and `.sl-cat-nav` gets its own explicit `display: block` (as does `/setup/advanced`'s `.ad-toc`, a second silent dependent of the same bare rule). A new contract test guards against a future bare element selector shipping the same way — with `header`, `footer` and `code` allowlisted as acknowledged DEBT rather than as innocents: they are live rules of the same bug class (`header {}` alone reaches eight bare `<header>` elements across three admin pages, `footer {}` every design-system page), and unpicking them means auditing each call site for a visual change. So this closes the reported bug and stops the next one, but does not clear the three that predate it. Closes #1207.
- **The `/admin/server-config` editor can no longer silently overwrite the
  experience preset.** The editable-field registry declared static defaults
  for the preset-coupled knobs, so on an `instance.experience: redesign`
  instance the stack-membership switch rendered OFF and `instance.theme`
  rendered `blue` while the runtime resolved ON/`paper` — and "Save section"
  persists every rendered leaf, so a routine save would have pinned the
  classic values over the preset. The `known_fields` payload now resolves
  those defaults per request through the same preset helpers the runtime
  getters use, and the theme select offers the full valid set
  (`blue`/`navy`/`dark`/`auto`/`paper`) instead of a stale pair.
- **The Library no longer claims granted-but-unsubscribed resources are "In
  Stack" under classic membership.** The redesigned Library stamped every
  access-granted data package and memory domain as a locked member — true
  under auto-membership, false under the classic default, where membership
  (and query authorization) is required ∪ subscribed. Rows now carry the
  resolver's real membership: members render exactly as before; a
  granted-but-unsubscribed row reads "Not in Stack", filters as addable, and
  its tooltip points at the Catalog to add it. The rail Catalog's Memory
  kind-tab follows the same mode fork as the Data grid (classic: full
  granted set; auto: addable-only), so a rail instance on the classic
  default no longer mixes two contracts on one page.
- The builder's Check panel no longer keeps faulting a name or category the author has already replaced. Editing the field cleared the inline alert but not the stored check result the panel re-renders from, so a red "fail" line about the old value stayed up with nothing to say it was stale short of re-running Check. A metadata edit now drops its own row from that result — the bundle's component and lint findings beside it survive, since only the edited field's verdict went out of date.
- **The author of a Private plugin can delete it, and add it to their own stack.** Choosing Private writes `visibility_status='hidden'` and nothing ever promotes it — but `hidden` is also what guardrail quarantine writes, and two gates read it as quarantine unconditionally. `DELETE /api/store/entities/{id}` therefore refused the owner with `quarantined_owner_cannot_delete` **permanently**, so a plugin nobody else could even see could never be deleted by the person who made it; and the marketplace detail page rendered "+ Add to my stack" disabled with "unavailable while under review", a state that would never end, even though the install endpoint already had the right exemption and would have accepted the request. Both now share one predicate — `is_own_unflagged_private`: owner, `hidden`, and no submission the review has rejected — so the evidence-preservation the delete gate exists for is unchanged (a genuinely quarantined entity still refuses its submitter), while the author's own Private row behaves like what it is. The detail feed carries the verdict as a new `installable` field rather than letting the front-end re-derive the rule from `visibility_status`, which is how button and endpoint came to disagree in the first place; `installable` defaults to `true`, so curated entries and older payloads are unaffected. The unlock lands on both looks: the two legacy templates carry their own button ladder, but the redesigned page draws the shared `detail.store_menu()` macro, which held a third copy of the gate still pinned to `approved` — so on a paper-theme instance the author saw a permanently greyed-out Delete while the API would have accepted the archive. Two more surfaces follow from letting a `hidden` row be archived at all. **The archive rollback no longer publishes what it was archiving**: when the on-disk rename fails, `delete_entity` reverts the row — and that revert hardcoded `approved`, which was accurate while only an approved row could reach it and would have flipped a Private entity to organization-wide visibility off a disk error the author only ever sees as a 500. It now restores the status the row actually had. And **the quarantine banner stands down for the author's own Private row**: it fell to the "Hidden" fallback, whose copy says "nobody can install it" — false since #1178, and rendered directly above the now-enabled "+ Add to my stack". A genuinely quarantined entity keeps its banner. Closes #1177, #1178.
- **"Check bundle" now checks the metadata too, not just the ZIP.** `POST /api/store/entities/preview` never declared the `name` / `description` / `category` form fields the builder had been posting all along, so FastAPI dropped them and the pre-flight validated strictly less than the save it was a pre-flight for: a check could come back clean and the very next click 409 on a name the author already owned. Preview now reports what `POST /entities` would refuse — `missing_name`, `invalid_name_format`, `conflict_owner_name`, `conflict_global_suffix`, `invalid_category` — as a new `field_issues` list, using the same precedence as the create endpoint (a typed name wins, the manifest's is the fallback) so it judges the name the save would actually use. The builder marks the offending field and lists the reason in the check panel. The guardrail pipeline and the per-submitter quota are deliberately not previewed: the first runs against the baked tree, the second is transient and not a property of what the author typed. Closes #1176.
- **A plugin bundle's manifest description pre-fills the builder's Description.** The preview endpoint has always parsed and returned the manifest's `name` and `description` for exactly this, but the builder's bundle branch kept only `.components` from the response — so an author retyped a description the server had in hand. Applied under the same only-fill-blanks rule as the Markdown path's frontmatter import (an attached bundle never overwrites what the author typed), and the toast names the fields it filled, because a field that fills itself while you are looking elsewhere reads as a glitch. Closes #1175.
- **Dark theme: revoked and expired token cards on `/me/profile#tokens` were unreadable.** The card's background was a hardcoded near-white while its text followed the theme-aware `--text-secondary` — so in dark theme the row went light-on-light, precisely on the cards the page most wants to de-emphasize rather than hide. The background is now `--ds-surface-sunken` (recessed in both themes), and the ink on the same card — the "Revoked/Expired/Expires" line and the last-used column's soon/expired/strike states — moves to `--ds-text-muted` / `--ds-accent-*-ink` for the same reason. The **status pills** on every token row went with them: written as a literal tint + a literal ink, they were a light-theme pair only, and measured **1.87–2.97:1** against the dark card — the badge naming a token's state was the least readable thing on its row. They now use the theme-resolved `--ds-accent-*` pairs (`revoked`, having no state to accent, takes the neutral surface/secondary pair), which measure 6.4–8.5:1 in dark. Guarded two ways in `tests/test_design_system_contract.py`: a structural check that these rules carry no colour literals, and one that resolves the dark-theme tokens out of `design-tokens.css` and asserts the computed contrast clears 4.5:1 — eyeballing is what let the original pair through. Closes #1193.
- **`docs/QUICKSTART.md`'s `agnes admin register-table` example could not be copy-pasted**: it omitted the required positional table name and passed `--table`, which is not a flag (the option is `--source-table`). **`docs/PLATFORM_SETUP.md` named `instance.yaml` fields that do not exist** — `instance.url` and `auth.google.domain` / `auth.email.allowed_domains`; the real keys are `server.hostname` / `server.public_url` and the flat `auth.allowed_domain`. Closes #1192. The frozen collection page also links its file rows: `/library/<slug>/f/<id>` is a redesign-era route, so the page being frozen had nothing to point at — but routing a default instance back to that copy orphaned the per-file page and its sharing controls, reachable only by typing the URL.

- **An agent persona no longer silently strips the platform's data-access rails.** A non-empty `agents.system_prompt` makes `ChatManager._spawn_live` materialize a persona `CLAUDE.md` that *replaces* the workspace one (`WorkdirManager._materialize_profile`) — by design, but it also took the analyst data rails with it. The sandbox still had the `agnes` CLI, the Agnes MCP server, and every granted passthrough tool, yet nothing left told the agent that the organization's data lives behind `agnes catalog`; the observed behavior was an agent hunting through whatever other MCP servers its scope exposed until a human said "use Agnes". `agent_profile.build_profile` now appends a compact `DATA_ACCESS_RAILS` section (discovery chain, "never enumerate from memory", canonical metric lookup, and a pointer to `agnes skills show agnes-data-querying`) to every persona, so a persona overrides the rails' tone and task but never their existence. Affects all four sandbox-spawning surfaces — web chat, Slack DM/thread, `agnes chat <slug>`, and the one-shot agent API (`POST /api/v1/agents/{slug}/responses`), where no human is in the loop to correct it. Agents with no persona are untouched (the workspace `CLAUDE.md` stays symlinked in), as are the built-in authoring profiles in `app/chat/profiles.py`, which are Agnes-authored and already scoped to their own non-analyst task. The `/agents` builder's Identity section now says so, so persona authors know not to restate data instructions in Instructions.
- **A failed action on `/admin/users` says what went wrong, instead of showing the envelope it arrived in.** Five handlers interpolated the raw response body into the toast, so creating a user with an address that already exists read `Failed: {"detail":"User with this email already exists"}` — the sentence was right there and nothing unwrapped it. All five now share one `errorText(r)` helper that reads FastAPI's `detail`, prefers the human half of the `{code, hint}` shape other routers answer with, and falls back to the status code when the body is not JSON at all (a proxy's HTML error page, which the raw-body version would have pasted into the toast wholesale). Closes #1172.
- **The login card is centred on rail-layout instances.** `rail.css` reserved 240px of body padding whenever `data-ui-layout="rail"` was stamped on `<html>` — but the rail nav itself renders only for a signed-in user, so on pre-auth pages the reservation survived with nothing to reserve for, and `/login/password` centred its card inside a box shifted a rail's width to the right. The clearance is now tied to the rail actually being present (`body:has(.rail)`), with the ≤1024px override kept at matching specificity so the top-bar layout still drops the padding. Closes #1170.
- The remaining read surfaces now see a partition-synced table's data, the way
  the preview already did in 0.83.0. That sync stores a table as a DIRECTORY of
  per-period parquets, so the single-file lookup found nothing and a healthy,
  fully-synced table looked empty everywhere else too: `GET /api/v2/schema/<id>`
  404-ed, `POST /api/v2/scan` 404-ed, and the catalog's `rough_size_hint` came
  back `null`. Schema and scan now resolve either layout and read every
  partition; the catalog reports the SUM of the partition sizes — the same
  rollup the extractor writes to `_meta.size_bytes` and the sync state to
